episodes.title: The Story of Luxembourg
episodes.blurb: Two hosts, Anna and Ben, tell the story of Luxembourg, from a Roman-era fortress and a medieval dynasty to a modern financial centre.
episodes.notes:
This is a conversation between two hosts, Anna and Ben, running roughly an hour and a quarter in eight chapters. Each chapter stands alone, so you can start anywhere. Everything from the Welcome section onward is written to be heard, with no tables or footnotes.

The conversation is voiced by a more expressive model than before, so the hosts react, laugh and sigh now and then. Text-to-speech voices sometimes stumble on Luxembourgish and French names such as Alzette, Vauban, Ermesinde and Echternach. You can add respellings in tools/pronunciations.json (for example Alzette = Al-zet) and the next audio run will use them.

On accuracy: the 1839 partition, the 1942 conscription figures, the 2025 abdication and the current government were checked against sources listed at the end. Older dates and details come from standard histories. They are reliable, but check anything you plan to repeat in print.

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.label: Welcome
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Luxembourg. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben.
Anna: I have to be honest with you, and with everyone listening. All I know about Luxembourg is that it's small and rich.
Ben: That's more than most people know.
Anna: How small, exactly?
Ben: You could drive across it in about an hour. Its whole population is smaller than that of many a single city.
Anna: So it's basically a very well-organized suburb. [chuckle]

Ben: Tell that to the emperors. For more than a thousand years, kings and emperors fought over this place. It's been a fortress, a province, a battlefield, a steel empire, a banking center, and a founding member of the European Union.
Anna: All of that, in a country you can cross before lunch.
Ben: And it's the last grand duchy in the world.
Anna: Wait. Were there a lot of grand duchies?
Ben: Quite a few, once. Now there's one.
Anna: Okay, I need to know how a place that small ended up that interesting.
Ben: Rock, iron, borders, and a great deal of stubbornness.
Anna: Right. New rule. I'm keeping an owner count. Every time somebody new takes over Luxembourg, it goes on the board.
Ben: You're going to need a big board.
Anna: Starting at zero.
Ben: Not for long. And their national motto, by the way, translates as "we want to remain what we are."
Anna: Which is a bold thing to say about a country that's changed hands more often than a second-hand bicycle.
Ben: Ha. Yes. Hold that thought.
Anna: So where do we start?
Ben: With a swap of land beside a river. But first, a few thousand years we shouldn't skip.

chapters.title: Before Luxembourg
chapters.label: Chapter 1: Before Luxembourg
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, quick quiz. When was Luxembourg born?

Ben: Depends who you ask. Some say 1815, when the Grand Duchy was created at the Congress of Vienna. Others say 1839, when its modern borders were drawn in London. Others point to 1867, when the great powers guaranteed its independence.
Anna: But you have your own answer.
Ben: I do. The story really starts in the year nine sixty-three, with a land swap.
Anna: A land swap. That's the founding moment. Not a battle, not a coronation.
Ben: Not a sword in sight.
Anna: Disappointing. I'd have bet on a sword.
Ben: You'd have lost. But before the land swap, there's a man we have to meet.
Anna: Who?

Ben: He has no name. Archaeologists call him Loschbour man, after the rock shelter near the village of Heffingen where his skeleton was found in 1935. He lived about eight thousand years ago, when this land was dense forest and people survived by hunting, fishing, and gathering.
Anna: And he made headlines.
Ben: Decades after his discovery, scientists sequenced his DNA. The result suggested that this early European had dark skin and blue eyes.
Anna: Huh. That's not the picture most of us have in our heads.
Ben: It overturned a lot of assumptions about what the first Europeans looked like.
Anna: Who came next?

Ben: Farmers, from the southeast. They cleared fields along the river valleys. Then the age of metal, first bronze and later iron. By the last centuries before Christ, the land of Luxembourg belonged to a Celtic people called the Treveri.
Anna: Who left something behind.

Ben: A fortified hilltop town called the Titelberg, in the far southwest of today's country, near the French border. High plateau, ramparts all around, a center for metalworking and trade, and one of the best cavalry traditions in Gaul.
Anna: Cavalry. Of course it was cavalry.
Ben: And then Rome arrives.
Anna: Naturally.

Ben: The first written mention of this land comes from Julius Caesar himself, in his account of the Gallic Wars. In the middle of the first century before Christ, he fought the Treveri. After years of rebellion and repression, the region was swallowed into the Roman Empire.
Anna: So what did the Romans build?
Ben: A city nearby, on the Moselle, just across what's now the German border. Augusta Treverorum. Today it's called Trier.
Anna: Trier. I've heard of Trier.
Ben: Within a few generations it was one of the great cities of the western empire. At one point it was home to emperors, and its Roman gates and baths still stand.
Anna: So where does Luxembourg fit in?

Ben: It's Trier's backyard. Farmland and forest, crossed by Roman roads, and dotted with country estates. One road ran from Reims, in what's now France, to Trier. Along it, near today's village of Dalheim, a small Roman town grew up, complete with a theater.
Anna: A theater, in the backyard of the backyard.
Ben: And villas. At Echternach and at Diekirch, wealthy landowners built grand ones. A Roman mosaic from one of the Diekirch houses survives, laid out in colored stone.
Anna: Sounds comfortable.
Ben: Settled, Latin-speaking, and for a few centuries, secure.
Anna: But it didn't last.

Ben: No. In the third and fourth centuries, raiders pushed across the Rhine, and Roman power along the frontier began to wear away. By the end of the fifth century the region belonged to the Franks, a Germanic people whose king, Clovis, was building a new kingdom out of the ruins of Roman Gaul.
Anna: Which brings a new religion.
Ben: Through some remarkable missionaries. The one that matters for us is a monk named Willibrord. Born in Northumbria, in England, trained in Ireland.
Anna: Well traveled.

Ben: He crossed the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians, and in the year six ninety-eight he founded a monastery at Echternach, on land given to him by a noblewoman from the Trier area. He died in seven thirty-nine, and he was buried there.
Anna: And Echternach became a big deal.
Ben: One of the great intellectual centers of medieval Europe. Its monks copied and illuminated manuscripts so beautiful that they're treasured in museums in Germany today.
Anna: And there's a dance. I've heard there's a dance.
Ben: Every year, on the Tuesday after Pentecost, thousands of people dance through the streets of Echternach in honor of Saint Willibrord. They hop in time to a simple, polka-like tune.
Anna: Hop. Thousands of people. In the street.
Ben: UNESCO recognizes it as part of humanity's living cultural heritage.
Anna: Okay, that's going on my list.
Ben: Now, Charlemagne.
Anna: Finally. A name I know.

Ben: In the late eighth and early ninth centuries, the Frankish kings became emperors, and this region sat comfortably inside their realm. But when Charlemagne's empire was split among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun in eight forty-three, the land that would become Luxembourg fell into the middle kingdom, named after the grandson Lothar.
Anna: Which didn't last either, did it?

Ben: It broke up over the following decades. The region became a borderland, a long-contested strip between the western Frankish kingdom, which would become France, and the eastern Frankish kingdom, which would become Germany.
Anna: So it was born in the middle of an argument.

Ben: It was. And in the year nine sixty-two, in Rome, a German king named Otto was crowned emperor. His realm would later be called the Holy Roman Empire, a loose, shifting collection of kingdoms, duchies, counties and church lands that would last more than eight hundred years.
Anna: And one year later?
Ben: A count named Siegfried made a small land deal that no one at the time could have thought important.
Anna: Okay, who was Siegfried?

Ben: He belonged to a noble family from the Moselle and Ardennes region, and according to tradition he had Carolingian blood. What he wanted was a stronghold. On the edge of his lands there was a rocky promontory above the river Alzette, with the ruins of an old fortification.
Anna: Which belonged to someone else.
Ben: To the abbey of Saint Maximin, in Trier. Siegfried offered other lands in exchange, and the monks said yes.
Anna: So the founding of Luxembourg is a property swap with monks.
Ben: And the charter survives. It's dated nine sixty-three, and it names the place: Lucilinburhuc. That means, roughly, little castle.
Anna: Little castle. Cute.
Ben: In time, the name softened and shortened into Luxembourg.
Anna: And the rock itself?

Ben: It's known as the Bock. Siegfried built a real fortress on it, and his family spread out from there across the surrounding land. The spot was so well chosen that armies would fight over it for the next nine hundred years.
Anna: And I have a feeling there's a legend.
Ben: Of course there is. It says Siegfried married a mermaid named Melusina, who agreed to live with him on one condition. He must never look at her on a certain day.
Anna: And he looked.
Ben: He looked. She vanished beneath the waters of the Alzette, and left him alone.
Anna: Classic.
Ben: And locals say she can still be seen, once every seven years, spinning at the bottom of the river.
Anna: Okay, I'm choosing to believe that. [chuckle]

Ben: The real story is even better. Because from this little rocky outcrop, Siegfried's descendants would rise to the heights of European power. They'd sit on the throne of Bohemia, and wear the imperial crown.
Anna: From a swap with some monks to an emperor's crown. I want to hear about that.
Ben: Next chapter. We meet the House of Luxembourg.
Anna: And I'm betting they're a lot of trouble.
Ben: Quite a family.

chapters.title: The House of Luxembourg, 963 to 1443
chapters.label: Chapter 2: The House of Luxembourg, 963 to 1443
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Siegfried has his little castle. Then what?
Ben: Then, for about two centuries, not much. A rocky fortress, a handful of villages, and a dynasty that married well and waited.
Anna: The long game.
Ben: The very long game. The counts slowly gathered land, and in 1136 an inheritance gave the county to Henry the Blind, count of Namur, who joined the two territories together.
Anna: Henry the Blind. Good name.
Ben: You'll meet another one in a minute. But the one to remember here is Henry's daughter. Ermesinde.
Anna: Ermesinde. I like her already.

Ben: She inherited the county in 1196, and ruled for more than fifty years, through two marriages and a great deal of politics. She's remembered for granting charters of freedom to the towns of her county.
Anna: Including the capital.

Ben: In 1244 she gave one to the city of Luxembourg. It freed its townspeople from many of the old obligations of serfdom, and let them organize themselves as a community, with a council of their own.
Anna: In 1244. That's early.
Ben: In a Europe where most people lived under their lord's thumb, it was a bold step. To this day, Luxembourg treats Ermesinde as one of its founding figures.
Anna: Good. A woman who ruled for fifty years gets her due.
Ben: Now. The little county is about to leap onto the continental stage.
Anna: How?

Ben: By accident, and by tragedy. In 1288, the count of Luxembourg was killed at the Battle of Worringen, in a war over who would inherit the neighboring duchy of Limburg. His heir was a boy of about thirteen, also named Henry. We know him as Henry the Seventh.
Anna: Thirteen. Yikes.
Ben: He grew up chivalrous, pious, and quietly ambitious. And in 1308, the German king was murdered. The electors of the empire looked around for someone who was capable, but not too powerful.
Anna: Not too powerful. Everyone's favorite job requirement.
Ben: And they chose the count of Luxembourg.
Anna: Wait. The little county on the western edge?

Ben: Suddenly, king of the Germans. And Henry did not waste it. He arranged for his teenage son John to marry Elisabeth, the heiress of the kingdom of Bohemia, which is roughly today's Czech Republic. John became King of Bohemia in 1310.
Anna: So in one marriage, a small county in the Ardennes gets one of the richest crowns in central Europe.
Ben: Exactly that.
Anna: And Henry?

Ben: He marched over the Alps into Italy, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312. He dreamed of restoring imperial glory. The poet Dante, who lived through those years and pinned his hopes on Henry, wrote that a seat was waiting for him in Paradise.
Anna: Oh. That's some endorsement.
Ben: But Henry died of a fever in 1313, near Siena, and the dream died with him.
Anna: Oh, no. And his son? The new King of Bohemia?
Ben: John the Blind.
Anna: Henry the Blind, John the Blind. Did they run out of nicknames? [chuckle]

Ben: Different men, a long time apart. Just a coincidence of the name. John was one of the great adventurers of the Middle Ages. Born in Luxembourg, raised partly at the French court. As King of Bohemia, he was almost never home.
Anna: Where was he?

Ben: Italy. Poland. Lithuania, fighting alongside the crusading Teutonic Knights. He loved tournaments, and he loved France. His daughter Bonne married the man who became King John the Second of France, and she became the grandmother of a future French king.
Anna: Busy man. When did he go blind?

Ben: By around 1340 he had lost his sight completely. It didn't slow him down. In 1340 he founded a fair in Luxembourg City that still exists. The Schueberfouer. It takes place every year in late August and early September, with rides, food stalls and traditional parades, and it's the biggest funfair in the country.
Anna: Wait. A blind king founded a funfair that's still running almost seven hundred years later?
Ben: Yes.
Anna: Okay. That's a legacy.
Ben: Now the war that defined his end. In 1346, England and France were fighting what we now call the Hundred Years' War. John, loyal to the French, rode to the battlefield of Crécy.
Anna: Blind.

Ben: Blind. According to the old account, he asked his knights to lead him into the fight. They tied their horses together by the reins, so he wouldn't be separated from them, and they charged straight into the English archers.
Anna: And then?
Ben: The next morning, John and his companions were found dead on the field.
Anna: That's a hard story.

Ben: It is. And there's a tradition that the English prince we call the Black Prince, who was just sixteen, took the three ostrich feathers from John's helmet and made them his own emblem. Historians argue about whether that's true. But in Luxembourg, John is remembered as the great national hero. His body rests in the crypt of Notre-Dame cathedral in the capital.
Anna: A symbol of bravery.
Ben: Of bravery, loyalty, and a certain doomed gallantry.
Anna: All right. Now the greatest of the Luxembourgers.

Ben: John's eldest son. Born in Prague, baptized Wenceslas, and he took the name Charles at the French court, in honor of his godfather and uncle. As Charles the Fourth, he became King of Bohemia after his father's death, and in 1355 he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome.
Anna: And what kind of emperor?

Ben: A different kind. A scholar, a builder, a patient politician. In 1356 he issued a famous decree called the Golden Bull, which fixed how emperors would be elected, by seven electors. That system more or less lasted until the empire itself ended.
Anna: Wow. Centuries of rules from one decree.
Ben: And in 1348 he founded Charles University in Prague, the first university in central Europe.
Anna: And there's a bridge, isn't there? Everyone has a Charles Bridge photo.

Ben: He started building the stone bridge across the Vltava that still bears his name. He turned Prague into one of the great cities of Europe. And he didn't forget the little county where his family began. In 1354, he raised Luxembourg to the rank of duchy, and installed his half-brother Wenceslas as its first duke.
Anna: So by the late fourteenth century, this is a mighty dynasty.

Ben: Its sons ruled Bohemia, and for a time Hungary, and sat on the imperial throne. In all, four Luxembourgers held the title of ruler of the Holy Roman Empire. Henry the Seventh, Charles the Fourth, Charles's son Wenceslas the Fourth, and Charles's other son Sigismund.
Anna: Four.
Ben: Though only three of them were actually crowned emperor in Rome. Henry, Charles, and Sigismund.
Anna: So Wenceslas never made it to the Rome ceremony.

Ben: Right. He was never crowned there. Which brings us to Sigismund, the last. A shrewd, restless man. King of Hungary from 1387, and King of the Romans from 1411. He called the great Council of Constance, which met from 1414 to 1418 and ended a split in the Catholic Church.
Anna: That's a big achievement.
Ben: It also burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus, which triggered the Hussite wars in Bohemia.
Anna: Right. So, mixed.
Ben: Very mixed. Sigismund was crowned emperor in 1433 and died in 1437, with no surviving son. And with that, the male line of the House of Luxembourg came to an end.
Anna: Okay, so what happened to the little duchy? Back home, in the Ardennes?
Ben: Its glamorous rulers were scattered across central Europe. They spent most of their time in Prague, Buda, or Rome, and they rarely visited the place that made them.
Anna: So they were absentee landlords.
Ben: To them, Luxembourg was a source of money, and they treated it that way. They mortgaged it. They pledged it as security for loans, and passed it around among cousins and creditors.
Anna: Does the owner count include creditors? Because that's a lot of paperwork.
Ben: Let's say no. We'll count real owners only.
Anna: Fair. So who ended up with it?

Ben: One of the holders was a woman named Elisabeth of Görlitz, a niece of Sigismund. She was widowed, remarried, and constantly short of money. In the end, she sold her rights to the most powerful figure in the region. Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
Anna: Ah. And that's the first real change of owner.
Ben: In 1443, his forces took possession of the city, reportedly by a surprise assault with the help of local nobles who were fed up with the unstable rule of the pledge-holders.
Anna: Owner count. One.
Ben: And just like that, the old era ended. The county that had given Europe emperors and kings was now one more piece in the growing Burgundian collection of lands.
Anna: Okay. Before we move on, there's something I want to ask about. The castles.

Ben: Ah. In the countryside of Luxembourg, medieval lords built castles that still stand. The most spectacular is Vianden, on a hill above a river in the north, one of the largest feudal residences in this part of Europe.
Anna: A castle on a hill. Obviously.
Ben: In the early fifteenth century, Vianden passed by inheritance to the family of Nassau.
Anna: Nassau. Why do I know that name?
Ben: It would later become the Dutch royal house.
Anna: Keep that name in mind.
Ben: Four hundred years later, it'll be central to our story.
Anna: And next, a fortress.
Ben: Next, a very big rock.

chapters.title: The Gibraltar of the North, 1443 to 1815
chapters.label: Chapter 3: The Gibraltar of the North, 1443 to 1815
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. If the first part of the story was about a dynasty, this part is about a rock.

Ben: A very big rock. For the next three and a half centuries, Luxembourg's main job in European politics was to be a fortress. And it was a good one. A great deal of the time, the Luxembourgers themselves weren't the ones deciding who owned it.
Anna: So this is where my owner count gets serious.
Ben: It does. And I should warn you, it moves fast.
Anna: We left off with Philip the Good of Burgundy in 1443. Count of one.

Ben: And for a while, Luxembourg was one piece in a glittering Burgundian empire that included Flanders, Brabant, and Holland. Burgundy was the richest, most fashionable court in Europe. But it didn't last. In 1477, Philip's grandson Charles the Bold was killed in battle outside the city of Nancy, and he left a single daughter. Mary.
Anna: Who married Maximilian of Habsburg.
Ben: She did. And through that marriage, the Burgundian lands, Luxembourg included, passed to the Habsburg family.
Anna: Two. I'm counting handovers, by the way. Not different owners. Handovers.

Ben: I'll allow it. And this was the beginning of an era in which Luxembourg belonged to the most powerful dynasty in the world. Maximilian and Mary's grandson was born in Ghent in the year 1500, and he grew up to be Charles the Fifth. He ruled Spain, much of Italy, the Netherlands, Germany, and the new Spanish lands in the Americas.
Anna: And Luxembourg was a tiny corner of all that.
Ben: A tiny corner. But it sat right on the road between his Netherlands and his Italian and Spanish possessions, so it mattered.
Anna: So what happened when Charles retired?
Ben: His empire was divided. His son Philip the Second took Spain and the Netherlands, and Luxembourg went with them.
Anna: Same family, different branch.
Ben: Right.
Anna: Counts as three.
Ben: Of course it does.
Anna: Hey, the rules are mine.

Ben: That put Luxembourg in the front row for one of the great conflicts of the age. The northern provinces of the Netherlands rose in revolt, turned Protestant, and eventually broke away to become the Dutch Republic.
Anna: But not the south.
Ben: The southern provinces, including Luxembourg, stayed under Spain, and stayed Catholic. Luxembourg's people had barely been touched by the Reformation, and they remained loyal.
Anna: Okay. Then the seventeenth century.

Ben: It was brutal. During the Thirty Years' War, armies marched back and forth across the Luxembourg countryside, looting and burning. Famine and plague followed the soldiers. In some parts of the country, the population fell by something like half.
Anna: Half.
Ben: Meanwhile Spain was declining, and France, under the Sun King, Louis the Fourteenth, was rising.
Anna: And France began nibbling.

Ben: In 1659, the peace treaty between Spain and France handed over a belt of towns along Luxembourg's southern border, including Thionville. It was the first of several times that Luxembourg would shrink.
Anna: Then Louis came for the fortress itself.
Ben: In 1684. French forces besieged the city for about a month and took it.
Anna: Four.
Ben: And here, the history of the place changes. Louis brought in the great military engineer Marquis de Vauban, the greatest builder of fortresses of his age, to rebuild the defenses.
Anna: Okay. What did Vauban do?

Ben: He dug ditches, raised massive walls, and tunneled deep into the rock. Within a few years, the capital of Luxembourg was one of the most formidable fortresses in Europe, with a nickname that would stick. The Gibraltar of the North.
Anna: Good nickname. So France kept it.
Ben: No. In 1697, after a long war, Louis gave Luxembourg back to Spain in the Treaty of Ryswick.
Anna: Wait. He builds up the whole fortress and then gives it back?
Ben: He did.
Anna: Five. That's a very expensive favor. [chuckle]
Ben: France held it again briefly in the early eighteenth century.
Anna: Six. Seriously, Ben?

Ben: I told you it moves fast. And when the great war over the Spanish throne was settled in 1713 and 1714, Luxembourg was handed to the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs, together with what is now Belgium. Those lands became the Austrian Netherlands.
Anna: Seven. Okay. How was the Austrian period?

Ben: About eight decades, and it's sometimes remembered as a relatively calm and prosperous time. Historians still debate whether it was really a golden age, but the evidence of peace is clear enough. The population recovered. Ironworks along the rivers produced cast iron, and farming improved.
Anna: And the fortress?

Ben: The Austrians kept strengthening it. In the seventeen-thirties they built a new fort on the plateau across the valley, called Fort Thüngen. Its restored towers, nicknamed the Three Acorns, still stand today, and they house a museum.
Anna: The Three Acorns. I'm sorry, that's adorable. [laugh]

Ben: And the real wonder is hidden. Over the generations, engineers dug a vast network of tunnels called casemates into the sandstone cliff of the Bock. They provided shelter for soldiers, space for cannon, and storage for supplies.
Anna: How much tunnel are we talking about?

Ben: At the height of the fortress, many miles. Today roughly seventeen kilometers survive, about ten and a half miles, and visitors can walk through them and look out over the valley through the gun slits.
Anna: Okay. That's going on the list too.
Ben: You have a long list.
Anna: It's getting very long. But Ben, I have a question. If it changed hands that often, how did anyone who lived there cope?

Ben: Not well. Its history reads like a revolving door. If you were an ambitious king, Luxembourg was a prize. If you lived in Luxembourg, it was a burden. The city was stuffed with soldiers, the townspeople paid for the upkeep of the walls, and every time a war broke out between France and its neighbors, armies tramped across your fields.
Anna: And the quiet ended in the seventeen-eighties.

Ben: Emperor Joseph the Second, who ruled from Vienna, was a reformer of the enlightened kind. He tried to modernize his lands all at once, closing monasteries, limiting the church's power, and reorganizing the courts.
Anna: All at once. That never goes well.

Ben: Many of his subjects in the Austrian Netherlands, including Luxembourg, were conservative and devout, and they were furious. In 1789, the same year the French Revolution began, a revolt broke out in the Netherlands. It was suppressed within a couple of years.
Anna: But the French Revolution wasn't so easily suppressed.

Ben: In 1794, French revolutionary armies swept through the Austrian Netherlands. The Luxembourg fortress held out. For about seven months, from the autumn of 1794, French troops surrounded it, while the Austrian defenders waited for relief that never came.
Anna: And it fell.
Ben: In June of 1795, starving and cut off, the garrison surrendered. The Gibraltar of the North had fallen, not to a great assault, but to hunger.
Anna: Eight.

Ben: And that was the end of the old duchy. In the autumn of 1795, France formally annexed the territory. In its place the French created a new administrative unit called the Department of the Forests, named for the heavily wooded Ardennes hills. It was ruled from the city of Luxembourg.
Anna: And the French years brought changes.

Ben: Profound ones. The old feudal rights were abolished. The church lost much of its land. A new system of laws, the Napoleonic Code, was introduced, and traces of it survive in Luxembourg's legal system to this day.
Anna: But there was a price.

Ben: A heavy one. The French demanded soldiers. Young men from Luxembourg were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came home. In 1798, the conscription law sparked a revolt in the countryside of the north. Peasants, armed with clubs, farm tools, and old hunting guns, rose up against the French.
Anna: The Peasants' War.

Ben: Or, more literally, the War of the Clubs. It was crushed within weeks, and the leaders were punished harshly. But the memory of it has never faded. For generations it was a reminder of how deeply the ordinary people of Luxembourg resented foreign rule.
Anna: And then, 1814.

Ben: After Napoleon's disastrous retreat from Russia and his defeat at Leipzig, the French withdrew. For the first time in centuries, the future of Luxembourg was up for negotiation among the great powers of Europe.
Anna: Okay, I'm nervous about what the count's going to be. What do they decide?
Ben: Something no one had ever seen before.
Anna: Go on.
Ben: A grand duchy.

chapters.title: A Grand Duchy Is Born, 1815 to 1867
chapters.label: Chapter 4: A Grand Duchy Is Born, 1815 to 1867
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Picture the scene. Vienna, the winter of 1814 and 1815.

Ben: Napoleon has been defeated and exiled. The diplomats of Europe, kings, princes, and ministers in glittering uniforms, gather for the Congress of Vienna to redraw the map. Their main goal is simple. Make sure France can never again conquer its neighbors.
Anna: And one way to do that is to put something strong on France's northern border.
Ben: Exactly. So they combine the Netherlands and Belgium into a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, ruled by William of Orange-Nassau, who became King William the First.
Anna: And Luxembourg?
Ben: William's family had lost its ancestral German lands, so the great powers looked for ways to compensate him. One of them was Luxembourg.
Anna: Nine. Owner count, nine.

Ben: And they made it a state in its own right. They raised it to the rank of grand duchy, a way of saying it was more than an ordinary duchy. A proper sovereign state, with a seat in the new German Confederation.
Anna: Okay, so what's a grand duchy, practically? Is it like a duchy, but with better snacks?

Ben: Ha. No. It's a duchy with a promotion. And William would be both King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg. A so-called personal union, in which the same man wore two crowns over two countries that were otherwise separate.
Anna: Two hats, one head.
Ben: Two hats, one head. And that's 1815. The Grand Duchy of Luxembourg came into being, and it remains the only grand duchy in the world.
Anna: But it was smaller than the old duchy.

Ben: Much smaller. Prussia, the rising power on the Rhine, demanded land, and Luxembourg lost its entire eastern border region, the territory east of the rivers Moselle, Sûre, and Our. About a quarter of its area.
Anna: And that's the second time it had been carved up?
Ben: In the modern era, yes. And the fortress became a fortress of the German Confederation, and a Prussian garrison moved in. The Grand Duke ruled the country. The Prussians held the rock.
Anna: So who actually owned it?
Ben: Depends who you asked, and on which day.
Anna: I'll count the Prussians as tenants.
Ben: Wise.
Anna: Then, 1830. The great shock.

Ben: In Brussels, riots broke out after an opera performance. Within weeks, the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands had risen up in revolution. They were Catholic and mostly French-speaking, and they resented rule by a Protestant, Dutch-speaking king. They declared independence as the new Kingdom of Belgium.
Anna: A revolution after an opera. That's very Belgian.

Ben: And Luxembourg joined in. Most Luxembourgers took part in the uprising, sent representatives to the Belgian national congress, and for several years almost the whole country was governed from Brussels. The only exception was the capital, where the Prussian garrison held the fortress firmly in the name of the German Confederation.
Anna: So it was unresolved.

Ben: For nearly a decade. Belgium claimed all of it. The Dutch king claimed all of it. The great powers met in London and eventually proposed a compromise. And in 1839, after King William finally accepted defeat, a treaty was signed in London that carved the country in two.
Anna: Who got what?

Ben: The western part of Luxembourg, the French-speaking part, went to Belgium. It included the towns of Arlon and Bastogne, a name we'll meet again in the Second World War. That was roughly sixty-five percent of the country's territory and about half its population, something like one hundred and seventy-five thousand people.
Anna: Sixty-five percent. That's not a trim. That's a haircut with a lawnmower. [laugh]
Ben: Ha. What remained was the eastern, German-speaking part, essentially the Luxembourg of today.
Anna: How was it decided?
Ben: The line was drawn in London, using maps that were out of date and inaccurate, by diplomats who had never visited the places they were dividing.
Anna: Never visited. Wow.

Ben: To compensate the German Confederation for the loss, part of the Dutch province of Limburg was attached to it. And the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, which had been a middling European territory, became a small, landlocked, mostly poor country, with about one hundred and seventy thousand inhabitants.
Anna: That's rough.

Ben: But there's a twist. The treaty of 1839 is often described as the moment Luxembourg's independence began, because it fixed the borders. For the first time there was a clear, internationally recognized line around a state called Luxembourg, the same line you can cross on a bridge or a country road today. It was a tragic loss, but it was also a beginning.
Anna: So how were the decades that followed?

Ben: Hard. Luxembourg was a farming country with little industry, and in the eighteen-forties, a potato blight and poor harvests pushed many families into hunger. In 1842, the Grand Duchy joined the German customs union, the Zollverein, which tied its economy to the German states and opened up markets for its goods. But it also meant that Luxembourg's economic fate was linked to its neighbor across the Moselle.
Anna: And people left.

Ben: Between about 1840 and 1890, tens of thousands of Luxembourgers emigrated. Many went to the United States and settled in the Midwest, especially in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, and the area around Chicago. For a country of fewer than two hundred thousand people, it was an enormous drain.
Anna: Meanwhile, the country was learning to govern itself.

Ben: In 1841, William the Second, the king who followed William the First, granted Luxembourg its first constitution, creating an assembly of the estates. In 1848, the year revolutions shook Europe, a more liberal constitution followed.
Anna: And the Dutch kings were fully engaged?
Ben: Not very. William the Third, who ruled from 1849, rarely visited. Day to day, the country was run by his brother Prince Henry as his representative.
Anna: Another absentee landlord.

Ben: Some things don't change. And then, a national consciousness woke up. Writers and poets began composing in Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect that ordinary people spoke at home and that had no official status.
Anna: What did they write?

Ben: In 1859, the poet Michel Lentz wrote a song Luxembourgers still sing, called the Feierwon, the Fire Wagon, about the arrival of the railway. Its refrain became the national motto. We want to remain what we are.
Anna: After nine changes of owner, that is a bold line.

Ben: It is. In the same decade, Lentz wrote the words of the song that would become the national anthem, Ons Heemecht, which means Our Homeland. It was officially adopted in 1895. And in 1872, Michel Rodange published Renert, a long satirical poem in Luxembourgish about a crafty fox, which many people consider the country's national epic.
Anna: A national epic about a fox. I respect that.
Ben: Now we come to the crisis that nearly started a war.
Anna: Oh no.

Ben: In 1866, Prussia defeated Austria in a short, decisive war, and the German Confederation, which had existed since 1815, was dissolved. Suddenly no one was sure what Luxembourg's status was. Was it part of Germany? Was it independent? And who owned the fortress, with its Prussian garrison?
Anna: And Napoleon the Third saw an opportunity.

Ben: Prussia had just become dramatically more powerful, and he wanted something in return to keep the balance, and to restore French prestige. He offered to buy Luxembourg from King William the Third of the Netherlands, who was short of money and had little emotional attachment to the place.
Anna: Wait. He tried to buy a country.
Ben: He did.
Anna: What was the price?
Ben: William agreed to the idea in principle.
Anna: So it was basically a garage sale for a fortress.
Ben: Ha. Just about. But then, Bismarck.
Anna: The Prussian chancellor.

Ben: Otto von Bismarck was not going to let France take a strategic fortress on the German frontier. He made sure that news of the sale leaked, and German public opinion exploded. Luxembourg is German soil, politicians and newspapers cried. And for a few weeks in the spring of 1867, Europe stood at the edge of war.
Anna: Over Luxembourg.
Ben: Over Luxembourg.
Anna: How did it end?

Ben: Diplomacy won. The great powers met in London in May of 1867, and agreed on a settlement that satisfied everyone and no one. The second Treaty of London, signed on the eleventh of May, declared that Luxembourg was an independent state, under the sovereignty of the House of Orange-Nassau, and that it would be perpetually neutral, under the collective guarantee of the great powers.
Anna: Perpetually neutral. I bet that works out well.
Ben: We'll get there.
Anna: And the fortress?
Ben: The Prussian garrison would leave. And the fortress, the Gibraltar of the North, would be dismantled, so that no one could use it as a weapon against their neighbors.
Anna: So Napoleon the Third didn't get it.
Ben: He didn't. So, for the owner count, an almost.
Anna: An almost doesn't count.
Ben: Right. Still nine.

chapters.title: Neutrality, Iron and a New Dynasty, 1867 to 1914
chapters.label: Chapter 5: Neutrality, Iron and a New Dynasty, 1867 to 1914
paragraphs: Anna: The treaty of 1867 promised that the fortress would be taken apart.
Ben: And it kept its word. Over the next sixteen years, work crews tore down walls, filled in ditches, and blew up forts and bastions. It was one of the biggest demolition projects in Europe.
Anna: Sixteen years of knocking things down.
Ben: And when it was done, a city that had been a cramped military stronghold for centuries was suddenly free to grow.
Anna: What did it do with the space?

Ben: Parks, boulevards, and building plots. New districts spread across the plateau, and the deep valleys that had been obstacles became green spaces. In 1903, the city opened the Adolphe Bridge, which sweeps across the Pétrusse valley in two graceful stone arches. At the time, it was one of the largest stone arch bridges in the world.
Anna: And not everything was destroyed.

Ben: Parts of the casemates survived, and so did the old town on its cliffs. In 1994, UNESCO recognized the old quarters and the surviving fortifications as a World Heritage site. The Gibraltar of the North had become, in the end, a beautiful ruin.
Anna: Okay. But the neutrality. That was a gamble, wasn't it?
Ben: A real one. The great powers had guaranteed it together, which in practice meant that if anyone broke it, no single power was obliged to punish them.
Anna: So it's a promise from everyone, which is a promise from nobody.
Ben: Pretty much. And the country had almost no army, only a small corps of volunteers and gendarmes. Luxembourg's safety depended on the goodwill of its neighbors.
Anna: Not a great strategy.
Ben: Not a great strategy. But while the diplomats worried, something was happening underground.
Anna: Ooh. What?

Ben: In the south of Luxembourg, running down into the French region of Lorraine, there is a belt of iron ore called minette, a reddish-brown stone. Local blacksmiths had known about it for centuries, but it was nearly useless, because it contained a lot of phosphorus, which made the iron brittle.
Anna: Until...

Ben: Until 1878. That year, an Englishman named Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and his cousin Percy Gilchrist developed a way to remove the phosphorus. Suddenly the poor ore of Luxembourg and Lorraine could be made into excellent steel.
Anna: So the worst rock in the country became the best one.

Ben: An industrial revolution in miniature. Blast furnaces went up along the Alzette and across the southwest corner of the country. Villages like Esch, Differdange, Dudelange and Rumelange swelled into industrial towns. The night sky over the south turned orange, and red dust settled on everything.
Anna: Red dust on everything. Lovely.
Ben: Within a generation, the country that had been exporting farmers to America was importing workers.
Anna: From where?

Ben: First from Germany, then from Italy. Italian laborers began arriving in large numbers in the eighteen-nineties and settled in the steel towns. They were the first of many waves. Luxembourg had a long tradition of sending its sons and daughters abroad. Now, for the first time, it began to receive people.
Anna: And the companies consolidated.
Ben: In 1911, the main steel producers merged into a single giant called ARBED, a name built from the French words for the united steelworks of Burbach, Eich and Dudelange.
Anna: Say that three times fast.
Ben: For most of the twentieth century, ARBED was practically a state within the state. Per head of population, few places in the world made more steel.
Anna: And who ran the country during all this?

Ben: A careful lawyer named Paul Eyschen, head of the government from 1888 until 1915. An extraordinary twenty-seven years. He guided Luxembourg through industrialization and the pressures of its neighbors.
Anna: Twenty-seven years. Imagine the paperwork.
Ben: Now, for the strangest episode. The change of dynasty.
Anna: Oh, I've been waiting for this.

Ben: In 1890, King William the Third of the Netherlands died. He had been King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg for forty-one years. But he had no surviving sons, only a ten-year-old daughter, Wilhelmina.
Anna: Who became Queen of the Netherlands.
Ben: But in Luxembourg, an old family law, the Nassau family pact, said only men could inherit. So the Grand Duchy and the Netherlands, united for seventy-five years, separated.
Anna: So who got Luxembourg?
Ben: A cousin. A distant one, named Adolphe, the former Duke of Nassau. His own duchy in Germany had been swallowed by Prussia in 1866, and he'd been living in exile.
Anna: Poor man. Homeless duke.

Ben: And now, at the age of seventy-three, he became Grand Duke of Luxembourg. For the first time, the country had a ruler who lived there, whose family belonged to it, and who wasn't the king of someone else.
Anna: So for the owner count?
Ben: Not a new owner. A new family, but the crown stays in the Nassau line.
Anna: Fine. A promotion, not a handover. Still nine.
Ben: It was the beginning of the modern Luxembourg monarchy. Adolphe reigned until 1905. His son William the Fourth followed, and he had no sons, only daughters.
Anna: Uh-oh.
Ben: So parliament changed the rules in 1907 to allow women to inherit. When William died in 1912, his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, became Grand Duchess at eighteen.
Anna: Eighteen. And the first woman to rule Luxembourg in her own right.

Ben: She was. And in these same years, this tiny country produced a few remarkable people who made their names abroad. In 1879, a boy named Edward Steichen was born in the village of Bivange. His family emigrated to the United States when he was a toddler, and he grew up to be one of the greatest photographers of the twentieth century.
Anna: And he organized a famous exhibition.
Ben: The Family of Man, in 1955. It toured the world, and today it is permanently displayed in a castle in the northern town of Clervaux.
Anna: Who else?

Ben: The physicist Gabriel Lippmann won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for a method of reproducing colors in photographs. And Hugo Gernsback, born in Luxembourg City in 1884, moved to the United States in 1904 and published some of the first magazines devoted to what he called scientifiction.
Anna: Scientifiction. Of course.
Ben: We call it science fiction. The Hugo Awards are named after him.
Anna: Wow. A tiny country, and it gave us the Hugo Awards. [chuckle]

Ben: So by 1914, Luxembourg was prosperous, stable, proud, and increasingly sure of its identity. It had a language its writers loved, a dynasty that was its own, and a fast-growing economy. But it still sat between France, Belgium and Germany, and the guarantee of the great powers was only as strong as their promises.
Anna: And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushed Europe toward catastrophe.
Ben: The neutrality of Luxembourg was about to be tested.
Anna: And I think we know how well that works.
Ben: We do.

chapters.title: Two World Wars, 1914 to 1945
chapters.label: Chapter 6: Two World Wars, 1914 to 1945
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. I'm putting the owner count away for this chapter.
Ben: Good idea. This one is hard.
Anna: On the second of August, 1914, German soldiers crossed the border into Luxembourg.

Ben: By road and by rail. They seized the capital's railway station and the key bridges within hours. It was a plain violation of the treaty of 1867. Germany claimed it was only protecting the railways, which were vital to its plan to invade France through Belgium.
Anna: And Luxembourg could do nothing.

Ben: The government protested, but it had no army worth the name. A popular story says that the young Grand Duchess Marie-Adélaïde drove to the Adolphe Bridge and tried to block it with her car. Whether or not that's exactly true, it captures the helplessness of the moment. A country that had trusted a piece of paper for fifty years was now occupied.
Anna: What was the occupation like?

Ben: Strange. Germany let the Luxembourg government keep operating, and promised not to harm the country. But the economy was tied into the German war machine, food grew scarce, and thousands of young men slipped away to join the French army, fighting under the French flag against the occupiers of their homeland.
Anna: And the Grand Duchess?

Ben: She was in an impossible position. Very young, very Catholic, very conservative. She stayed in the country and kept up official contacts with the occupiers, including meeting the German Crown Prince.
Anna: And that came back to haunt her.
Ben: When the war ended in November 1918, France and Belgium especially accused her of being pro-German. Crowds demonstrated against her, and the French and the Americans refused to deal with her.
Anna: So she stepped down.
Ben: In January 1919, she abdicated in favor of her younger sister Charlotte, who was twenty-two. Marie-Adélaïde left the country, entered a convent in Italy, and died in 1924, aged only twenty-nine.
Anna: But the monarchy itself was now in question.

Ben: In September 1919, Luxembourgers voted in a double referendum. The first question asked whether they wanted to keep the dynasty, and about seventy-eight percent said yes. The second asked what kind of economic union they wanted with a larger neighbor, and about seventy-three percent chose France.
Anna: And France said no.

Ben: So Luxembourg turned to Belgium. In 1921, the two formed an economic union, with a shared customs area and a Luxembourg franc tied to the Belgian franc. It lasted until both countries adopted the euro.
Anna: And 1919 brought a political revolution, too.
Ben: A revised constitution introduced universal suffrage, including women. That year, women voted in Luxembourg for the first time, and a woman was elected to parliament.
Anna: What were the next two decades like?

Ben: A quiet transformation. Charlotte, a poised and popular young monarch, married Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma in 1919, and their son Jean was born in 1921. The family became beloved symbols of national unity. The steel industry prospered, then suffered in the Depression. And in 1929, a new law made the country unusually attractive for holding companies, the first small step toward its future as a financial center.
Anna: And I've heard about radio.

Ben: In 1933, Radio Luxembourg began broadcasting from the country, with a powerful transmitter and programs in several languages. It was a business as much as a broadcaster, selling advertising across the borders, and in time it became one of the most famous radio stations in Europe.
Anna: But the shadow of Germany was growing again.
Ben: And on the tenth of May, 1940, it fell. German forces invaded at dawn, as part of their attack on France and the Low Countries. The country was overrun in a single day.
Anna: And Charlotte?

Ben: Grand Duchess Charlotte and her government escaped across the border into France, then to Portugal, then to London. She spent much of the war in exile in Britain and Canada, and her BBC radio addresses were heard in secret by people in the occupied country. They gave courage to many.
Anna: And this occupation was worse than the first.

Ben: Far worse. Hitler's Germany didn't treat Luxembourg as a neutral occupied country. It treated it as German. Gustav Simon, the Nazi governor of the neighboring Koblenz-Trier district, was given authority over Luxembourg in the summer of 1940, and his goal was to make the country fully German.
Anna: What did that look like?

Ben: Thorough, and petty at once. The French language was banned. People were told to change their names, street signs were repainted, and even a polite merci had to become danke. Political parties and trade unions were abolished, and Luxembourgers were declared to be Germans of the Moselle region, who would sooner or later be expected to join the German war effort.
Anna: Then there was the census.

Ben: In October 1941, the Nazi authorities arranged a census with three questions. Your nationality, your mother tongue, and your ethnicity. They expected everyone to answer German, which would prove that Luxembourg was a German land.
Anna: And that's not what happened.

Ben: Resistance organizers spread the word quietly, and the answer they urged was Luxembourgish, three times. More than nine in ten people wrote Luxembourgish on every line. The Germans were furious, and canceled the census.
Anna: And the Jewish community?

Ben: It numbered a few thousand before the war, and it was persecuted from the first days of the occupation. Many managed to flee. But more than a thousand were deported to ghettos and camps in the East, and only a small number survived.
Anna: And then, the summer of 1942.

Ben: On the thirtieth of August, Simon announced that young Luxembourgers would be drafted into the German army. Within hours, a spontaneous general strike began. It started in the northern town of Wiltz, and spread to the steel towns, the mines, the schools, the government offices. Workers walked off their jobs, and trains stopped.
Anna: How did the Nazis respond?

Ben: Simon declared a state of emergency, and the Gestapo moved in. A special court sentenced about twenty strikers to death, and they were shot within days. The strike was crushed, but it remains one of the proudest moments in Luxembourg's national memory. An act of mass defiance in the middle of a brutal occupation.
Anna: And the draft went ahead anyway.

Ben: Around twelve thousand Luxembourgers were forced to serve in the German army. About thirty-five hundred deserted or went into hiding, and their families were deported to labor camps in Germany and Silesia. Somewhere between twenty-five hundred and twenty-eight hundred conscripts were killed or went missing at the front.
Anna: That's so many families.
Ben: It divided families, and left a scar that took generations to heal.
Anna: But many Luxembourgers fought on the other side, too.

Ben: A small Luxembourg unit served in the Allied armies in Britain. And Charlotte's son, Prince Jean, joined the British Army's Irish Guards, and took part in the advance after the Normandy landings.
Anna: And liberation came in September 1944.

Ben: American troops entered Luxembourg City on the tenth, to scenes of wild celebration. But the ordeal wasn't over. In December, Hitler launched his last great offensive in the Ardennes forests, the Battle of the Bulge, and the fighting swept across northern Luxembourg.
Anna: And the towns in its path.
Ben: Wiltz, Clervaux and Vianden were battered. Wiltz, the cradle of the 1942 strike, was nearly destroyed, and earned the title of martyr town.
Anna: And General Patton was there.

Ben: His Third Army made its headquarters in Luxembourg City, and from there launched the counterattack that helped save the besieged town of Bastogne, just across the border in Belgium. When the battle ended in January 1945, Luxembourg was free again, but exhausted and scarred.
Anna: And Patton himself is buried there.

Ben: He died in December 1945, after a car accident in Germany. And he was buried, at his own wish, among his soldiers, in the American military cemetery at Hamm, just outside the capital. More than five thousand American servicemen rest there today.
Anna: So in barely a quarter of a century, Luxembourg had been invaded twice by its giant neighbor.
Ben: The old strategy of neutrality, of staying quiet and hoping to be left alone, had failed twice, catastrophically. The country needed a new way to survive.
Anna: And it found one. Next, we meet the Luxembourgers who decided that the answer wasn't to hide from Europe, but to help build it.

chapters.title: Rebuilding and Founding Europe, 1945 to 1980
chapters.label: Chapter 7: Rebuilding and Founding Europe, 1945 to 1980
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. The owner count is back, but this time I think it's going to stay at nine.
Ben: It will. Because when the war ended, Luxembourg drew a conclusion that shaped the rest of its history. A small country cannot protect itself by standing alone.
Anna: Neutrality had failed twice.

Ben: So the Grand Duchy threw itself into international cooperation, with an enthusiasm few larger countries could match. It started before the war even ended. In September 1944, with the exiled governments of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg still in London, they signed an agreement to create a customs union.
Anna: What did they call it?
Ben: A combination of their initials. Benelux.
Anna: Oh, that's good. That's a very efficient name.
Ben: Fourteen years later, they turned it into a full economic union.
Anna: Then a flurry of firsts.

Ben: In 1945, Luxembourg became a founding member of the United Nations. In 1948, it rewrote its constitution to remove the clause that made it perpetually neutral. And in 1949, it was one of the twelve founding members of NATO. For a country with a tiny army, that was a bold declaration. Luxembourg was firmly part of the Western camp.
Anna: Okay, but you said the most important step had a Luxembourg connection.

Ben: Robert Schuman. He was born in 1886 in Clausen, a neighborhood of Luxembourg City, to a Luxembourg mother and a father from the French region of Lorraine. He grew up speaking German, French and Luxembourgish, studied in Germany, and eventually became a French politician. After the Second World War, he served as France's foreign minister.
Anna: And on the ninth of May, 1950...

Ben: Schuman proposed something remarkable. That France and Germany, who had fought three wars in less than a century, should place their coal and steel production under a single common authority, open to other European countries.
Anna: Because if you share the raw materials of war...
Ben: Another war between them would become unthinkable. That is the Schuman Declaration, and May ninth is celebrated today as Europe Day.
Anna: And the result?
Ben: The European Coal and Steel Community, set up in 1951 by six countries. France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.
Anna: Luxembourg was a natural fit.

Ben: It made more steel per head than almost anyone, ARBED was one of the giants of the sector, and its leaders had learned that tying themselves to bigger neighbors in shared institutions was the best way to stay free.
Anna: And there was another key figure.

Ben: Joseph Bech, Luxembourg's foreign minister for more than thirty years, from 1926 to 1958. In 1955, at a conference in the Sicilian town of Messina, he helped push forward a plan for a wider common market. That led to the Treaties of Rome in 1957, which created the European Economic Community. The direct ancestor of today's European Union.
Anna: Small country, skilled diplomats.

Ben: They made themselves useful as mediators between France and Germany. And Luxembourg was rewarded. The High Authority of the Coal and Steel Community was based there from 1952. So was the Court of Justice, which still sits in Luxembourg today.
Anna: Wait. The EU's highest court is in Luxembourg?

Ben: Yes. In 1968, the European Investment Bank set up its headquarters there, and in 1977 the European Court of Auditors followed. Parts of the European Parliament's administration are there too, along with Eurostat, the EU's statistics office.
Anna: So in a continent full of enormous capitals...
Ben: The little city on the Alzette had quietly become one of the capitals of Europe.
Anna: And it lent its name to a famous diplomatic fix.
Ben: In 1965, France's president Charles de Gaulle was furious about plans to give the European institutions more power, and he boycotted meetings for months. That was the empty chair crisis.
Anna: Hang on. A crisis named after a chair. [chuckle]

Ben: It's a very diplomatic name for a very stubborn absence. The crisis was settled in January 1966 at a meeting in Luxembourg. The deal, known as the Luxembourg Compromise, effectively let a country block a decision if its vital national interests were at stake.
Anna: That sounds like it might cause problems.
Ben: For decades afterwards, it shaped how Europe made decisions.
Anna: Meanwhile, back home, the country was rebuilding.

Ben: The north, devastated by the Battle of the Bulge, was rebuilt town by town. Steel boomed in the postwar decades, as Europe needed girders, rails and machinery. Wages rose, new housing went up, and the standard of living climbed steadily.
Anna: And the throne changed hands.

Ben: Grand Duchess Charlotte, who had reigned for forty-five years and become the symbol of the country's survival, abdicated on the twelfth of November, 1964, in favor of her son Jean. Jean, who had fought alongside the Allies, was forty-three, and he would reign for thirty-six years.
Anna: And there was a quieter change, too.

Ben: The steel mills needed workers, and Luxembourg's own population was too small to supply them. Starting in the nineteen-sixties, thousands of people arrived from Portugal, escaping poverty and a dictatorship at home. They worked in construction, in the mills, in hotels and restaurants.
Anna: And they stayed.
Ben: They became the largest foreign community in the country, and today people of Portuguese origin make up about one in seven residents.
Anna: So Luxembourg was multicultural long before that was fashionable.

Ben: And then there was a financial first. In 1963, an Italian motorway company raised money through a new kind of bond, sold outside its home country and denominated in a foreign currency. It was the first so-called Eurobond, and it was listed on the Luxembourg stock exchange.
Anna: Why Luxembourg?

Ben: Simple. It was friendly, flexible, discreet, and lightly regulated. Over the next decade, banks from Germany, the United States and elsewhere arrived to set up shop. It was the seed of a new economy.
Anna: And somebody saw where this was going.

Ben: Pierre Werner, prime minister and finance minister for much of the sixties and seventies. In 1970, European leaders asked a committee chaired by Werner to design a path toward a single European currency. The Werner Report mapped out a step-by-step plan for monetary union by 1980.
Anna: By 1980? That's ambitious.

Ben: It was shelved after the monetary chaos of the early seventies and the oil crisis. But its ideas came back twenty years later. The euro, launched in 1999, owes something to the plan sketched by a Luxembourg politician in 1970.
Anna: Then the oil crisis hit.

Ben: The crisis of 1973, and the global steel crisis that followed, hit Luxembourg hard. Steel demand collapsed, and the southern mills were in danger. In 1977, rather than let mass unemployment tear society apart, the government brought unions and employers together in a standing body called the Tripartite.
Anna: Three parties at the table.

Ben: They negotiated early retirements, retraining and state support, and avoided the bitter strikes and layoffs that wrecked other industrial regions. This approach of consensus became known as the Luxembourg model.
Anna: All right. Now, a lighter note. I want to hear about the music.

Ben: In these same years, Luxembourg quietly became a pop music superpower. Radio Luxembourg, broadcasting in English by night on medium wave, was one of the few ways British teenagers could hear the latest records. Many remember listening under the blankets with a transistor radio.
Anna: Under the blankets. That's adorable.
Ben: And Eurovision.
Anna: No.
Ben: Luxembourg won five times. In 1961, 1965, 1972, 1973, and 1983.
Anna: Five times?! [chuckle]

Ben: One winner was the French singer France Gall, who won in 1965 with a song written by Serge Gainsbourg. A country of a few hundred thousand people won more often than many far larger ones, helped by its commercial radio, and its talent for hiring great singers from abroad.
Anna: Smart. If you're small, hire the best.

Ben: So by 1980, the Luxembourg that had been invaded and half-destroyed was a comfortable, cosmopolitan little state with a seat at Europe's table. But the steel that had made it rich was in decline.
Anna: And what replaces steel?
Ben: Money.

chapters.title: From Steel to Finance, and Luxembourg Today, 1980 to 2026
chapters.label: Chapter 8: From Steel to Finance, and Luxembourg Today, 1980 to 2026
paragraphs: Anna: So. The early nineteen-eighties. The steel that built modern Luxembourg is shrinking.

Ben: Blast furnaces closed, and thousands of jobs vanished. In many European industrial regions, that kind of decline led to decades of misery. Luxembourg took a different path, because a new industry was already growing in its shadow. Banking and finance.
Anna: The seeds went back to the first Eurobond.

Ben: Over the following decades, the Grand Duchy built itself into a major international financial center. Banks from around the world set up offices, attracted by its stability, its multilingual workforce, its flexible laws, and its famously strong banking secrecy. In 1988, Luxembourg was the first country to write a 1985 European directive on cross-border investment funds into national law, which gave it a head start in that business.
Anna: And today?

Ben: It is the largest center for investment funds in Europe, second in the world only to the United States. By common estimates, the financial sector accounts for roughly a quarter of the whole economy.
Anna: What happened to the steel company?

Ben: In 2002, ARBED merged with Spanish and French rivals to form Arcelor. In 2006, Arcelor was taken over by the steel group of the Indian-born businessman Lakshmi Mittal. The result was ArcelorMittal, one of the largest steelmakers in the world, still headquartered in Luxembourg City.
Anna: And the old steel country found new uses for its industrial heritage.

Ben: At Belval, in the far south near Esch, one of the biggest steelworks was shut down. Its enormous blast furnaces weren't demolished. They were preserved as monuments, and around them rose a whole new district, with offices, a concert hall called the Rockhal, and the campus of the University of Luxembourg, which was founded only in 2003.
Anna: So where workers once tapped molten iron...
Ben: Students now study for exams.
Anna: I love that. Okay. Europe.
Ben: In June 1985, on a passenger boat anchored on the Moselle near the Luxembourg village of Schengen, five European countries signed an agreement to gradually abolish border checks among them.
Anna: Wait. On a boat?

Ben: On a boat. Schengen is a tiny wine-growing village where the borders of Luxembourg, France and Germany meet. The Schengen Area, which now lets millions of people cross borders without passport control, was born on that boat.
Anna: So the borders of Europe came down on a river cruise. [laugh]
Ben: More or less, yes.
Anna: And then the euro.

Ben: In the early nineties, as leaders negotiated the Maastricht Treaty, which set the path to a single currency, Luxembourg's finance minister was a young politician named Jean-Claude Juncker. A crafty, informal negotiator, he helped broker the compromises that made the deal possible.
Anna: And he went on to bigger things.

Ben: He became prime minister in 1995 and held the job for eighteen years, longer than any other head of government in the European Union at the time. He later chaired the eurozone finance ministers through the debt crisis, and in 2014 he was chosen as President of the European Commission.
Anna: He wasn't the first Luxembourger in that job.
Ben: No. Gaston Thorn led the Commission from 1981 to 1985, and Jacques Santer from 1995 to 1999. Three presidents from one of the smallest countries in the union is an extraordinary record.
Anna: How does a country that small pull that off?
Ben: It reflects what Luxembourg has always been good at. Making deals among bigger partners, and making itself indispensable.
Anna: And the language? I'm curious how people actually talk there.

Ben: In 1984, Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect spoken at home for centuries, was formally recognized as the national language. French and German remained the languages of law and administration. Children grow up with three languages in school, and many speak English, Portuguese or Italian at home as well.
Anna: Three languages in school. I barely survive one. [chuckle]
Ben: In few countries is multilingualism such a normal part of daily life.
Anna: And the country grew rich, and crowded.

Ben: Luxembourg has about two thirds of a million residents, and nearly half hold a foreign passport. On top of that, around two hundred thousand people cross the border every day from France, Belgium and Germany to work.
Anna: Two hundred thousand. Every day.
Ben: Per head, it has one of the highest standards of living in the world, but also some of the highest housing costs in Europe, and legendary traffic jams on the roads into the capital. [sigh]
Anna: That's the cost of being popular.
Ben: And in 2020, the government made all public transport free for everyone, the first country in the world to do so.
Anna: Okay, that's a good solution. And it looked to the sky.

Ben: A Luxembourg-based company, SES, launched the Astra satellites in the nineteen-eighties, one of Europe's great satellite television success stories. In 2017, the government passed a law on space resources, and in 2018 it created its own space agency, hoping to become a hub for the new space economy.
Anna: From fortress to satellites. Not everything has been smooth, though.

Ben: No. In 2008, Grand Duke Henri, who had come to the throne in 2000 when his father Jean abdicated, announced that his conscience would not allow him to sign a bill legalizing euthanasia. The government responded by changing the constitution, so that the Grand Duke simply promulgates laws rather than approving them. A quiet change that further reduced the monarch's role.
Anna: And LuxLeaks.

Ben: In 2014, a leak of confidential documents revealed that Luxembourg had signed tax deals with hundreds of multinational companies, allowing them to pay very low taxes. The outcry across Europe was fierce, and many officials elsewhere said the Grand Duchy had been undermining its neighbors.
Anna: How did Luxembourg respond?

Ben: The government defended its legal framework, but came under heavy pressure. In 2015, it joined an international system for the automatic exchange of bank account information, effectively ending the era of strict banking secrecy for foreign account holders. The debate over what is fair in international taxation continues.
Anna: And the politics today?

Ben: The Christian Social party dominated for most of the twentieth century. From 2013 to 2023, a three-party coalition of liberals, Greens and social democrats governed under Prime Minister Xavier Bettel. In the election of October 2023, the Greens lost heavily and the coalition lost its majority.
Anna: So who's in charge now?

Ben: A new government took office in November 2023, led by Luc Frieden of the Christian Social party, in coalition with Bettel's Democratic Party. Frieden is prime minister, and Bettel is deputy prime minister and foreign minister.
Anna: And one more big moment. The most recent chapter of the oldest story.

Ben: On the twenty-third of June, 2025, Luxembourg's National Day, Grand Duke Henri announced that he would step down after twenty-five years on the throne. On the third of October, 2025, in a ceremony at the Grand Ducal Palace, he formally abdicated in favor of his eldest son, Guillaume.
Anna: Who was forty-three.

Ben: He swore an oath to the constitution before parliament, and greeted crowds from a balcony of the palace with his Belgian-born wife, Stéphanie, and their two young sons beside him. He is the seventh grand duke of the modern line that began with Adolphe in 1890.
Anna: Seventh, in a line going back to 1890.
Ben: Voluntary abdication has become something of a tradition in this family, since Henri himself took the throne when his father stepped aside in 2000.
Anna: All right. Let's step back and look at the whole journey.

Ben: It began in nine sixty-three with a count and a rock. It passed through a golden age of emperors who sat on the thrones of Prague, Budapest and Rome. It became a fortress that foreign armies fought over for centuries, passed from Burgundy to Spain to France to Austria and back to France again.
Anna: Then it was created as a grand duchy in 1815.

Ben: Carved in half in 1839, saved from a war in 1867, occupied by Germany twice, and each time it recovered. It turned from farms into steel, from steel into finance, and from a nation guarding itself into one of the founding pillars of a united Europe.
Anna: And the owner count, final tally.
Ben: Go on.
Anna: Nine handovers. And one grand duchy that's still standing.

Ben: And through all of it, one thing stayed consistent. The people of this small land, who have spoken three languages and lived under a dozen flags, never stopped insisting on being themselves. The line from that old song, written in the eighteen-fifties, still works as a national motto.
Anna: We want to remain what we are.
Ben: That is the story of Luxembourg.
Anna: Thank you for listening, and safe travels.

episodes.title: Amsterdam by Day: Rijksmuseum, Heineken and Ribs
episodes.blurb: An all-day walk through the museum quarter and De Pijp, from the Rijksmuseum to the Heineken rooftop tour and a ribs dinner at Cafe de Klos, with art, architecture, a few dark corners and a champagne break. Allow a full day with long pauses.
hints: Museumplein side of the building, Museumstraat. Your reserved 1 PM ticket is for the main entrance under the arch in the center of the building.

Walk out of the museum garden side onto the big open lawn behind the museum. The Van Gogh Museum is the modern building on the far side, the Concertgebouw is the red brick hall at the top of the square.
From Museumplein go east along the canal side, then into the Albert Cuypstraat, the long market street in De Pijp.
Walk back toward the canal, the Stadhouderskade. The brewery is the big old brick building at number 78, with a red star on the front. Your rooftop tour is at 4:45 PM.

Walk north toward the center, aiming for Kerkstraat, a street between the canals. The cafe is at number 41, a small bar with a pink and gold front. No reservations, so go early. Positions are approximate, so check the address on a map.
episodes.notes:
A day walk through the museum quarter and De Pijp, in five stops. Three of them come from your plans: the Rijksmuseum at 1 PM with tickets, the Heineken rooftop tour at 4:45 PM with tickets, and dinner at Cafe de Klos at 6:30 PM, walk-ins only. The two in between, Museumplein and the Albert Cuyp market, are suggestions to fill the afternoon with sights and a champagne break, and you can skip either one. Distances are short, about two kilometers in all, so most of your day is spent standing still.

Stop positions are approximate, good to about 50 meters at best, and the position of the dinner stop is the least certain, so use the street address on a map. Opening hours, ticket rules, tour times and what is on show change often, so check them on the day. The museum may rearrange its rooms. This episode was written without being able to open web pages, so every fact comes from well-known reference history and should be checked against the list at the end. We found no famous ghost story attached to these places and did not invent any. The spooky material is real art and real history, and the one frightening true story, at the brewery, is told plainly.

chapters.title: Welcome and how this works
chapters.label: Welcome and how this works
paragraphs: Anna: Hello, and welcome to a walk. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. Today is a long, lazy day in Amsterdam, in five stops.
Anna: Three of them are booked. A museum, a brewery and a dinner.
Ben: And two we added, so the gaps in the afternoon aren't just waiting around.
Anna: Which sounds like me, standing around, with a beer.
Ben: Eventually. First the art.
Anna: Each chapter is one stop. You press pause when you arrive, stare as long as you like, and press play when you want to walk.
Ben: We give loose directions. Please keep a map open as well. The canals have no railings, and the bicycles have no brakes.
Anna: That's not true.
Ben: It's true in spirit.
Anna: I'll make a bet. Somebody nearly gets run over by a bike before the brewery.
Ben: And it will be a tourist, and it will be you.
Anna: Rude.
Ben: We'll get there.
Anna: Shoes?
Ben: Comfortable. Hours standing in front of paintings are harder than hours walking.
Anna: Okay. First stop, one o'clock.
Ben: The Rijksmuseum.

chapters.title: Stop 1: The Rijksmuseum
chapters.label: Stop 1: The Rijksmuseum
paragraphs: Anna: So, can I ask a rude question about the biggest museum in the country?
Ben: Always.
Anna: Why does it look like a cathedral that took a wrong turn?
Ben: Ha. People said that when it opened.
Anna: Really?

Ben: Really. The architect was Pierre Cuypers, a Catholic from the south of the Netherlands. The museum opened in 1885. Some Protestant critics in Amsterdam thought it looked far too much like a church.
Anna: To a country that had spent centuries being proudly Protestant.
Ben: Not quite proudly. Very, very seriously.
Anna: Fair.
Ben: And here's a thing. Cuypers also designed Amsterdam Central Station.
Anna: Wait. Both buildings?
Ben: Both. The station where you arrived, and the museum where you're standing. Same architect, same red brick, same fussy towers.
Anna: So he basically bookended the city.
Ben: More or less. The station is the front door, and this is the family treasure room.
Anna: Okay, where are we exactly?

Ben: You should be on the side facing Museumplein, the big lawn behind the museum, or at the main entrance. With a ticket for one o'clock, you go to the entrance, and you go in. We'll tell you the story while you queue, or later, if you pause us.
Anna: And the collection started where?
Ben: Not in Amsterdam. In 1800 it was founded in The Hague, as a national gallery.
Anna: Then it moved.

Ben: In 1808. Louis Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother, was king of the Netherlands, and he moved it to Amsterdam. For a while, it lived in the Royal Palace on the Dam. Then in a different old building, and finally here.
Anna: A museum that had to find a home.
Ben: Like a very expensive student.
Anna: Ha. Okay, so what do I look at?
Ben: Let's choose three things, because nobody can see all of it in an afternoon.
Anna: Three. Bet I get one right.
Ben: Go on.
Anna: The Night Watch.
Ben: Yes. Rembrandt, finished in 1642. And here's something people get wrong.
Anna: It's not at night.
Ben: It's not at night.
Anna: Ben!

Ben: It was a daytime scene. Over the centuries, the varnish darkened and the painting looked like a night scene, and the name stuck. The real title is much longer, something like the militia company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.
Anna: So a group portrait of a neighborhood militia.
Ben: Exactly. Amsterdam's civic guard companies commissioned group portraits, and Rembrandt made his dramatic instead of lined up in rows.
Anna: And people liked that?
Ben: History is mixed. We do know it's a huge painting, and it was cut down on the sides, in 1715, when it moved to the Town Hall on the Dam, because it didn't fit between two doors.
Anna: Wait. They cut a Rembrandt to fit a wall?
Ben: They did.
Anna: That is the least Dutch thing I've ever heard, and the most Dutch.
Ben: Practical to the bone. Look at the faces, and look for the girl in yellow, who gets lots of attention. Our advice is to go there first, before the crowds thicken.
Anna: And the other two?
Ben: Something quieter. Vermeer's painting of a kitchen maid pouring milk. It's small, and everybody who sees it stops talking.
Anna: And the third is for the spooky request.
Ben: Right. You wanted spooky.
Anna: I did.
Ben: So find a vanitas. That's a type of still life, very popular in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century. A table with fruit, flowers, a pocket watch, sometimes a skull.
Anna: A skull on a table.
Ben: As a reminder. The word means emptiness, or vanity. The message is that wealth and beauty don't last, so enjoy them but don't be fooled. The Latin phrase is memento mori, remember you will die.
Anna: That's very cheerful for a lunch break.
Ben: To be fair, it was the opposite of a threat. It was a gentle reminder, painted by artists who were selling to rich merchants.
Anna: Rich merchants who wanted a skull above the fireplace.
Ben: Next to the silver. Yes.
Anna: Okay, I love it. What else?
Ben: The model rooms. A cabinet house of the early eighteenth century, with tiny furniture, belonging to a woman named Petronella Oortman. It cost about as much as a real house.
Anna: A toy house the price of a house.
Ben: And the Gallery of Honour, the long hall leading to the Night Watch. It's the museum's spine.
Anna: And I've heard about the bicycles.
Ben: Ah. The passage.
Anna: There is a passage?
Ben: There's a tunnel under the central part of the building, with a public road and a bike path. For over a hundred years, people have cycled and walked straight through the museum.
Anna: Through it, not around it.
Ben: And when the museum was rebuilt, with work that started in 2003 and finished in 2013, a long ten years, a plan to close the passage ran into the cycling lobby.
Anna: Of course.
Ben: Of course. They won, and the passage stayed open.
Anna: So the national treasure house has a bike lane.
Ben: And it works. When you walk out the door, you'll see.
Anna: Okay. How long do we stay?
Ben: Your ticket is for one o'clock. Two hours is comfortable. Three if you love it. There's a garden outside, free to walk into, with sculptures, if you need air.
Anna: And then?
Ben: And then we leave through the back and go onto the lawn. Pause here as long as you like, and when you're out, press play.
Anna: Ben, one thing. A small question for the audience.
Ben: Go ahead.
Anna: Look at the Night Watch, and count the hands in the painting.
Ben: Oh, that's good.
Anna: I'm going to lose count.
Ben: You'll lose count, and you'll lose track of time. Go.

chapters.title: Stop 2: Museumplein
chapters.label: Stop 2: Museumplein
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, I'm out. I need to sit down.
Ben: You did well. Welcome to Museumplein.
Anna: Museum square.
Ben: A big open lawn, with the Rijksmuseum at one end, the Van Gogh Museum along one side, and the Concertgebouw at the top.
Anna: What's the red brick one?
