Ben: That's the Concertgebouw, the concert hall. It opened in 1888, just three years after the Rijksmuseum. Its orchestra is among the best known in the world, and the acoustics are famous.
Anna: A neat little quarter.

Ben: A deliberate one. This was open ground at the edge of the city in the nineteenth century. In 1883 it was a world fair site, and then it was turned into this cultural district, so the museums stand together.
Anna: Not a stage for tourists.
Ben: Though that has happened. You may have seen photos of a giant sign here spelling out "I amsterdam".
Anna: I have.
Ben: It stood on this lawn for years, a favorite for pictures. It was removed in 2018, and the city decided that it brought too many crowds.
Anna: So if you came for the photo.
Ben: Sorry, no photo. But look around. There's a pond in winter that becomes an ice rink, and a lawn where people lie down and eat sandwiches.
Anna: And the Van Gogh Museum?
Ben: It opened in 1973. It holds the largest collection of Van Gogh's work anywhere, thanks to his family, who kept the paintings and later gave them to the nation.
Anna: His brother.

Ben: His brother Theo, who supported him, and then Theo's family. It's a moving place, and it needs a ticket booked long in advance, so we're not planning it today, but look at the building as you pass.
Anna: Okay, I need a coffee.
Ben: Or champagne.
Anna: Wait. Is that allowed?
Ben: You told us in the request that you care about champagne.
Anna: I did. Because I'm a person with priorities.

Ben: Right. So here's the plan. In De Pijp, the neighborhood just east of here, there are plenty of cafes with small glasses and nice terraces. You've got about two hours before the brewery. Sit somewhere, order a glass, and watch the bicycles go by.
Anna: And we continue.
Ben: We continue. Walk east along the canal side, toward the Albert Cuyp market.
Anna: How far?
Ben: Ten minutes. Pause now if you'd like to sit on the grass.
Anna: Pausing. Don't talk.
Ben: I wouldn't dream of it.

chapters.title: Stop 3: The Albert Cuyp Market and De Pijp
chapters.label: Stop 3: The Albert Cuyp Market and De Pijp
paragraphs: Anna: Ben, why is this neighborhood called the Pipe?
Ben: Good question. De Pijp. The name means the pipe, and the story is that the streets are long and narrow, straight and tall, like a pipe, with rows of tall houses.
Anna: Are you sure?
Ben: It's the common explanation. There's some doubt about the exact origin.
Anna: Okay. And it's a pipe with a market in it.
Ben: Right. The Albert Cuypstraat. You're probably on it by now.
Anna: I can hear it.
Ben: It runs for nearly a kilometer. The market has been here since 1905, and it's named after Albert Cuyp, a painter of the seventeenth century, who painted rivers and cows.
Anna: Cows.
Ben: Beautiful cows. A calm, golden-light painter. You might even have seen one of his paintings in the museum.
Anna: Cows then, cows now.
Ben: The market is mostly food and goods. Cheese, fish, flowers, and stroopwafels. A stroopwafel is a thin waffle with syrup between two layers, and if you find a stand making them fresh, buy one.
Anna: Is that the real thing?
Ben: Warm, yes. Cold, it's a cookie.
Anna: I'm going to bet that I buy three.
Ben: I'm not taking that bet.
Anna: Where's the champagne?
Ben: Side streets. Look for a small bar with a terrace. If you'd rather beer, nobody will stop you, and the brewery is coming.
Anna: One more question. De Pijp used to be a poor area?

Ben: In the nineteenth century, yes. It was built fast, in the 1870s and 1880s, as housing for workers outside the old canal ring. These days it's one of the most popular neighborhoods, with artists, students and cafes.
Anna: Who moved in?
Ben: Everyone. It's a standard story. First the workers, then the artists, then the people who like artists.
Anna: Then the people who like the people who like the artists.
Ben: Then the tourists.
Anna: Hello.
Ben: Hello. Enjoy it. The tour at the brewery is at 4:45 PM, so aim to be walking by 4:15.
Anna: Ten minutes?
Ben: From the western end of the market, ten minutes. Pause and eat something. We'll be here.

chapters.title: Stop 4: The Heineken Brewery and the Rooftop Tour
chapters.label: Stop 4: The Heineken Brewery and the Rooftop Tour
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, this is huge. A giant brick building with a red star.
Ben: Number 78, Stadhouderskade. The old Heineken brewery.
Anna: It looks like a factory.
Ben: It was one. It sits right next to the canal that marks the old edge of the city.
Anna: So it's the actual place where beer was made.
Ben: For over a hundred years. The story starts in 1864. A young man named Gerard Adriaan Heineken, just twenty-two years old, bought a brewery called De Hooiberg, which means the haystack.
Anna: He bought a brewery at twenty-two.
Ben: With help. His mother put up money. And the family had money.
Anna: Naturally.
Ben: He soon built a new brewery on this spot, and it began producing in 1867. The city was growing, and beer was a big business.
Anna: And the beer is the one with the star.
Ben: The red star, yes. That became the trademark, and it's still on every bottle.
Anna: What's special about the beer?
Ben: One thing is the yeast. In the 1880s the company hired a scientist, Doctor Elion, who isolated a pure strain of yeast. The company calls it the A-yeast, and still uses a descendant of it.
Anna: Like a family pet.
Ben: Rather like a family pet. And a company secret.
Anna: Huh. So a brewery, a hundred years, then?
Ben: Then it closed. Making beer here ended in 1988, because the plant was too small for a modern brewery. The beer moved to bigger sites elsewhere in the country.
Anna: And the building became a museum.
Ben: A visitor attraction, now called the Heineken Experience. The tour is the main thing.
Anna: And we have the rooftop version.
Ben: Yes. Your ticket is for 4:45 PM. Don't be late, because tours start on the dot. Details vary, so follow the instructions you were given when you booked.
Anna: And what's on top?

Ben: We're not going to describe what we can't confirm. What we can say is that the building is one of the tall brick landmarks of the neighborhood, so a roof gives you a view over the south of the city.
Anna: And beer.
Ben: Tastings are part of the experience, yes. Please enjoy them responsibly, and get home safely.
Anna: Fair. Okay, but you promised spooky, and I think there's something here.
Ben: There is. It's not a legend. It's real, and it's serious, so we're going to talk about it plainly.
Anna: Okay.

Ben: In November 1983, the owner of the company, Freddy Heineken, was kidnapped, together with his driver, Ab Doderer. They were taken from the street near the company's offices and held captive for about three weeks.
Anna: By whom?
Ben: A group of Dutch criminals. They demanded a very large ransom, around 35 million guilders at the time, which was one of the largest ransoms ever paid in the world.
Anna: And they were freed?
Ben: Yes. Both men were released at the end of November. The kidnappers were later caught, and several were convicted.
Anna: That must have been terrifying.
Ben: It was. The case is still remembered here as one of the most shocking crimes in modern Dutch history.
Anna: Thank you for telling it straight.
Ben: It's part of the story of the place. We'll say no more.
Anna: Okay. Let's gather ourselves. Enjoy the tour.
Ben: Pause here for as long as the tour takes. About an hour and a half should be plenty, and then, dinner.
Anna: I'll be the one humming.
Ben: Of course you will.

chapters.title: Stop 5: Cafe de Klos
chapters.label: Stop 5: Cafe de Klos
paragraphs: Anna: Tour done, a few beers in. And it's evening. How are we doing for dinner?
Ben: Dinner is at 6:30 PM, at Cafe de Klos, and it's walk-ins only.
Anna: So no booking.
Ben: No booking. You turn up and wait. It's a small place and it fills up fast, so we'd suggest going straight there from the brewery.
Anna: How far?

Ben: About a kilometer, fifteen minutes on foot. Walk north, away from the canal, into the old town. Keep a map open. You're aiming for Kerkstraat, a long street between the canals, near the Vijzelgracht.
Anna: And the cafe?
Ben: Kerkstraat 41. It's a small, dark, cozy bar with a lot of character.
Anna: And what do we eat?
Ben: It's known in Amsterdam for spare ribs. Big plates of them, grilled, with sauces, and garlic. Local guides often mention the garlic.
Anna: Garlic. Spooky, if you think about vampires.
Ben: Ha. Nicely done. Garlic against vampires is folklore, and of course there are no vampires here. But if you ate a lot of garlic tonight, they'd leave you alone.
Anna: So the spooky request is covered.
Ben: Technically.
Anna: You said walk-ins only. What if there's a queue?

Ben: Then wait, or have a drink nearby. There are plenty of bars on the nearby streets. We can't promise a table, and we can't promise opening hours, so please check before you leave the brewery. A phone call or a look at a map will do.
Anna: Do we have to eat ribs?
Ben: No. They have other dishes. But you don't get this reputation for nothing.
Anna: What do you drink with ribs?
Ben: You've just come from a brewery.
Anna: Right. Beer. Or if I'm brave, champagne.
Ben: With ribs.
Anna: I like to live dangerously.
Ben: It would be unusual. But it's your holiday.
Anna: Okay. Now, Ben, a bet.
Ben: Go on.
Anna: I'll lose a napkin before the end of the meal.
Ben: You'll lose three, and a sleeve.
Anna: Probably true.
Ben: Pause now. Eat. We'll come back at the end.

chapters.title: Wrap-up
chapters.label: Wrap-up
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Full. Happy. A bit sticky.
Ben: A good day, then. A museum with a Rembrandt cut to fit a wall, a lawn with a missing sign, a street market with warm waffles, a brewery with a haystack in its past, and a plate of ribs.
Anna: And no one got run over by a bike.
Ben: Not yet. The walk home is still ahead.
Anna: Oh no.
Ben: Look both ways. Then look again. Then look up, because the next bicycle might come from the sky.
Anna: That doesn't happen.
Ben: In Amsterdam, you can never be sure.
Anna: Thank you for walking with us.
Ben: If you'd like another tour, ask for one. There's a night walk through the old center, for the spooky side of the city.
Anna: Safe travels.
Ben: And safe walking.

episodes.title: The Story of Brussels
episodes.blurb: Two hosts, Anna and Ben, walk through the history of Brussels, from a marsh settlement to the capital of Europe.
episodes.notes:
This is a conversation between two hosts, Anna and Ben, running roughly an hour and a quarter in eight chapters. Each chapter stands alone, so you can start anywhere. Everything from the Welcome section onward is written to be heard, with no tables or footnotes.

Text-to-speech voices sometimes stumble on Flemish and French names such as Senne, Coudenberg, Egmont and Anspach. You can add respellings in tools/pronunciations.json (for example Senne = Senn) and the next audio run will use them.

On accuracy: the 1695 bombardment, the 2016 attacks, today's population figures and the current governments were checked against the sources listed at the end. Older dates and details come from standard histories. They are reliable, but check anything you plan to repeat in print.

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.label: Welcome
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Brussels. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. And I'll admit, I've been looking forward to this one.
Anna: Why? It's the city with the waffles and the... what is it, the European Union?
Ben: Ha. Yes. The waffles and the European Union.
Anna: It's a good pairing. Breakfast and paperwork.

Ben: Well, the same city also has a Gothic town hall, a glass tower full of EU officials, a medieval square that was rebuilt in four years after a bombardment, and a whole boulevard built on top of a river.
Anna: Wait. A river?
Ben: A river. We'll get there.
Anna: You say that a lot, don't you? "We'll get there."
Ben: It's a long story. I'm pacing myself.
Anna: And I've heard every street sign has two languages.
Ben: Two languages on the signs, and nearly four in ten residents hold a foreign passport.
Anna: Four in ten. That's a lot.
Ben: It is. So here's what I want to know. How does a small town on a muddy river end up as the working capital of Europe?
Anna: Trade, I'm guessing.
Ben: Trade. Guilds. Dukes. Emperors. Revolutionaries.
Anna: Ooh. Revolutionaries.
Ben: And a great deal of stubbornness.
Anna: Okay, I'm keeping count of that. Stubbornness tally, starting now. Zero.
Ben: It won't stay at zero.
Anna: Right, I'm sold. Where do we start?
Ben: With the mud, naturally.

chapters.title: A Settlement in the Marsh
chapters.label: Chapter 1: A Settlement in the Marsh
paragraphs: Anna: So. Mud. Walk me through it.

Ben: The river is called the Senne. And you have to imagine it as nothing like a proper river. It's a small, slow stream that used to wander across a wide, wet valley, splitting into channels, making little islands as it went.
Anna: Not exactly a glamorous start.

Ben: Not at all. But people had been living around the edges of that valley for a very long time. There are traces of Iron Age settlers at a site called Champ Saint-Anne, in the neighborhood of Anderlecht.
Anna: And the Romans? Because the Romans always show up. I'd bet money on a Roman town.
Ben: You'd lose.
Anna: Ugh.

Ben: Roman farms and country houses were scattered across the countryside, but no real Roman town on the spot. After the empire faded, Frankish settlers moved in. And in that same field in Anderlecht, they've found a Frankish cemetery with more than three hundred graves, from roughly the years five hundred to seven hundred.
Anna: Three hundred graves. So that's not a passing visit.
Ben: No. That's farmers and fighters living in small villages on the dry ground above the river, inside the new Frankish kingdom. The one that eventually grows into Charlemagne's empire.
Anna: Okay. I can feel a legend coming.
Ben: You're right. There's a legend.
Anna: Go on.
Ben: Tradition says that around the year five eighty, a holy man named Gaugericus, known in French as Saint Géry, who was bishop of Cambrai, built a little chapel on an island in the Senne.
Anna: Is that true?

Ben: Honestly? Historians are cautious. The sources are later, and a bit shaky. But it's a good candidate for the seed of the city. And the nice part is, you can still go there. It's a square in the old center called Place Saint-Géry, with an old market hall close to where the island used to be.
Anna: What about the name, though? Brussels.
Ben: The earliest forms look something like Bruocsella. And most scholars read that as a home in the marsh. Or a dwelling by the swamp.
Anna: Oh, that's honest.
Ben: It's what a farmer would call a wet bit of ground.
Anna: "Welcome to Swampville. Population: wet."
Ben: Roughly that. But it tells you something true. This was a place that had to deal with water.
Anna: But hang on. If it's a swamp, why would anyone build a town there?

Ben: Geography. The Senne valley sat on an important route. Trade roads ran from the cloth-making cities of Flanders in the west, to Cologne and the Rhine in the east. Merchants went through carrying wool, cloth, wine, metalwork.
Anna: And they needed somewhere to stop.
Ben: Exactly. A place to cross the river, or bring boats upstream. And the islands gave them safe ground.
Anna: And the hills?
Ben: The hills to the east were a good place for a fortress.
Anna: So it's a market town waiting to happen.
Ben: Waiting to happen, yes. But for a long time it's still small, in a much bigger political world. In the ninth century, Charlemagne's empire gets divided among his heirs.
Anna: As happens.

Ben: As always happens. And the region that becomes Belgium gets caught in the middle, in a long contested territory called Lotharingia, named for the Frankish king Lothar. It bounces back and forth between the western and eastern halves of the old empire.
Anna: Who's actually in charge, though? On the ground.
Ben: Not the dukes, really. They ruled Lotharingia on behalf of the German emperors, but with a loose grip. So local lords hold most of the real power.
Anna: Right. So when do we get a proper date?

Ben: Late tenth century. In the year nine seventy-seven, the German emperor Otto the Second gives the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which is roughly Belgium and part of the Netherlands, to a man called Charles.
Anna: Who's Charles?
Ben: A member of the old Carolingian family. A son of one French king and a brother of the next one. Basically an exile from the throne of France, hunting for a power base.
Anna: Oh, so he needs a castle.
Ben: He needs a castle. And within a couple of years, he builds a fortification on one of the islands in the Senne. The same island as the old chapel.
Anna: Is that the founding?

Ben: Hold on. Because something else matters even more. In about the year nine seventy-nine, Charles moves the relics of a saint named Gudula, a pious woman from the seventh century, to the chapel on the island.
Anna: Gudula! I love Gudula. Is it true she went to church before dawn carrying a lantern?
Ben: So the story goes. And the devil kept blowing out her light.
Anna: Every time?
Ben: Every time. And every time, an angel lit it again.
Anna: I like the angel.
Ben: Everyone likes the angel. Anyway, Gudula becomes the patron saint of Brussels. And that move of her relics is the date most often given as the official founding of the city.
Anna: But I sense a caution.

Ben: Always. Modern historians point out that the story of Charles building a castle and founding the city rests on sources written long afterwards. The real picture is probably messier. A growing settlement, a chapel, a market, local lords, all developing over several generations.
Anna: So nobody cut a ribbon.
Ben: Nobody cut a ribbon. But nine seventy-nine is the date that stuck. Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.
Anna: Okay, and the relics moved again, didn't they? They get around.

Ben: They really do. In 1047, a powerful nobleman named Lambert the Second, Count of Leuven, which is a city about twenty-five kilometers to the east, moves them to a new church on a hill overlooking the valley. And he sets up a college of priests there, called canons, to look after it.
Anna: Wait, so that's the cathedral?
Ben: That's the ancestor of the cathedral. The hill church was dedicated to Saint Michael, and in time to Saint Gudula too. It grows into the twin-towered cathedral you can still see today.
Anna: And Saint Michael is the dragon slayer.
Ben: He is. He becomes the other patron saint of the city. And he ends up standing on top of the town hall, which we'll get to.
Anna: Of course we will.
Ben: Of course we will.
Anna: Okay, so by now, the pieces are in place.

Ben: They are. A lowland market settlement on the river, with merchants and craftsmen. A church on the hill, with money and influence. A castle for protection. And the counts of Leuven, who increasingly see this place as an important part of their growing territory.
Anna: What about walls?

Ben: Around the year eleven hundred, the people build their first defensive wall. Nothing grand, a modest circuit around the main settlement. Inside, maybe a few thousand people. They make cloth, bake bread, brew beer, trade.
Anna: A few thousand. So, not a great city. Not yet.
Ben: Not yet. But a real town now. Walls, a market, a church, a lord.
Anna: Stubbornness tally?
Ben: Surviving in a swamp for a thousand years? I'd say it's one.
Anna: Fair. One.
Ben: Next time, the counts become dukes, and the craftsmen start flexing their muscles.
Anna: And that muddy market square...
Ben: Begins turning into one of the most famous squares in the world.

chapters.title: Dukes, Guilds and the Grand Place, 1100 to 1430
chapters.label: Chapter 2: Dukes, Guilds and the Grand Place, 1100 to 1430
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, I want to start with a bet. The Grand Place. I bet it began as a field of mud.
Ben: You're learning.
Anna: Ha! Finally.

Ben: But we'll get to it. First, the family that rules the place. In the twelfth century, Brussels falls into the hands of the counts of Leuven, and they just keep climbing. They become dukes of Lower Lotharingia, and then, as that old title stops meaning anything, dukes of Brabant.
Anna: And Brabant is a big deal.

Ben: One of the richest territories in northwest Europe. It stretched across the heart of what's now Belgium and part of the southern Netherlands, with great towns like Leuven, Antwerp, and Brussels. For a long time, Leuven is the leading city. But gradually the dukes start spending more time in Brussels, in a castle on a hill called the Coudenberg.
Anna: Which means?
Ben: Cold hill.
Anna: Cold hill. I love how nobody in this region tried to oversell anything.
Ben: Swamp, cold hill. They called it as they saw it.
Anna: So the dukes move in. And?
Ben: And by the late Middle Ages, Brussels is the main seat of the dukes, and with the dukes come money, officials, and prestige.
Anna: But the dukes can't be the only reason it grows.

Ben: No. Brussels owes just as much to its own people. The town makes cloth. Wool comes in from England, weavers and dyers turn it into fabric, merchants sell it across Europe. And around that grows everything else. Brewing, baking, butchery, metalwork, carpentry, and eventually luxury goods like tapestries.
Anna: And the people doing those jobs organized themselves.
Ben: Into guilds. Part trade union, part business association, part social club, part political party.
Anna: So, basically, a LinkedIn group, but with swords.
Ben: Not quite. But I'm going to think about that.
Anna: So where does the Grand Place come in?

Ben: At the center of it all is the market. Down in the valley, on low ground by the river, there's an open space called the Lower Market. Traders set up stalls, townspeople do business. Over the centuries, wooden stalls turn into stone halls, and the guilds build meeting houses around the edges.
Anna: So it did begin as a muddy field.
Ben: It did. By the end of the thirteenth century, the drapers' guild has its own hall there, and the foundation of the square's future is laid.
Anna: Okay. Who actually runs the town?

Ben: A narrow elite. A handful of wealthy families, known as the Seven Lineages of Brussels, who hold the city council and the best offices. Below them are the guilds, which have economic muscle but very little say in government.
Anna: Oh, that's going to end well.

Ben: It does not end well. But first we meet one of the great documents of Brussels history. In 1355, the Duke of Brabant, John the Third, dies without a male heir. His eldest daughter, Joanna, becomes duchess. And her husband is a man listeners of our Luxembourg episode will remember. Wenceslas of Luxembourg, half brother of the Emperor Charles the Fourth.
Anna: Oh! Small world.
Ben: It's a very small world. Everyone is somebody's half brother.
Anna: So what happens?

Ben: In January of 1356, before they can take up their rule, Joanna and Wenceslas have to sign a charter promising to respect the rights of the towns and nobles of Brabant. It's called the Joyous Entry, named for the ceremonial entry a new ruler made into the cities of the duchy.
Anna: Joyous Entry. It sounds like a party.

Ben: It's a contract. A very polite contract. It limits the power of the duke. He can't declare war, sign treaties, or raise taxes without the consent of the estates. And it even includes a remarkable clause allowing the people of Brabant to withdraw their obedience if the duke breaks the rules.
Anna: That sounds like the Magna Carta.

Ben: People often compare them. Historians do caution that its later reputation was somewhat inflated by romantic writers in the nineteenth century. But it remained an important symbol for centuries, and Brabantine rulers swore to uphold it for generations.
Anna: And I'm guessing someone tested it right away.
Ben: Immediately. Louis of Male, the Count of Flanders, a powerful neighbor with his own claim to Brabant, invades and seizes Brussels in 1356.
Anna: That was fast.

Ben: But he doesn't hold it long. A citizen named Everard t'Serclaes, from one of the great families, leads a night raid with a small band of men, slips into the city, and drives out the Flemish garrison.
Anna: Okay, that's a folk hero.

Ben: Absolutely. He's killed by a rival lord a few decades later, and today there's a bronze monument to him lying against a wall just off the Grand Place. According to local custom, rubbing the bronze arm of the statue brings good luck.
Anna: And I'll bet it's polished bright.
Ben: It's shining. Generations of hands. Anna, stubbornness tally?
Anna: Oh, a night raid against an occupying army? Two. Easily two.

Ben: Now, the liberation helps fuel another great project. The city is growing quickly, and the old walls are too small. Between 1356 and 1383, the people of Brussels build a second, much larger ring of walls, with seven main gates and dozens of towers.
Anna: That's a huge undertaking for a town that size.

Ben: It encloses about eight kilometers of ground. Most of it is torn down in the nineteenth century, and its path is now traced by a ring of boulevards around the old center. The Petite Ceinture. The small ring.
Anna: So if I look at a map of central Brussels, that five-sided shape of boulevards is the medieval city?
Ben: Exactly. And one gate survives. The heavy, castle-like Porte de Hal, on the southern side of the ring.
Anna: Okay. And the Town Hall. That's from this period too.

Ben: The early fifteenth century is the great age of civic building. In 1402, work begins on the Brussels Town Hall, on the Grand Place. The left wing goes up first, and the right wing follows in the fourteen-forties. In 1449, the architects begin the soaring tower, a lace of stone rising about ninety-six meters, topped by a gilded statue of Saint Michael slaying the dragon.
Anna: And there's a famous quirk.

Ben: There is. The tower isn't centered over the main doorway, and the two wings are slightly different lengths. According to an old story, the architect was so horrified by the asymmetry that he threw himself from the tower.
Anna: Oh no.
Ben: Historians think that's just a legend.
Anna: Thank goodness. Although, it's a very dramatic way to say "I should have measured twice."
Ben: It is a good legend.
Anna: And then there's the smallest landmark in the city.

Ben: The Manneken Pis. A fountain figure of a little boy relieving himself into a basin, first mentioned in a document from 1388. The bronze you can visit today is a copy of a version made in 1619 by the sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy. It stands on a street corner a few minutes from the Grand Place.
Anna: And he has a wardrobe.
Ben: Well over a thousand costumes, changed on special occasions.
Anna: A thousand outfits! He's a small bronze boy with a better closet than me.

Ben: And lots of legends try to explain him. In one, a small duke of Leuven, hung in a basket from a tree during a battle, relieves himself on the enemy and inspires his soldiers. In another, a boy puts out a burning fuse and saves the city.
Anna: So which is true?
Ben: Nobody knows. And Brussels doesn't seem to mind.
Anna: Which is the right attitude, honestly. Okay, but now the tension between the lineages and the guilds.

Ben: Boils over. In 1421, a group of guildsmen, angry about the patricians' control of the government and rising taxes, storm the town hall, and several city magistrates are killed. The duke, John the Fourth, steps in to restore order. But the result is a victory for the craftsmen.
Anna: So what changes?

Ben: From then on, the guilds, organized into nine groups called the Nations of Brussels, have a formal share of power on the city council. For the first time, Brussels has a government in which ordinary working people have a say.
Anna: That's a big deal.
Ben: It's a very big deal. Out of a muddy marsh town, a real city is growing, with a strong sense of its own rights.
Anna: And money. Don't forget the money.
Ben: Never. And money is exactly what the next chapter is about.
Anna: Because in 1430, someone very rich and very ambitious walks in.
Ben: And Brussels becomes a capital.

chapters.title: Capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, 1430 to 1568
chapters.label: Chapter 3: Capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, 1430 to 1568
paragraphs: Anna: In 1430, Brussels hits the jackpot.

Ben: It really does. The duchy of Brabant passes to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest and most glamorous princes in Europe. And Philip makes a choice that changes the city's destiny. Out of all his great towns, he picks Brussels as his main residence.
Anna: Okay, I have to ask. What was the Burgundian state? Because it sounds like a wine region.

Ben: Ha. Not quite. It wasn't a kingdom on a map the way we think of kingdoms. It was a patchwork of territories collected through marriage, inheritance, and purchase. Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, and soon the duchy of Luxembourg, which Philip took in 1443, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode.
Anna: So roughly modern Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

Ben: Plus a good slice of northern France. And Philip ruled it all from the most dazzling court in Europe. Knights, painters, musicians, diplomats. In 1430, the same year he inherited Brabant, he founded a famous chivalric brotherhood, the Order of the Golden Fleece.
Anna: Every club needs a good name. And the heart of that court was Brussels.

Ben: More and more. The dukes lived at the Coudenberg Palace, on the hill above the town, and enlarged it into a huge complex of halls, chapels, and courtyards. Government offices followed the court. Money followed the offices.
Anna: And artists followed the money.
Ben: Artists always follow the money.
Anna: So let's talk art, because this is a golden age.

Ben: It's extraordinary. In 1436, the city appoints a painter named Rogier van der Weyden as its official city painter. He was born in Tournai, trained there, and became one of the great masters of what we now call Early Netherlandish painting.
Anna: His portraits have those sharp, searching faces. Like they know what you did.
Ben: And emotional religious scenes, admired across Europe. For the town hall, he painted a series of panels about justice, scenes of rulers hearing the cases of ordinary people.
Anna: Can we go and see them?
Ben: No. They were destroyed in 1695. We'll get to that.
Anna: Of course we will.
Ben: The artist's reputation lived on, though. Rogier is buried in the cathedral of Brussels.
Anna: And then there's tapestry.

Ben: Brussels becomes famous for it. Weavers in the city produce huge, richly colored wall hangings, made of wool, silk, and threads of gold and silver. Tapestries were the luxury art of the age. A prince would pay more for a fine set than for a painting.
Anna: Wait, more than a painting? For a rug on the wall?
Ben: For a very, very good rug on the wall. And they could be rolled up and carried from palace to palace. It was a portable fortune.
Anna: Okay, that makes sense. And I remember a Sistine Chapel connection.

Ben: In the second decade of the sixteenth century, Pope Leo the Tenth commissions a set of tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, from designs by Raphael. And the weaving is done in Brussels. The city soon introduces a quality mark, a pair of the letter B around a red shield, woven into the edge of authentic pieces to protect the brand.
Anna: A brand mark. In the fifteen hundreds. That's very modern.

Ben: Very. But the Burgundian dream ends abruptly in 1477. Philip's grandson, Charles the Bold, is killed fighting the Swiss and the Lorrainers outside the city of Nancy. And he leaves a single daughter, Mary of Burgundy.
Anna: Who was born in Brussels.

Ben: And she's the most eligible heiress in Europe. She marries Maximilian of Habsburg, an Austrian prince who will become Holy Roman Emperor. And when she dies in a riding accident in 1482, her lands pass to their children. Through that marriage, the Burgundian Netherlands falls into the hands of the Habsburgs, the most powerful dynasty of the next three centuries.
Anna: And the Habsburg who matters most for Brussels?

Ben: Mary's grandson, Charles. He's born in Ghent in the year 1500, but he's raised in the Netherlands, and he sees Brussels as home. When he's six, he inherits the Burgundian lands. In 1516, he's proclaimed King of Spain, in a ceremony in the church of Saint Gudula in Brussels.
Anna: Wait. King of Spain. In Brussels.
Ben: In Brussels. And in 1519, he's elected Holy Roman Emperor, as Charles the Fifth.
Anna: So a boy from Ghent, raised in the Netherlands, ends up ruling an enormous empire.
Ben: From Spain and Italy to Germany, the Netherlands, and the new Spanish colonies in the Americas.
Anna: He can't have been in Brussels very often.

Ben: He was usually traveling, so he needed trusted regents to govern the Netherlands in his absence. His aunt Margaret of Austria ruled from nearby Mechelen. Later, his sister Mary of Hungary took over. And in 1531, the central government institutions are fixed in Brussels.
Anna: So that's the moment it becomes the capital of the Low Countries.
Ben: A role it has kept, in one form or another, ever since.
Anna: And it's a brilliant time intellectually, isn't it?

Ben: It is. In 1521, the great humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam, the most famous scholar in Europe, spends several months in Anderlecht, then a village outside Brussels. In a house you can visit today as a museum.
Anna: And Vesalius was a Brussels boy.

Ben: Andreas Vesalius, born in Brussels in 1514. He grows up to be a pioneer of modern anatomy. His groundbreaking book on the structure of the human body, published in 1543, corrected centuries of errors by examining real corpses.
Anna: Which I imagine did not go down well at dinner parties.
Ben: It went down very well in the history of medicine.
Anna: And Bruegel.

Ben: In 1563, Pieter Bruegel the Elder moves to Brussels. He marries the daughter of a well-known local artist, and in the remaining years of his short life, he paints some of his most famous scenes of peasant life and village feasts. He dies in Brussels in 1569, and he's buried in a church in the Marolles district.
Anna: Charles left another mark on the city, didn't he? A festival.

Ben: In 1549, there's a great festival in Brussels to present his son and heir, Philip, to the people of the Netherlands. The procession of guilds, nobles, and giant figures that winds through the streets is remembered today in a summer pageant called the Ommegang, held every year on the Grand Place.
Anna: Giant figures. I'm in.
Ben: It's a good one.
Anna: And then the abdication. That's such a scene.

Ben: It is. In October of 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace, Charles gives up his crown. Exhausted, ill, and weary of ruling, he announces he's handing the Netherlands over to Philip the Second. Witnesses record that he leaned on the shoulder of a young nobleman, the twenty-two-year-old William of Orange, and that the hall wept as he spoke.
Anna: And then he retired to a monastery.
Ben: Soon afterward he handed Spain over too. And yes, a monastery.
Anna: The most dramatic retirement in history. "I'm tired. Here is most of the world."
Ben: Take it, I'm going to lie down.
Anna: But the picture isn't all golden, is it? The Reformation arrives.

Ben: By now Brussels is a city of tens of thousands of people, a great center of government, art, and trade. But dark clouds are on the horizon. In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther challenged the Catholic Church, and the new Protestant ideas spread quickly through the Low Countries.
Anna: And the authorities reacted.

Ben: They did. And this part is not funny. In 1523, in the very center of Brussels, two young Augustinian monks, Henry Voes and Johannes van den Esschen, were burned at the stake on the Grand Place for refusing to renounce Luther's teachings.
Anna: Right here. In the square we've been joking about.
Ben: In the same square. They're considered the first martyrs of the Protestant Reformation. It was a sign of things to come.
Anna: And the new ruler?

Ben: Philip the Second is a devoutly Catholic king who lives in Spain and never really understands the Netherlands. He intends to stamp out heresy, enforce Catholic orthodoxy, and tighten royal control over the proud cities.
Anna: And the cities, with their ancient privileges, weren't going to take that lying down.
Ben: Not without a fight.
Anna: Okay. If someone wants to touch this chapter, where do they go?

Ben: The Place Royale, at the top of the hill. Under the square, an archaeological site called the Coudenberg lets you walk through the surviving cellars and streets of the old ducal palace. You'll be standing on the same ground where Charles the Fifth gave up the biggest empire in the world.
Anna: Stubbornness tally?
Ben: Philip the Second against every city in the Netherlands? I think we're about to jump.
Anna: Next time, revolt, execution, bombardment, and an elegant rebuilding.
Ben: A busy century and a half.

chapters.title: Revolt, Bombardment and Reinvention, 1568 to 1795
chapters.label: Chapter 4: Revolt, Bombardment and Reinvention, 1568 to 1795
paragraphs: Anna: So the Netherlands of the sixteenth century is a powder keg.

Ben: And the spark comes from Spain. Philip the Second sends troops and a harsh general, the Duke of Alba, to put down any sign of rebellion. Alba sets up a special court in Brussels that the locals call the Council of Blood. It tries thousands of people for heresy and treason.
Anna: That's a name that tells you what you need to know.

Ben: It is. And it catches some very prominent people. Two of the most important noblemen in the country, the Count of Egmont and the Count of Hoorn. Both were Catholics, loyal subjects, who had only asked the king to show some moderation.
Anna: And that was enough.

Ben: It made no difference. On the fifth of June, 1568, Egmont and Hoorn were beheaded on a scaffold in front of the town hall, on the Grand Place. The execution shocked the Netherlands. Egmont became a martyr, and in later centuries his story inspired a play by Goethe and an overture by Beethoven.
Anna: And politically?

Ben: It helped turn a local protest into a full-scale war. The Eighty Years' War. Long and bloody. In the north, the Dutch provinces under William of Orange eventually break away and form the Dutch Republic. In the south, the fighting seesaws.
Anna: And Brussels?

Ben: Brussels itself joins the rebels, and for a few years in the fifteen-seventies and fifteen-eighties it's run by a militant Calvinist regime. But in 1585, a Spanish army under the Duke of Parma retakes Brussels after a long siege.
Anna: Which had consequences beyond Brussels, I think.

Ben: Big ones. Many Protestants flee north, taking their skills and their money with them, and they help build the great Dutch cities of the seventeenth century. The southern Netherlands, including Brussels, stays under Spanish control and stays Catholic. A border has been drawn through the Low Countries, and it's roughly the border between Belgium and the Netherlands today.
Anna: Wow. So one execution on a square, and eventually a country border.
Ben: It's not that simple. But it's part of the story.
Anna: Okay. Did Brussels recover under the Spanish?

Ben: Slowly. From 1598 to 1621, the southern Netherlands are governed by a popular and cultured couple, the Archduke Albert and the Archduchess Isabella. And they make Brussels a glittering capital again. Their court attracts artists, including the great Peter Paul Rubens, who paints for them. A wave of baroque churches and palaces rises across the city.
Anna: That sounds like a golden age.
Ben: It looks like one. But Spain is in decline, and a new threat is rising in the south. France, under King Louis the Fourteenth, the Sun King.
Anna: Oh no. Not the Sun King.

Ben: Louis wants to push France's frontiers north and east, and the Spanish Netherlands lie right in his path. For decades, French armies march back and forth across the region, and the country suffers from endless war.
Anna: And then 1695.
Ben: The worst blow. August of 1695, during a conflict called the Nine Years' War. A French army of tens of thousands, under Marshal Villeroi, marches on Brussels. Not to capture it. To punish it.
Anna: Punish it? Why?
Ben: The French want to draw their enemies away from another city under siege, the fortress of Namur. And Brussels is rich and poorly defended, so it makes a tempting target.
Anna: What happened?

Ben: On the evening of the thirteenth of August, French cannons and mortars begin to fire red-hot shot and incendiary shells into the city. The bombardment goes on for about two days and nights. The spire of the town hall is the obvious target, because it's the tallest landmark, and the shells rain down around it.
Anna: And the streets were narrow, and medieval.

Ben: So the fires spread. When it's over, about a third of the buildings in Brussels have been destroyed or badly damaged. The Grand Place is in ruins. All that remains of the town hall is the shell of its stone walls, still standing, the spire miraculously intact.
Anna: That must have been terrible.

Ben: It was the most destructive event in the city's long history. A warning had been sent ahead, so the casualties were far fewer than they might have been. But the damage to property was staggering.
Anna: And now the part I love. Because what happens next is the best part of the story.

Ben: It is. The people of Brussels don't despair. They don't abandon the center. And they don't rebuild on a brand new plan. Instead, the guilds, which own the plots around the Grand Place, get to work. The city council and the governor require that every plan be submitted for approval. Which means the new buildings will fit together.
Anna: How long does it take?
Ben: Within about four years, the square has risen again. In stone, this time, rather than wood. Each guildhall is a showpiece, decked with gilded statues, carvings, and symbols of its trade.
Anna: Four years. I can't get a bathroom renovated in four years.
Ben: Well, they had a motivation.
Anna: Stubbornness tally. This one has to be three.
Ben: Or four. Rebuilding the whole square from ash, and making it prettier? That's stubbornness with style.
Anna: So you can read the trades on the facades.

Ben: Butchers, bakers, brewers, boatmen, cabinet-makers, painters. The house that belonged to the guild of the boatmen has a gable shaped like a ship's stern. Another crowned its roofline with a golden phoenix, rising from the flames, as a symbol of rebirth.
Anna: A phoenix. Subtle.

Ben: Very subtle. And all those different styles stand side by side. Gothic, baroque, and Louis the Fourteenth styles. The mixture shouldn't work. But it does. In 1998, UNESCO placed the Grand Place on its World Heritage list.
Anna: Okay. Into the eighteenth century.

Ben: The Spanish Habsburg line dies out, and after a long war of succession, the southern Netherlands pass to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1714. For the next eighty years, Brussels is the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and the country enjoys a long period of relative peace and prosperity.
Anna: Who's the beloved ruler?
Ben: Charles of Lorraine. A brother-in-law of the Empress Maria Theresa, who governs from 1744 to 1780. A genial, sociable man who loves hunting, science, and a good table.
Anna: So, the kind of governor you'd want to have dinner with.

Ben: I think so. And under him, the city gets a makeover. In the elegant neoclassical style. In 1731, the old Coudenberg Palace had been destroyed by a fire, and its ruins were cleared away and covered over. In its place, the authorities build a handsome new district. The Place Royale, a harmonious square lined with uniform facades, and a park laid out in geometric patterns, now the Parc de Bruxelles, with straight avenues and statues.
Anna: Which are among the most graceful spaces in the city today.

Ben: And they date from this period. But the old order is about to crack. The Enlightenment has arrived. And the Emperor Joseph the Second, who rules from Vienna starting in 1780, tries to modernize his lands at breakneck speed. Closing monasteries, reorganizing the courts, curbing the power of the church.
Anna: And people didn't like that.

Ben: Many in the Austrian Netherlands, who loved their ancient privileges, are furious. In 1789, the year the French Revolution begins, a rebellion breaks out in Brabant. It drives the Austrians out, and in January of 1790 a new state, the United Belgian States, is proclaimed.
Anna: The first time the word Belgian appears in a country's name.
Ben: But the republic quickly collapses in quarrels between conservatives and democrats. And the Austrians return in December of 1790.
Anna: And then France arrives.

Ben: Right. The Austrians don't last long. In 1792, French revolutionary armies march in, and after a few years of back and forth, they win a decisive victory in 1794. In 1795, France formally annexes the southern Netherlands, just as it did the Duchy of Luxembourg, which became the Department of the Forests.
Anna: And Brussels?

Ben: Brussels becomes the capital of a French department called the Dyle. The old privileges of the Joyous Entry are swept away. The old order is gone, and Brussels, like the rest of what will become Belgium, is now part of a new France.
Anna: Next time, Napoleon, Waterloo, and a night at the opera that changed the map of Europe.
Ben: Which sounds like a joke. But it isn't.

chapters.title: Napoleon, Waterloo and the Revolution of 1830
chapters.label: Chapter 5: Napoleon, Waterloo and the Revolution of 1830
paragraphs: Anna: The French years were short. But they changed Brussels more than almost any other period, didn't they?

Ben: They did. After the annexation of 1795, the revolutionary government sets about erasing the old order. Monasteries and convents are closed, and their lands and buildings sold off. Many medieval churches and abbeys, some of them centuries old, are demolished or turned into barracks, warehouses, and factories.
Anna: Ouch. And the guilds? The ones that rebuilt the Grand Place?
Ben: Abolished. Feudal privileges disappear. In their place, France introduces new laws, new weights and measures, and eventually the Napoleonic Code, which becomes the basis of Belgian civil law.
Anna: What did ordinary people think?
Ben: The most unpopular novelty was conscription. Young men from Brussels and its countryside were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came back.
Anna: Did Napoleon himself ever come to Brussels?

Ben: More than once. He used the royal estate at Laeken, on the northern edge of the city, as a residence. It would later become the home of the Belgian royal family. And even after his fall, the artist who had painted his coronation, Jacques-Louis David, chose Brussels as his place of exile. He lived there from 1816 until he died in 1825.
Anna: So the emperor's painter retires to Brussels.
Ben: It was a good place to be an exile. And the end of the empire came uncomfortably close.
Anna: How close?

Ben: Very close. In 1814, Napoleon is defeated and exiled, and the Congress of Vienna, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, redraws the map. The great powers decide France's northern neighbors need to be stronger. So they combine the old Austrian Netherlands with the Dutch Republic to create a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, under King William the First.
Anna: With two capitals, I seem to remember.
Ben: Government and parliament met alternately in The Hague and in Brussels.
Anna: That sounds exhausting. Imagine the moving vans.
Ben: Every session, off they go.
Anna: And then Napoleon comes back.

Ben: In March of 1815, he escapes from the island of Elba and returns to France. For about a hundred days, he rules again, and he marches north to strike the allied armies gathering in Belgium, under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Field Marshal Blücher.
Anna: And Brussels in June of 1815 is full of British officers and their families.

Ben: Allied officers and their families, yes. On the evening of the fifteenth of June, the Duchess of Richmond holds a famous ball in the city for Wellington and his officers. And in the middle of the evening, news arrives that Napoleon's army has crossed the border and is advancing.
Anna: And they just left?

Ben: Officers slip out of the ball, still in their dress uniforms, and march south to fight. The scene becomes so famous that the poet Lord Byron, who visits Brussels a year later, writes some of his best-known verses about that night of dancing and the sound of guns.
Anna: That's one way to leave a party.
Ben: It's the most famous early exit in history.
Anna: And three days later, Waterloo.

Ben: On the eighteenth of June, the decisive battle is fought at a village about fifteen kilometers south of Brussels. On that field, the Allied armies, with Wellington's British, Dutch, and Belgian troops and Blücher's Prussians, crush Napoleon's army and end his career for good.
Anna: And in Brussels, they could hear it.
Ben: People could hear the cannon. And in the days that followed, the city was filled with thousands of wounded soldiers, treated in houses, churches, and makeshift hospitals.
Anna: So then the new kingdom gets to work.

Ben: King William is a hardworking, practical ruler who promotes industry, canals, schools, and a modern economy. Brussels flourishes. The city gets a new opera house, the Théâtre de la Monnaie, which opens in 1819, on the site of the old royal mint.
Anna: But the kingdom had a flaw built in. Didn't it?

Ben: A basic one. The north is mostly Protestant and Dutch-speaking. The south is mostly Catholic, with a French-speaking upper class and a Dutch-speaking Flemish population. And the king favors the Dutch language and the north in appointments and taxation.
Anna: So who's angry?

Ben: French-speaking liberals resent his controls over the press and the schools. Catholics resent his interference in the church. And in 1828, these two groups, who normally dislike each other, join forces against the king. It's the beginning of the end.
Anna: Okay. A king so unpopular that liberals and Catholics team up. That's an achievement.
Ben: A very unusual one.
Anna: And then, the night at the opera.

Ben: On the twenty-fifth of August, 1830, there's a performance at the Monnaie of a popular French opera called The Mute Girl of Portici. It tells the story of a revolt in seventeenth-century Naples against Spanish rule, and it contains a stirring duet about love of country.
Anna: And the audience got carried away.

Ben: As the singers reach that number, the audience is swept up. They pour out of the theater into the streets, shouting, and join crowds that are already angry about food prices and unemployment. Over the next days, mobs attack the houses of unpopular officials and the offices of a pro-government newspaper. Similar riots break out in other towns.
Anna: So a revolution started because of a song.
Ben: A song, and food prices, and a lot of resentment. But, yes. The song lit the match.
Anna: Was it meant to be a revolution?

Ben: At first it was a protest, and its leaders wanted autonomy, not independence. But King William hesitates, then sends troops under his son, Prince Frederick, to restore order. On the twenty-third of September, some ten thousand Dutch soldiers enter Brussels through the gates on the upper side of the city and try to push down the hill toward the old center.
Anna: And who stopped them?

Ben: A ragged force of volunteers. Workers, students, craftsmen, and men from other towns, including Liège, who had come to help. For four days, from the twenty-third to the twenty-sixth of September, the fighting rages around the Royal Park, in the streets, from house to house, over barricades made of paving stones, carts, and furniture. By the end of the fourth night, the Dutch have pulled back.
Anna: Stubbornness tally?
Ben: Volunteers with paving stones beating a trained army? That's five. At least.
Anna: Five. I'm writing it down.

Ben: A provisional government has already taken control in Brussels. And on the fourth of October, it declares Belgium independent. A National Congress is elected, and in February of 1831 it adopts a constitution that's among the most liberal in Europe. Guarantees of freedom of the press, of religion, and of association, and a king with limited powers.
Anna: Who did they pick as king?

Ben: The Congress chooses Brussels as the capital, and it needs a king acceptable to the great powers. After much negotiation, they pick a German prince, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, a widower of the British royal family and an uncle to the future Queen Victoria.
Anna: Imported king. Okay.

Ben: And the date everyone in Belgium knows. On the twenty-first of July, 1831, Leopold stands on the steps of a church on the Place Royale and swears an oath to the constitution. That day, July twenty-first, is still Belgium's National Day.
Anna: But the Dutch weren't ready to accept it.

Ben: No. A few weeks later, in August of 1831, the Dutch army invades, in what's called the Ten Days' Campaign. A French army has to march in to save Belgium. It takes years of negotiation before the Dutch accept the loss.
Anna: And it was settled in 1839.

Ben: By a treaty signed in London that finally confirms Belgium's independence, and guarantees the new country's perpetual neutrality, under the protection of the great powers. The same treaty, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, splits the old duchy of Luxembourg in two, and hands its western half, including the town of Bastogne, to Belgium.
Anna: Two places to visit for this chapter?

Ben: At the Place des Martyrs, a quiet neoclassical square near the city center, a monument and a crypt honor the fighters who died in the September days of 1830. And in the Parc de Bruxelles, the same park where the Dutch troops fought their way in and lost, you can walk among the trees and statues where the battle for Belgian independence was won.
Anna: Next, the capital of a new kingdom grows into a modern metropolis.
Ben: And the king who rules it from 1865 turns it into a showcase. Financed, in part, by a colony of terrible cruelty.

chapters.title: Leopold's Capital, the Belle Époque and the Congo, 1831 to 1914
chapters.label: Chapter 6: Leopold's Capital, the Belle Époque and the Congo, 1831 to 1914
paragraphs: Anna: The new Belgium turned out to be a remarkable success story. Didn't it?

Ben: And Brussels is its showcase. Belgium is the first country on the European continent to undergo an industrial revolution, following the example of Britain. Coal and iron in the south, textiles in Flanders, and a good banking system. Real wealth.
Anna: And the railways.

Ben: In 1835, the first railway on the continent opens, between Brussels and the nearby city of Mechelen. And within a few years, the country has a dense network of tracks, with Brussels at the center. The population grows fast, and the capital swells with civil servants, bankers, merchants, and workers.
Anna: It also became a refuge for ideas.

Ben: In 1834, liberal Brussels founds a new university, the Free University of Brussels, dedicated to free inquiry, independent of both state and church. And because the new Belgian constitution is so liberal, the city attracts writers, thinkers, and political refugees from across Europe.
Anna: Baudelaire, Victor Hugo.

Ben: Charles Baudelaire stayed there. Victor Hugo lived for a time on the Grand Place. And in 1873, in a Brussels hotel room, the poet Paul Verlaine shot and wounded his young lover, the poet Arthur Rimbaud. Then went to jail in Belgium.
Anna: Okay, that is dramatic. I was not expecting that.
Ben: Poets. What can you do.
Anna: But one exile, above all, left a mark.

Ben: In 1845, the young German philosopher Karl Marx, expelled from France, comes to Brussels with his wife and family, and he stays until 1848. With his friend Friedrich Engels, he writes a pamphlet in Brussels, in the winter of 1847 and 1848, called the Manifesto of the Communist Party.
Anna: Published elsewhere, though.
Ben: In London, in February of 1848. And Marx is expelled from Belgium a few weeks later. The pamphlet went on to shape the history of the twentieth century.
Anna: And that's one very productive winter.
Ben: Well, he did get thrown out.
Anna: Meanwhile, the river had become a problem.

Ben: A disaster. The Senne, which made Brussels possible, runs through the middle of the city, an open sewer, choked with refuse, and it floods regularly. It carries cholera. And the stench in summer is notorious.
Anna: So they buried it.

Ben: In the eighteen-sixties, the city's reforming mayor, Jules Anspach, decides to bury it. Between 1867 and 1871, the river is covered with a long brick vault. And above it, the city builds a grand new avenue lined with elegant buildings, modeled on the Paris boulevards of Baron Haussmann.
Anna: The Boulevard Anspach.

Ben: Named after the mayor who built it. The river is still there today, flowing in a tunnel beneath the city. They also build a stock exchange, the Bourse, in the heart of the new district, and the whole center is transformed.
Anna: So that's the river I said sounded impossible in the Welcome.
Ben: That's the river. See? We got there.
Anna: We got there. It sounds like a triumph.
Ben: It was an enormous achievement. And also a loss. Hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods were torn down, and whole communities were uprooted.
Anna: And there was another giant project, the Palace of Justice.

Ben: In 1866, work begins on a vast new Palace of Justice, designed by the architect Joseph Poelaert, on a hill above the Marolles. When it's finished in 1883, it's often described as the largest building constructed anywhere in the nineteenth century. A colossal mass of columns, domes, and staircases that dwarfs the city around it.
Anna: I bet the neighbors weren't thrilled.
Ben: To build it, the authorities flattened part of the old working-class Marolles district. Locals have grumbled about it ever since.
Anna: Fair enough. Now, we get to Leopold the Second.

Ben: In 1865, Leopold the First dies, and his son takes the throne as Leopold the Second. He reigns for forty-four years, and he's ambitious in a way his father wasn't. He feels his country is too small, and he dreams of an empire. The great European powers are carving up Africa, and Leopold wants a piece of it.
Anna: And this is a hard part of the story.

Ben: It is. At a conference in Berlin in 1884 and 1885, the great powers recognize Leopold as the ruler of a vast territory in central Africa, about eighty times the size of Belgium. It was not a Belgian colony. It was the king's personal property, called the Congo Free State.
Anna: And what followed?

Ben: One of the worst atrocities of the colonial era. Leopold's agents forced villagers to collect rubber and ivory, under a system of terror. Hostages were taken, villages burned, and people who failed to meet quotas were beaten, mutilated, or killed. Historians estimate that millions of Congolese died from violence, starvation, and disease during these years, although the exact numbers are debated.
Anna: How did the world find out?

Ben: Reports by missionaries, journalists, and the British diplomat Roger Casement, and a campaign led by the journalist Edmund Morel, eventually produced an international outcry. In 1908, under heavy pressure, the Belgian state took over the colony from the king, and it became the Belgian Congo, which Belgium ruled until 1960.
Anna: And that money ended up in Brussels.

Ben: Partly. The money that Leopold drew from the Congo went partly into building, and into impressing. He built the great Cinquantenaire park and its triumphal arch, to commemorate fifty years of Belgian independence. He built wide avenues, such as Avenue Louise, and monuments, and royal greenhouses at Laeken, and a huge museum of Central Africa in the suburb of Tervuren.
Anna: And the world's fair.

Ben: For the Brussels world's fair of 1897, he organized a colonial exhibition in which Congolese people were put on display in a replica village. The grand showpiece of Belgium's capital had been paid for, in part, by a terrible human cost. And that's a story Brussels has been grappling with ever since.
Anna: Meanwhile, something very different was happening in architecture.

Ben: In the eighteen-nineties, a group of young architects, led by Victor Horta, create a new style that rejects the heavy historical imitations of the time. They use iron, glass, and sweeping curves inspired by plants and flowers, in what comes to be known as Art Nouveau, or the new art.
Anna: The Tassel house.

Ben: In 1893 and 1894, Horta builds a townhouse for a professor named Emile Tassel, in which iron columns shaped like stems, and stairs twining like vines, flow through the whole house, with light pouring in from above. It's widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.
Anna: Others followed.

Ben: Paul Hankar and Henry van de Velde, among others. The style spreads to Paris, Vienna, and Barcelona. But it started in Brussels. Several of Horta's townhouses are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Anna: So by 1900, what kind of city is Brussels?

Ben: A prosperous, confident metropolis of more than half a million people in its wider urban area. A city of cafés, department stores, glass-roofed shopping arcades, and boulevards. And a French-speaking city. At the time of independence, a large share of ordinary Brusselers spoke a Dutch dialect, but French was the language of government, business, education, and prestige. And over the nineteenth century, it steadily took over.
Anna: And today it's officially bilingual.
Ben: And the question of language, which was just beginning to stir in the late nineteenth century, will return again and again in the story of modern Belgium.
Anna: But the fates of small countries rest on the decisions of large ones.

Ben: The guarantee of Belgian neutrality, signed in 1839, is now seventy-five years old. And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushes Europe toward war. Germany's plan to defeat France calls for an army to march through neutral Belgium.
Anna: If someone wants to see this chapter in stone?

Ben: Walk the Boulevard Anspach and look at the grand facades of the Bourse. Visit the Palace of Justice, whose terrace has a famous view over the whole city. And if you have time for one museum, make it the Horta Museum in Saint-Gilles, the house where the architect lived and worked.
Anna: Next, two wars, a world's fair with a giant atom, and a city that becomes the capital of Europe.
Ben: A lot to cover. Let's go.

chapters.title: Two Wars, Expo 58 and the Capital of Europe, 1914 to 1989
chapters.label: Chapter 7: Two Wars, Expo 58 and the Capital of Europe, 1914 to 1989
paragraphs: Anna: We left off in the summer of 1914, with Germany's plan requiring an army to march through Belgium.

Ben: On the fourth of August, 1914, German troops cross into Belgium. The German government had offered the Belgians a deal. Let our army pass through your country to attack France, and you will be spared. King Albert the First refuses. The Belgians, he says, will defend their independence.
Anna: And the neutrality treaty?
Ben: Germany's chancellor dismisses the treaty that Germany itself had signed, the treaty of 1839, as nothing more than a scrap of paper. Britain, which had guaranteed it, declares war.
Anna: How did Brussels fare?

Ben: The Belgian army fights hard, and the German advance is slowed, but it can't be stopped. On the twentieth of August, German troops march into Brussels, which had been declared an open city to spare it from destruction. The occupation lasts more than four years. Curfews, requisitions, food shortages, and harsh punishments.
Anna: And the king?
Ben: King Albert and what's left of the Belgian army hold a narrow strip of land in the far west of the country, along the river Yser, for the entire war.
Anna: The occupation gave Brussels one of its best-known heroines, Edith Cavell.

Ben: An English nurse who had come to Brussels in 1907 to run a training school for nurses. When the war began, she and a network of Belgian and French helpers started hiding Allied soldiers who had been cut off behind enemy lines, and guiding them across the border into the neutral Netherlands. She's believed to have helped about two hundred men escape.
Anna: And she was caught.

Ben: In August of 1915, the Germans arrest her. She openly admits what she has done. She's tried, sentenced to death, and on the twelfth of October, 1915, shot by a firing squad, in the early morning, at a shooting range in the Brussels suburb of Schaerbeek. Her execution causes an outcry around the world.
Anna: What she said the night before is remembered.
Ben: She told a chaplain that patriotism was not enough, and that she must have no hatred or bitterness toward anyone.
Anna: When does the war end for Brussels?

Ben: In November of 1918. On the twenty-second of that month, King Albert rides into a liberated Brussels. And the next two decades are a time of recovery and glamor. Art Deco buildings appear across the city. The great Palais des Beaux-Arts, designed by Victor Horta, opens in 1928.
Anna: And the science.

Ben: In 1927, the fifth Solvay Conference gathers in Brussels. The leading scientists of the age, including Einstein, Bohr, Marie Curie, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger, debate the strange new science of quantum mechanics.
Anna: I would pay a lot to be a fly on that wall.
Ben: A very confused fly.
Anna: And the arts?

Ben: The surrealist painter René Magritte lives and works in the city. And a young Brussels cartoonist named Georges Remi, who signs his work Hergé, publishes the first adventure of a young reporter with a quiff of red hair in a children's supplement of a newspaper, in January of 1929.
Anna: Tintin!
Ben: Belgium's comic strip tradition, which will make Brussels a world capital of the form, has begun.
Anna: Then the Germans came again.

Ben: On the tenth of May, 1940, they invade Belgium. King Leopold the Third, who had succeeded his father Albert, surrenders the army eighteen days later, against the wishes of his government, which goes into exile in London. The king stays in Belgium as a prisoner. That decision will split the country for years afterward.
Anna: What was the occupation like?

Ben: Four years. Resistance networks spring up, helping Allied airmen escape, hiding Jewish children, and publishing underground newspapers. But the occupation was brutal. Tens of thousands of Belgians were sent to forced labor in Germany. And about twenty-five thousand Jews, most of them from Brussels and Antwerp, were deported to the death camps through a transit camp in the city of Mechelen.
Anna: How many survived?
Ben: Only a small fraction. And many Belgian families risked their lives hiding Jewish neighbors.
Anna: And liberation?

Ben: On the third of September, 1944, British tanks of the Guards Armoured Division roll into Brussels to scenes of overwhelming joy. Compared to many other European cities, Brussels comes through the war relatively unscathed. Its buildings are mostly intact, and its position in the center of Western Europe is about to become its destiny.
Anna: But first, there was the question of the king.

Ben: After the war, many Belgians, especially in Wallonia and in Brussels, want to punish Leopold the Third for his surrender and for some of his actions during the occupation. Others, mostly in Catholic Flanders, defend him. In 1950, a referendum shows that a majority of Belgians want him back, but the split follows the language line almost perfectly. Strong support in Flanders, and a majority against him in Wallonia and in Brussels.
Anna: And it turned violent.
Ben: Strikes, riots, and violence follow. In 1951, Leopold abdicates in favor of his twenty-year-old son, Baudouin, to calm the country. It's an early sign of how deeply the language divide can cut.
Anna: Meanwhile Belgium changed course on neutrality.

Ben: It becomes a founding member of NATO in 1949 and of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951. And a Belgian socialist politician, Paul-Henri Spaak, becomes one of the leading architects of European unity. In 1955 and 1956, Spaak chairs the committee that writes the report that leads to the Treaties of Rome of 1957, creating the European Economic Community, the ancestor of today's European Union.
Anna: And that's how Brussels got the Commission.
Ben: When the new community needs a home for its executive, the Commission, it's set up in Brussels in 1958, intended as a temporary arrangement.
Anna: Temporary.
Ben: It never left.
Anna: Of course it didn't. The most permanent temporary arrangement in history. And that same year, there was the world's fair.

Ben: Expo 58, the first world's fair after the Second World War, opens in April on the Heysel plateau, on the northern edge of the city. It's meant to show a confident new age of science and peace. The pavilions of the United States and the Soviet Union stand across from each other, in the middle of the Cold War.
Anna: And the Atomium.

Ben: The most striking structure of all. A giant model of an iron crystal, magnified about a hundred and sixty-five billion times, made of nine shining steel spheres linked by tubes, rising a hundred and two meters into the air.
Anna: A hundred and sixty-five billion times. Imagine being the person who had to say that out loud in the meeting.
Ben: It was supposed to be demolished after the fair. But Brusselers loved it too much. It's now the most recognizable symbol of the city.
Anna: Stubbornness tally?
Ben: Refusing to tear down a giant atom? I'd say six.
Anna: Six. Then 1960, and the end of an empire.

Ben: On the thirtieth of June, 1960, the Belgian Congo becomes independent. At the ceremony, King Baudouin praises Belgium's colonial work, and Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the new country, gives an angry reply about the humiliations and brutality of colonial rule.
Anna: And what happened to Lumumba?

Ben: Within months, the Congo collapses into crisis, and in January of 1961, Lumumba is murdered. Decades later, a Belgian parliamentary commission concluded that Belgian officials bore a moral responsibility for his death, and the Belgian government apologized in 2002. In 2022, Belgium returned a tooth, a relic of his remains, to his family.
Anna: The nineteen-sixties are when Brussels starts to look like the capital of Europe.

Ben: In 1967, NATO moves its political headquarters from Paris to Brussels, after the French president, Charles de Gaulle, withdraws France from the alliance's military command. The European Commission moves into a huge, star-shaped office building called the Berlaymont, finished in 1967. And a whole district of offices spreads across the eastern side of the city, around the Rue de la Loi.
Anna: But the building boom had a cost.

Ben: In the nineteen-sixties and seventies, developers and the government tore down entire neighborhoods and many fine old buildings to make room for offices, highways, and towers. One of the most painful losses was Victor Horta's Maison du Peuple, a masterpiece of Art Nouveau, demolished in 1965 despite protests.
Anna: And there's a word for it.

Ben: Bruxellisation. The careless, speculative destruction of a historic city. By the late nineteen-sixties, citizens' groups fight back and begin to protect the old districts. The metro opens in 1976, and the city starts, slowly, to be more careful with its past.
Anna: And all the while, language politics was getting hotter.

Ben: In 1962 and 1963, Belgium fixes a border between its Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, and Brussels is left as a bilingual island inside Flemish territory. In 1968, the great Catholic university in Leuven splits in two, along language lines.
Anna: And the constitution followed.

Ben: Over the next two decades, a series of constitutional reforms gradually turns Belgium from a centralized country into a federation of regions and language communities. In 1989, the third region takes shape. The Brussels-Capital Region, made up of nineteen municipalities, officially bilingual. And in 1993, Belgium formally becomes a federal state.
Anna: How would someone see this chapter?

Ben: Take the metro to Schuman station. Walk out and you'll face the Berlaymont, with its star-shaped wings, the headquarters of the European Commission. Nearby is the Cinquantenaire park, where Leopold the Second's arch stands. And if you have time for a trip to the north end of the city, the Atomium is still there, with a view from the top sphere over the whole region.
Anna: In the final chapter, we come to the Brussels of today.
Ben: Which is a lot to take in.

chapters.title: Brussels Today, 1989 to 2026
chapters.label: Chapter 8: Brussels Today, 1989 to 2026
paragraphs: Anna: So, Ben. After all that, what is Brussels now?
Ben: On paper, the Brussels-Capital Region. Nineteen municipalities, about one and a quarter million people.
Anna: And the Grand Place?
Ben: Is in the City of Brussels. Which is only one of those nineteen.
Anna: So when someone says Brussels, they could mean three different things.
Ben: At least three.
Anna: The other eighteen have their own mayors and councils, don't they?

Ben: And names that Brusselers use as proudly as the name of the city itself. Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, Schaerbeek, Anderlecht, Molenbeek, Uccle, and more. The region is the capital of Belgium. It's the capital of the Flemish Community and of the French Community. And, informally but unmistakably, the capital of Europe.
Anna: Four capitals in one. That's a lot of hats.
Ben: And one very small head.
Anna: Okay, but the governance. Explain it to me like I'm five.

Ben: Belgium is a federation of three regions and three language communities, layered on top of each other. Brussels sits where they all overlap. The regional parliament has a French-speaking group and a Dutch-speaking group, and the government has to include members of both.
Anna: Which sounds like a clever safeguard.
Ben: It is. It also makes things slow.
Anna: Very slow, recently.
Ben: After regional elections in June of 2024, the parties couldn't agree on a coalition. It took 613 days. More than twenty months.
Anna: Six hundred and thirteen days.

Ben: A seven-party government finally took office in February of 2026, led by a French-speaking liberal, Boris Dilliès. The parties had to promise to balance a budget that was deeply in deficit, and to merge various regional agencies.
Anna: So for almost two years, the capital of Europe ran on a caretaker government.
Ben: It did.
Anna: Stubbornness tally. I think we have to.
Ben: Twenty months without a government, and the trams still ran? I'd say seven.
Anna: Seven. And that's just the region.

Ben: At the national level, the story was similar. After elections in June of 2024, it took more than two hundred thirty days to form a federal government. In February of 2025, Bart De Wever was sworn in as prime minister by King Philippe, in a five-party coalition.
Anna: And De Wever is a Flemish nationalist.
Ben: Who had long dreamed of a more independent Flanders. The first Flemish nationalist to lead the Belgian government.
Anna: Running the country he'd like to split.
Ben: The kind of irony Belgian history delivers on a regular basis.
Anna: And the king?
Ben: Philippe, who succeeded his father Albert the Second in 2013. The seventh king of the Belgians.
Anna: Okay. Governments come and go. Who actually lives here?
Ben: On the first of January, 2025, the region counted about one million, two hundred fifty-six thousand people. A bit over thirty-seven percent of them held a foreign passport.
Anna: And that doesn't count the Belgians with a foreign background.
Ben: No. Residents come from about a hundred and eighty-three different nationalities.
Anna: A hundred and eighty-three. There are only a hundred and ninety-some countries.
Ben: So almost the whole world is represented in one very small region.
Anna: Who are the biggest groups?
Ben: The largest foreign group is French. Then Romanians and Italians, then Spaniards and Moroccans. Brussels also has an important Congolese community, centered on a district called Matongé.
Anna: And I read something surprising about the population.
Ben: In 2025, for the first time since the mid-nineteen-nineties, it stopped growing.
Anna: And a lot of those foreign residents work for the institutions.

Ben: The European Commission, the Council of the European Union, and parts of the European Parliament all have their seats here, around the Schuman roundabout and the Rue de la Loi. NATO's headquarters, a striking new complex in the north of the city, opened in 2018.
Anna: How many people work for international institutions?

Ben: By the most recent count, more than fifty thousand in the region. Around them are embassies, trade associations, law firms, think tanks, and the lobbyists who try to influence the laws of the European Union.
Anna: So a city that once lived by cloth and tapestries.
Ben: Now lives largely by words and rules.
Anna: Which is still a kind of weaving, if you think about it.
Ben: With a lot more meetings.
Anna: It hasn't all been easy, though. The city has had dark days.

Ben: It has. In November of 2015, after the terror attacks in Paris, some of whose planners had lived in the Brussels district of Molenbeek, the city went into a security lockdown that lasted days. Soldiers on the streets, the metro closed.
Anna: And then, in March.
Ben: On the eighteenth of March, 2016, police captured one of the key suspects, Salah Abdeslam, in Molenbeek. Four days later, on the morning of the twenty-second, three suicide bombers struck.
Anna: Where?

Ben: Two bombs exploded in the departure hall of Brussels Airport at Zaventem. An hour later, a third went off on a metro train leaving Maalbeek station, in the heart of the European Quarter, among the offices of the institutions.
Anna: How many people were killed?
Ben: Thirty-two people, not counting the attackers. More than three hundred were injured. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility.
Anna: And the city remembers.
Ben: Every year since, the city has marked the anniversary. And the little statue of the Manneken Pis has been dressed in a firefighter's uniform to honor the rescuers.
Anna: And yet life goes on, and the city keeps reinventing itself.

Ben: It does. In 2015, the central boulevards around the Bourse were closed to cars, creating one of the largest pedestrian zones in Europe. The old Boulevard Anspach, built over the buried Senne, became a place to walk and sit.
Anna: The river we buried.
Ben: Now with a sidewalk café on top.
Anna: And the rest of the city?
Ben: A low-emission zone limits older cars. And a traffic plan called Good Move, which reduces through traffic in residential neighborhoods, has been bitterly debated.
Anna: Like most such efforts.
Ben: Brussels is trying to become a city for people rather than just for commuters. And, like most such efforts, it's argued over fiercely.
Anna: Let's turn to the fun. Because the culture is as eclectic as the population.

Ben: Brussels is the capital of the comic strip. There are dozens of giant murals of comic heroes painted on building walls across the city, a museum devoted to the art form, and a tradition that gave the world Tintin and the Smurfs.
Anna: Okay, I would like to do a comic-strip wall walk right now.
Ben: It exists. You can.
Anna: And beer and chocolate.

Ben: In 2016, UNESCO recognized Belgian beer culture as part of the world's cultural heritage.
