And according to tradition, the praline, the filled chocolate, was invented in 1912 by a Brussels chocolatier named Jean Neuhaus, in the elegant glass-roofed Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert. One of the oldest covered shopping arcades in Europe.
Anna: Waffles. Fries. Mussels.
Ben: And a small green vegetable that carries the city's name.
Anna: The Brussels sprout.
Ben: Which was grown in the area around the city centuries ago.
Anna: The vegetable everyone loves to hate, named after the city that loves everything.
Ben: I'd say that's unfair to the sprout.
Anna: Fair. Now, the city is also reckoning with its past.

Ben: Yes. The Royal Museum for Central Africa, in Tervuren, which Leopold the Second built as a showcase of his colony, was closed for years. It reopened in 2018 after a major renovation that tried to confront its colonial origins.
Anna: And the statues.
Ben: In 2020, during worldwide protests against racism, statues of Leopold the Second in Belgium were defaced, and some were removed.
Anna: And there was a royal apology.

Ben: A parliamentary commission examined Belgium's colonial past. In 2022, King Philippe visited the Democratic Republic of the Congo and expressed deep regret for the suffering caused by colonial rule. The debate is ongoing, and it will shape how the city understands itself in the years ahead.
Anna: Okay. If you had to pick one symbol for Brussels, what would it be?
Ben: Not a lion, or a saint, or a king.
Anna: A dog.
Ben: A dog. In the local dialect, a zinneke is a mongrel. A mixed-breed street dog that belongs to no one breed.
Anna: And Brusselers say it with affection.

Ben: For their city. A place of mixed languages, mixed origins, and mixed styles, where no one is quite purebred. There's a small bronze statue of a dog, relieving itself against a post, on a street in the old center. And a colorful parade, held every two years, that celebrates the zinneke spirit.
Anna: A dog that is also, let's be honest, a bit rude.
Ben: A very Brussels dog.
Anna: All right. Let's step back and look at the whole journey.
Ben: It began as a settlement in a marsh, with a chapel on an island. It became a market town on the road between Flanders and Cologne, and a ducal capital. Its guilds won a seat at the table.
Anna: It became the capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, the home of great painters and weavers.
Ben: It was nearly erased in 1695, and rebuilt in four years into one of the most beautiful squares in the world.
Anna: It passed from Spain to Austria to France to the Dutch.
Ben: And in 1830, after a night at the opera and four days of street fighting, it became the capital of a new nation.
Anna: It grew rich under Leopold, on the profits of an empire built on terrible cruelty.
Ben: It was occupied twice, and spared the worst of two world wars. And then, almost by accident, it became the working capital of a united Europe.
Anna: Through all of it, Brussels has been a place where different peoples and languages meet, argue, trade, and build together.
Ben: It has never had one identity.
Anna: And perhaps that is its identity.
Ben: Which brings us to the final stubbornness tally.
Anna: Final count. Eight.
Ben: Eight. For a city that survived fire, bombardment, two occupations, and a government that took twenty months to form. And somehow still serves excellent fries.
Anna: That is the story of Brussels. Thank you for listening.
Ben: And enjoy the city.

sources.title: Non-Belgian EU nationals in Brussels (Brussels Times)

episodes.title: Walking Antwerp's Old Town
episodes.blurb: A stop-by-stop walk from the river and Het Steen through the Grote Markt and the cathedral to the printing museum and the Rubens House. Allow about two hours with pauses.
hints: From the river dock, walk along the waterfront to the small stone fortress at the Steenplein. The giant statue stands by the entrance bridge.
Leave the Steen by the street that runs straight inland, the Suikerrui. It opens into the Grote Markt after a few minutes, with the town hall on your left as you enter.
From the Grote Markt, keep the cathedral tower in front of you. It rises over the rooftops, and the short streets lead straight to the church and the Handschoenmarkt.
Leave the cathedral square to the south and a little west, through the lanes toward the Vrijdagmarkt. Signs for the Plantin-Moretus Museum help.
The museum is on the Vrijdagmarkt itself. For the last stop, head east on foot toward the Meir shopping street. The Rubens House is just off it, on the Wapper.
episodes.notes: A walking tour of the old center of Antwerp, about two kilometers in all, in six stops. It is planned for a river cruise day: you start at the river dock and end near the Rubens House, with an easy walk back to the ship. Each chapter is one stop, so you can pause between them, and the audio carries on as you walk. Streets and landmarks are described loosely, and the stop positions on the map are approximate, good to about 50 meters at best, so keep a map open as well. If a guided tour fills part of your morning, you can do this walk in the afternoon, or do only the stops you have time for. If it rains, the cathedral, the Plantin-Moretus Museum and the Rubens House are all indoors. At the time of writing, the main artist's residence section of the Rubens House is closed for renovation, so check what is open before you go. Opening hours, queues and any construction change often, so check them on the day.

chapters.title: Welcome and how this works
chapters.label: Welcome and how this works
paragraphs: Anna: Hello, and welcome to a walk. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. This is a walking tour of old Antwerp, in six stops.
Anna: Starting at the river, where your ship is.
Ben: And ending near the home of the most famous painter this city ever had.
Anna: And you're not sitting down.
Ben: You're out on the street, with headphones. Each chapter is one stop. We tell you where you are, what you're looking at, and the story behind it. Then we point you toward the next one.
Anna: And if I want to stand there and stare?
Ben: Press pause. Stare as long as you like. The tour waits for you.
Anna: What do I need?
Ben: Comfortable shoes, because it's cobblestones. Something for the rain, because you might need it. And a map on your phone, because we describe where things are, but we'd rather you not get lost.
Anna: And what if the weather is bad?
Ben: Three of the stops are indoors. The cathedral, the printing museum, and the Rubens House. We'll flag them as we go.
Anna: Right. And I'll make a bet with you, right now. Before this walk is over, we will see more than one giant hand.
Ben: Is that a bet?
Anna: It's a bet. I'm keeping a hand tally.
Ben: Fine. Then let's find the first one. Stand by the river, near the little stone fortress, and press play when you're ready.

chapters.title: Stop 1: Het Steen and the Scheldt riverfront
chapters.label: Stop 1: Het Steen and the Scheldt riverfront
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Where are we?
Ben: On the riverbank, beside the Scheldt. The wide brown river in front of you is the reason this city exists.
Anna: It's not very blue.
Ben: It's a working river. Blue is not its job.
Anna: And that small stone building behind us?
Ben: That's Het Steen. The name means, roughly, the Stone. Look at the gateway, the arched part by the bridge. It was built between 1200 and 1225.
Anna: So it's older than almost everything we'll see today.
Ben: Older than the town hall, older than the cathedral's tower, older than the printing houses. People say it's the oldest building in Antwerp. We'll say by some counts.
Anna: Why the hedge?

Ben: Because the whole site is older than the gateway. There was a settlement and a fortification here by the 9th century. The gateway is what survives of a bigger castle of the Dukes of Brabant. The rest was torn down in the 19th century.
Anna: So it's the one piece left.
Ben: The front door. Then around 1520 it was rebuilt under Emperor Charles V, and that's when the name Het Steen took hold.
Anna: And what did they use it for?
Ben: Many things. A place for the city's aldermen and a court of justice. And from 1303 to 1827, a prison.
Anna: That's over 500 years of prison.

Ben: Yes. Then an archaeology museum from 1890, and a maritime museum annex from 1952. After a big renovation that finished in October 2021, it reopened as a visitor center, with a modern concrete extension.
Anna: Can we go in?
Ben: It's worth checking. It works as a gateway for visitors now. But for this walk, the outside is enough.
Anna: Now look at the bridge. There's a statue.
Ben: A giant. That's Lange Wapper.
Anna: Is that the giant from the legend?
Ben: Not quite. Different giant. Lange Wapper is a figure from local folklore who is said to have terrorized the medieval townspeople. He's not the one with the toll.
Anna: There's more than one giant?
Ben: It's a big city. Now, the giant with the toll. This is where the city's name story starts.
Anna: The hand.
Ben: The hand. The legend says a giant called Druoon Antigoon lived by the Scheldt, right about here. Any ship that wanted to pass had to pay a toll.
Anna: And if you didn't pay?
Ben: He cut off your hand.
Anna: Charming man.
Ben: Then a hero named Brabo came along. He fought the giant, cut off his hand, and threw it into the river.
Anna: That's one hand, in the river. My tally says one.
Ben: Hold the tally. The story says that's how the city got its name. Hand throwing. Whether that's true, nobody knows. But the city likes the story so much that it keeps telling it.
Anna: A city founded on a throw.
Ben: A good throw.
Anna: And the river itself. How big a deal was it?
Ben: Enormous. About 1500, the channel to the old trading city of Bruges silted up. Foreign merchants moved their trading houses here, because Antwerp's river was deep.
Anna: So this spot was the front door of a trade empire.
Ben: For a while. By 1560, Antwerp was the second-largest city in Europe north of the Alps.
Anna: And then?
Ben: And then came the Spanish Fury in 1576, a siege in 1585, and in 1648 the river itself was closed to shipping by a treaty. We'll hear about the Fury in a minute, at the town hall.
Anna: What happened to the river afterward?
Ben: Napoleon eased the restrictions and built docks. The last restriction ended in 1863. Today Antwerp is one of the major seaports in the world, which is a nice kind of revenge.
Anna: So the river made it, broke it, and made it again.
Ben: That's the whole city in one sentence.
Anna: Okay. Time to pause. Look at the river. Look at the gateway. Find the giant by the bridge.

Ben: When you're ready, here is the way on. Turn your back to the water and look for the street that runs straight inland from the square, the Suikerrui. It leads toward the church towers. A few minutes' walk, a little uphill, and it opens into the main square.
Anna: Is that the one with the fountain?
Ben: It is. And the fountain has Brabo on top, holding up something.
Anna: Oh no. Is it the hand?
Ben: We'll get there.

chapters.title: Stop 2: The Grote Markt, with the town hall and the Brabo fountain
chapters.label: Stop 2: The Grote Markt, with the town hall and the Brabo fountain
paragraphs: Anna: And we've arrived. Wow. That's a lot of gold.
Ben: That's the Grote Markt, the Great Market. The main square of the old city.
Anna: It's a bit of a stage set.
Ben: In a good way. Turn around slowly. On one side, the town hall. On the other sides, tall narrow houses, with gilded statues on the roofs. Those are guild houses.
Anna: Guild houses. So, clubs for craftsmen.
Ben: Associations for trades. Each one wanted a grand house on the best square. It was a way of showing off.
Anna: So it's the original who-has-the-nicest-front-door contest.
Ben: Basically.
Anna: Now the big building. The town hall. When was that built?
Ben: It was inaugurated in 1565. It's a Renaissance building, designed by Cornelis Floris and Willem van den Broeck.
Anna: And it's still standing.
Ben: It is, but not without trouble. And this is the part where we stop joking.
Anna: Understood.
Ben: In November 1576, Spanish troops sacked Antwerp. It's known as the Spanish Fury. About 6,000 people were killed and about 800 houses burned.
Anna: And the town hall?
Ben: The courtyard of the town hall had been used as an arsenal, and the fire in the sack gutted the building. It was rebuilt in its original style in the years that followed.
Anna: That's hard to imagine, standing here.
Ben: Most of what you see around you was either built before that, rebuilt after it, or both. The city lost something that day it never fully got back.
Anna: And then it got worse.

Ben: A few years later, in 1585, a long siege ended with Alessandro Farnese, the Duke of Parma, taking the city for Spain. Protestants were forced to leave. Many of the skilled people and their money moved north, to Amsterdam.
Anna: And that's the end of the golden age.
Ben: It's the beginning of the end. Then in 1648 the river was closed. By 1800, fewer than 40,000 people lived here.
Anna: So the grand square we're standing in was built by a city at the top of its power.
Ben: And has outlived it. Now. Let's lighten things up a little. Turn to the fountain in the middle.
Anna: Okay. That's dramatic. A man on top, throwing something.
Ben: That's Brabo. The fountain was made by the sculptor Jef Lambeaux in 1887. And Lambeaux lived in a house right on this square.
Anna: So the artist could look out the window at his own fountain.
Ben: I'd have done the same. Now look at the figures.
Anna: A man at the top. And a giant at the bottom, lying on the rocks.
Ben: Without his head and without his hand. And Brabo, up high, is just about to throw that hand into the river.
Anna: Oh, so it's the moment before the throw.
Ben: The moment of the throw. Look at the arm.
Anna: Okay, so that's my second hand. My tally says two. Even if one's on a statue.
Ben: I'll allow it. Statues count.
Anna: And the women?
Ben: Three nude women, around the base. They're holding symbols of Antwerp, a boat, and a fort, which is Het Steen, where we just were.
Anna: So it ties up the whole story. Boat, fort, giant, hero.
Ben: It's an advertisement for the town, in bronze.
Anna: Anything else to spot?

Ben: Look up at the guild house roofs. The golden figures. Look at the town hall's front, the flags, and the central tower of the building. And notice how much of it is a pedestrian zone. You can wander the whole square.
Anna: And terraces. I can see cafés.

Ben: Plenty of them. A coffee here is a fair price for the view. There's also a famous old brown café on the square, Den Engel, at number 3, a historic place with a smoke-darkened ceiling and a mix of locals and visitors. If you want to sit for ten minutes, that's the sort of place.
Anna: Is that the champagne spot?
Ben: No. Save that one. We'll point you at one near the end.
Anna: Good. I'm saving myself.
Ben: Pause here as long as you like. Walk around the fountain. Take your photo.
Anna: Where next?
Ben: Look over the rooftops. You'll see a very tall tower. That's the cathedral. Keep it in front of you, and take the short streets toward it. You'll be at the church in about three minutes.
Anna: Just follow the tower.
Ben: Just follow the tower.

chapters.title: Stop 3: The Cathedral of Our Lady
chapters.label: Stop 3: The Cathedral of Our Lady
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. That is a very big tower.
Ben: The north tower is 123 meters tall. It's the tallest in the city.
Anna: And it looks a bit lopsided. There's another one next to it.
Ben: There is. The southern tower is shorter, and it has a wooden lantern on top.
Anna: A wooden lantern. On a stone cathedral.
Ben: It was meant to be temporary. In 1533, a fire destroyed the wooden roof. Money meant for a big expansion went to repairs instead. In 1536, they put up a wooden lantern as a stopgap.
Anna: And?
Ben: It's still there.
Anna: Nearly 500 years. That's one very successful stopgap.
Ben: It's a very Belgian solution. Temporary, and permanent.
Anna: How old is the church?
Ben: The story goes back to 1124, when a Romanesque church was founded. The Gothic church began in 1352, with the choir. The big north tower was started in 1420 and finished in 1518.
Anna: So almost 100 years on the tower alone.
Ben: And in 1521, Emperor Charles V backed a project called the Nieuw Werck, the New Work, which was meant to make the church about three times larger.
Anna: Three times? It's already huge.
Ben: And then the fire came, and the money went elsewhere. Today the church has six naves and it's 53.6 meters wide. The part that was never finished is now a garden.
Anna: I love that. A cathedral extension that became a garden.
Ben: Now, if you're going in, here is what to look for. There are four paintings by Rubens inside.
Anna: Four in one church. That's a good start.

Ben: Over the high altar, The Assumption of Mary. To the left of the altar, The Raising of the Cross. To the right, The Descent from the Cross. And in a chapel on the right, The Resurrection of Christ.
Anna: Do they still hang where they were meant to?
Ben: Three of the four hang in their original settings, which is rare.
Anna: And the Resurrection?
Ben: That one was commissioned as a memorial for the son-in-law of a printer called Plantin. We'll meet his house in a few stops. Remember the name Moretus.
Anna: Moretus. Printer. Got it.
Ben: Rubens himself is buried in a different church, Saint James's, not here.
Anna: So don't go looking for his tomb in the cathedral.
Ben: Correct.
Anna: And practical bits?
Ben: Check the opening hours and whether there's a ticket. Churches can close for services or events. And if it's raining, this is your first dry stop of the day.
Ben: These paintings were made for people to pray in front of, so give them a few quiet minutes.
Anna: Of course.
Ben: Pause here. Go in, if you can. Take your time.
Anna: And outside, afterward?
Ben: Step out into the small square by the church front. That's the Handschoenmarkt, the Glove Market. That's where we'll start the next stop.

chapters.title: Stop 4: The Handschoenmarkt and the old lanes to the Vrijdagmarkt
chapters.label: Stop 4: The Handschoenmarkt and the old lanes to the Vrijdagmarkt
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Glove Market. I'm guessing there were gloves.
Ben: That's what the name says. The Handschoenmarkt, the market for gloves, right at the foot of the church.
Anna: And this is a really tiny square.
Ben: Small and sheltered, right under the cathedral. Look up, and you'll see the tower from very close.
Anna: Why is it called the glove market? Because the church hung gloves outside?
Ben: I can't tell you. We only know the name. We'd rather not make up a story.
Anna: Good rule.
Ben: Now. This stop is mostly a walk. From here to the Vrijdagmarkt, the Friday Market, it's a few minutes through the old lanes.
Anna: Which way do we go?

Ben: With the cathedral behind you, head south and a little west. The lanes here are narrow and cobbled, and they bend. If you lose your way, look for signs to the Plantin-Moretus Museum. Or keep your map open.
Anna: And what are we looking at as we go?
Ben: The small things. Old gables. Little shop windows. Doorways with carved details. This is a part of town that was rebuilt over and over, so you'll see different centuries in one street.
Anna: Which is why my tally still says two.
Ben: I'll give you a hint. Look at the wall plaques and the corner statues. Some of them carry the hand.
Anna: Really?
Ben: I can't promise. But the symbol is all over the city.
Anna: And what's the Friday Market? Is it a market on Fridays?
Ben: It was a market square, and the name comes from that. The Vrijdagmarkt is still an open square with old buildings around it, and the Plantin-Moretus Museum stands on it.
Anna: Does anything still happen on Fridays?

Ben: I can't confirm the current market days, so check locally. But the square is a good place to pause, and there's a bar on it, Marigold, at number 18, listed by a local magazine among the city's cocktail bars.
Anna: Cocktails at lunchtime. I'm tempted.
Ben: Hold on. We said we'd point you to the champagne one near the end.
Anna: Right. I'm being good.
Ben: Now, a little thread to carry through the lanes. Remember Christophe Plantin?
Anna: The printer. Moretus's father-in-law.
Ben: Right. He wasn't from Antwerp. He moved here from France around 1550, and started in the lace trade and in printing.
Anna: Lace. Of all things.
Ben: And in 1576, the same year as the Spanish Fury, the family moved into the building we're walking to. It was called De Gulden Passer, the Golden Compass.
Anna: The same year as the sack.
Ben: The same year. It's a reminder that life carried on, even in the bad years.
Anna: Alright. Walk with me. Which way again?
Ben: South and a little west, down the lanes, toward the Friday Market.
Anna: And while we walk, give me something to think about.
Ben: Think about how many hands it took to print a book in the 1500s. Every letter was set by hand, one at a time.
Anna: There it is. Another hand.
Ben: You're counting that one?
Anna: Tally says three. Don't argue.
Ben: I won't. Pause the tour here, and press play again when you reach the open square with the museum.

chapters.title: Stop 5: The Plantin-Moretus Museum
chapters.label: Stop 5: The Plantin-Moretus Museum
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Arrived. It looks like a normal house.
Ben: From the outside, it does. But this is one of the most important buildings in the history of printing. It's a World Heritage Site, listed in 2005.
Anna: A house?
Ben: A house, a workshop and a printing business, all together. The family lived above and printed below, for about four centuries.
Anna: Four hundred years in one building.
Ben: Plantin moved in in 1576. After he died, his son-in-law Jan Moretus took over the business, and the Moretus family kept it going, generation after generation.
Anna: Until when?
Ben: In 1876, Edward Moretus sold the company to the city of Antwerp. And a year later, in 1877, the public could visit the living rooms and presses.
Anna: So it has been a museum for nearly 150 years.
Ben: Over 140, yes. Now, here is the headline. The museum holds the two oldest surviving printing presses in the world.
Anna: The oldest in the world. In Antwerp.
Ben: In a house on a market square. Not in a grand hall.
Anna: What else is in there?
Ben: A Gutenberg Bible, the 36-line one. And the rooms where the family lived and worked.
Anna: So it's a time capsule.
Ben: A very good one. And there's a courtyard garden, so even if you're short on time, it's a calm place to stand for a minute.
Anna: Why was a printer so important to Antwerp?
Ben: Because in the 16th century, Antwerp was a place where ideas and goods and money moved fast. Printing is the same business. You make something, you send it far.
Anna: A bit like the port.
Ben: A paper port. Books left Antwerp the way pepper and cloth did.
Anna: And what's the link to Rubens?
Ben: This is the thread we promised. The Resurrection of Christ in the cathedral was painted as a memorial for Jan Moretus. So the painter and the printer worked in the same circle of the same city.
Anna: Good. The printing house, the painter, the church. All connected.
Ben: One city, one small world.
Anna: Practical?
Ben: This is an indoor stop, so it's your rain plan. Check the opening hours and ticket details before you go. It's a place where you could spend an hour or more if you read the labels.
Anna: And I should stay under an hour, I guess, because of the schedule.
Ben: If you're short on time, go for the presses, the printing room, and the courtyard.
Anna: Wait. A thought. The first printers made their letters by hand. They cut them in metal, they set them by hand, they pulled the press by hand.
Ben: And you're counting it.
Anna: Tally says four. Including that one.
Ben: I'm not sure that's what the bet meant.
Anna: The bet said hands. I'm just being generous.
Ben: Pause here. Go in if you can.
Anna: And then, the last stop?

Ben: Walk east, toward the shopping street called the Meir. It's about 10 minutes on foot. The Rubens House is just off it, on a short street called the Wapper. If you lose the way, ask for the Rubenshuis. Everybody knows it.

chapters.title: Stop 6: The Rubens House
chapters.label: Stop 6: The Rubens House
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. We're at the last stop. Is that it?
Ben: That's the front of the Rubens House. In Dutch, the Rubenshuis. It's on the Wapper, which used to be called Vaartstraat.
Anna: And this was his house?
Ben: In 1610, Rubens bought the property. A year earlier, in 1609, he'd married Isabella Brant. And he rebuilt it in the style of an Italian palace.
Anna: A palace in Antwerp.
Ben: With a studio, a portico, a courtyard, and a Baroque garden.
Anna: So he wasn't just a painter. He was a developer.
Ben: A very successful painter, with a studio full of students and assistants. A lot of his famous works came out of here.
Anna: So it was a workshop.
Ben: A workshop, a home and a showroom in one. He lived here for most of his life, until he died in 1640.
Anna: What happened to it after?
Ben: His widow, Helena Fourment, leased the house to William Cavendish and his wife Margaret. After Margaret left in 1660, the house was sold.
Anna: And how did it end up a museum?
Ben: A legacy from an architect named Henri Blomme helped the city buy the house in 1937.
Anna: Good for him.
Ben: And after extensive restoration, it opened as a museum in 1946, with period furniture and works by Rubens and his contemporaries.
Anna: Can we go in?

Ben: This is where I have to be careful. At the time of writing, the main section, the artist's residence, is closed for renovation. So please check the official website before you plan on going inside.
Anna: And if it's closed?
Ben: Look at the outside, and think about the garden. The courtyard opens onto the Baroque garden Rubens planned himself. Behind it is the Rubenianum, a study center and archive for scholars.
Anna: Right. So even if the house is shut, we've got the story.
Ben: And the four paintings in the cathedral. If you went inside earlier, you've already seen Rubens at work.
Anna: What else should we know about him?

Ben: He led the Antwerp school of painting in the 17th century. Another painter, Anthony van Dyck, belongs to the same school. And Rubens is buried in Saint James's church. If you have time left, ask for directions and check the hours.
Anna: And the city around his house. What did it look like in his day?
Ben: Poorer than in the golden age. The river was closed after he died, in 1648. But the art, the printing, and the sense of itself as a great city stayed.
Anna: So Rubens was at the end of the story.
Ben: Rather the middle of the story. The city came back, later, in a different way.
Anna: Okay. I think we need to do the tally.
Ben: Go on.
Anna: The hand in the river. The hand on the fountain. The printers' hands. The painter's hands. That's four. I won.
Ben: You said more than one giant hand. You got one in the legend, one on the fountain. Technically, yes.
Anna: I'll take it.
Ben: Pause here. Look at the house. Walk through the doorway, if you can.
Anna: And then?
Ben: Then one more thing, a drink. You said you'd been good.
Anna: I've been very good.
Ben: There's a champagne bar called the Laurent-Perrier Champagne Bar, at Meir 78, inside the old Stadsfeestzaal shopping building. It's a few minutes' walk from here, on the same shopping street.
Anna: Champagne. At last.

Ben: Check its opening hours first. It was listed as open until 6:30 in the evening on the day we looked, but hours change. And I can't promise it serves cocktails. If you want a cocktail with a view, there's a small bar called Jones and Co, on Pelgrimstraat, with a terrace that looks toward the cathedral. Again, check hours.
Anna: A toast to Rubens.
Ben: A toast to Rubens.

chapters.title: Wrap-up
chapters.label: Wrap-up
paragraphs: Anna: That's the walk. What have we done?

Ben: About two kilometers, in six stops. A riverside gateway from the 1200s. A square with a fountain and a rebuilt town hall. A cathedral with a lantern that was meant to be temporary. A lane to a printing house with the oldest presses in the world. And the home of a painter.
Anna: What's the theme?
Ben: That Antwerp is a city made by a river. It got rich when the river opened, it suffered when the river closed, and it came back when the river did.
Anna: And the hand?
Ben: The hand is the joke it tells about itself.
Anna: Final tally.
Ben: Four, according to you.
Anna: Four, according to me. Which means I won, and you owe me a drink.
Ben: I'm paying for champagne?
Anna: You said it, not me.

Ben: Back to the ship now. From the Rubens House, it's an easy walk back toward the river. Head west along the shopping street, then down to the water. Give yourself 20 minutes or more, and keep a map open.
Anna: And if you still have energy?
Ben: If you want the whole story of the city before tonight, play Antwerp in 15 Minutes. It covers the history in short.
Anna: Thank you for walking with us.
Ben: Safe travels, and enjoy your drink.

episodes.title: "Dark Antwerp: Legends and Ghost Stories"
episodes.blurb: A one-day briefing on Antwerp's spookiest side. A giant with a taste for hands, a shapeshifter by the river, and the real dark chapters, with legend and history kept apart.
episodes.notes: An overview for a one-day visit to Antwerp, about twelve minutes, for people who want the spooky side. It keeps two things apart on purpose: legends, which are stories people tell, and documented history, which is what the sources support. The legends are labelled as legends. Where the sources were thin, the script says less rather than guessing. For the general briefing, play "Antwerp in 15 Minutes".

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.label: Welcome
paragraphs: Anna: Evening. You're nearly in Antwerp. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. You have one day, and tonight we have about twelve minutes.
Anna: And tonight's theme is the spooky stuff. Ghosts. Giants. Dark history.
Ben: With one rule. We keep legend and history in separate boxes.
Anna: Boring.
Ben: Useful. When you stand in front of a statue tomorrow, you'll know which kind of story you're hearing.
Anna: Fine. I'll say it out loud. A legend is a story. History is the paperwork.
Ben: Close enough.
Anna: Five chapters. A giant, a shapeshifter, a stone fortress, a riot, and a massacre.
Ben: The first three are legends. The last two are real.
Anna: Cheerful. Let's go.

chapters.title: The giant and the hand
chapters.label: Chapter 1: The giant and the hand
paragraphs: Anna: Start me with the big one. Literally.
Ben: Okay. This is a legend, not history. Long ago, a giant called Druon Antigoon lived by the river Scheldt.
Anna: Of course he did.
Ben: He guarded a crossing and charged a toll. Anyone who couldn't pay lost a hand. He cut it off and threw it into the river.
Anna: That's a very specific business model.
Ben: Then a young Roman soldier called Silvius Brabo arrives. He beats the giant, cuts off the giant's own hand, and throws it into the river.
Anna: Poetic justice. With a knife.
Ben: And the story says that's how the city got its name. The Dutch name is Antwerpen. The tale reads it as "hand werpen," which means hand throwing.
Anna: Oh, that's good. So the whole city is named after a thrown hand.
Ben: Not quite. That's the folk explanation. The sources I checked say some specialists dispute it. Another idea connects the name to a word for a jetty or landing place by the water.
Anna: A jetty. Much less fun.
Ben: Much less fun.
Anna: So where do I see the hand?

Ben: The main square, the Grote Markt, in front of the town hall. There's a fountain by the sculptor Jef Lambeaux, put up in 1887. Brabo stands on top, about to throw. At the bottom, the hand is already in the air.
Anna: And I'm not allowed to pretend it's real.
Ben: You can pretend. Just remember it's a legend.
Anna: Noted. Bet number one. Somebody tonight mentions another hand.
Ben: We'll get there. Next, a tall one.

chapters.title: The shapeshifter at the castle
chapters.label: Chapter 2: The shapeshifter at the castle
paragraphs: Anna: Tall? Another giant?
Ben: A different one. Lange Wapper. Another legend, from Antwerp's folklore.
Anna: Give me the short version.
Ben: He's a shapeshifter. In the version I found, he starts as a baby, raised by an Antwerp family, and grows into a giant who can change size and shape.
Anna: Is he nice?
Ben: Mixed. He helps people at first. Later he's a trickster. He frightens drunks at night, and plays tricks on children.
Anna: So, a night-time prankster.
Ben: And a nuisance. One detail people like: he disliked the Virgin Mary. So the story goes that residents put little statues of her on their houses to keep him away.
Anna: Wait. That's why there are Madonnas on the corners of the buildings?
Ben: Not quite. Antwerp does have many street-corner Madonnas, but I can't tell you from my sources that Wapper is the reason. That's the story. Treat it as a story.
Anna: Fair. And how does it end?
Ben: Two endings. He leaves the city for good. Or he drowns in the Scheldt.
Anna: Two endings is cheating.
Ben: It's folklore. It does that.
Anna: Where do I find him?
Ben: By the river, in front of Het Steen, the old fortress. There's a bronze statue of him by the sculptor Albert Poels, from 1963. You can't miss it. He's a giant.
Anna: I'll keep my eyes up.
Ben: And Het Steen is next, because it has its own dark side.

chapters.title: The stone fortress
chapters.label: Chapter 3: The stone fortress
paragraphs: Anna: Het Steen. Is that the castle?
Ben: What survives is the gateway to a bigger castle. It was built between 1200 and 1225. The rest was torn down in the 1800s.
Anna: And the dark part?
Ben: Now we're back in history. It was used as a prison. From 1303 to 1827.
Anna: That's more than five hundred years.
Ben: Five hundred and twenty-four, if you count it. I don't have good sources on who was held there or how they were treated, so I'm not going to make that up.
Anna: Good. No invented dungeon.

Ben: There's also an odd carved relief over the archway. It's a figure called Semini. The story is that women once prayed to him for children, and later church people disapproved. Citizens were even called children of Semini.
Anna: Is that real?
Ben: The tradition is old. The details, including where the figure came from, are murky. Call it a local tradition and leave it there.
Anna: So three layers at one gate. A real prison, a tangled tradition, and a giant out front.
Ben: Right. Take a photo, and then walk up to the cathedral.
Anna: Teaser?
Ben: In the cathedral, there's a night in 1566 when the church looked like hell. That's from a witness.

chapters.title: The night the saints fell
chapters.label: Chapter 4: The night the saints fell
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Real history now. No jokes?
Ben: No jokes. Not for this one, and not for the next.
Anna: Understood.

Ben: In the summer of 1566, a wave of attacks on Catholic churches swept the Low Countries. It's called the Beeldenstorm, which means the storm of images. People smashed statues, altars and church fittings.
Anna: Why?
Ben: It was part of the religious conflict of the Reformation. Some Protestants considered religious images idolatry.
Anna: And it reached Antwerp.

Ben: On 20 August 1566. The Cathedral of Our Lady was badly damaged inside. An English merchant, Richard Clough, was there. He wrote that the church looked like a hell, with above 10,000 torches burning.
Anna: That's a line you don't forget.
Ben: It's one reason this night is remembered. Statues fell. Organs were wrecked. Books were burned.
Anna: And the building today? It looks perfect.

Ben: It survived, and was repaired, and it survived more. In 1794, French revolutionary troops plundered it and did serious damage. Around 1798 the French authorities even planned to demolish it. It was spared.
Anna: And the cathedral itself has one more odd feature.
Ben: The towers. Two were planned, equal in height. Only the north tower was finished, rising 123 meters. A fire in 1533 delayed the second, and it was never completed.
Anna: So it's lopsided on purpose?
Ben: On purpose is too strong. It's lopsided because of fire, money and time.
Anna: And the well?

Ben: Next to the cathedral on the Handschoenmarkt there's an ornate iron well cover, from the 1500s. It is traditionally attributed to Quinten Matsys, the artist. Only traditionally. I couldn't confirm it from a firm source.
Anna: Tradition again.
Ben: It's that kind of city.

chapters.title: The Spanish Fury
chapters.label: Chapter 5: The Spanish Fury
paragraphs: Anna: And the other real one.
Ben: This is the darkest chapter of the day, and we'll tell it plainly.
Anna: Go on.
Ben: In 1576, Spain was fighting in the Low Countries and its soldiers had not been paid. Troops mutinied. In November, mutinous Spanish troops came to Antwerp.
Anna: And then?
Ben: They attacked the city. It's known as the Spanish Fury. They killed people and burned buildings. The town hall was damaged by fire.
Anna: How many died?
Ben: Estimates differ widely. Some accounts say about 6,000 people. Others go much higher, up to 17,000 men, women and children. Around 800 to 1,000 buildings were burned, depending on the source.
Anna: That's a huge range.
Ben: It is. Nobody counted carefully in the middle of a massacre. The honest answer is that we don't know the exact number. We do know it was a catastrophe.
Anna: And what came after?
Ben: It shocked the region. Within days a treaty called the Pacification of Ghent was signed, calling for the expulsion of Spanish troops.
Anna: So it changed the politics.
Ben: Yes. And it still shapes how people remember the city.
Anna: Where do I feel it tomorrow?
Ben: On the Grote Markt, in front of the town hall. It's the same square as the fountain with the thrown hand. A legend on one side, a real tragedy on the other.
Anna: Hm. That's a strange square.
Ben: It is.

chapters.title: Wrap-up
chapters.label: Wrap-up
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. Let's put it in boxes.
Ben: Legends. Brabo and the giant's hand. Lange Wapper. The tales around Semini. The idea that a thrown hand named the city.
Anna: And history.
Ben: The prison at Het Steen, from 1303 to 1827. The Beeldenstorm on 20 August 1566. The French plundering in 1794. And the Spanish Fury, in November 1576.
Anna: And my bet. Somebody mentioned a hand. Twice.
Ben: Technically it was the same hand.
Anna: I'll take it.
Ben: Have a good day tomorrow. Look up at the towers, and read the plaques.
Anna: And be kind to the giants.

sources.title: The Legend of Brabo and Antigoon, Belgique Insolite
The Metsys Well at Antwerp, Dulwich Picture Gallery

episodes.title: Brussels in 15 Minutes
episodes.blurb: A quick briefing for your day in Brussels. What the city is, what to see, and the stories that make it make sense.
episodes.notes: An overview for the morning of a Brussels day, about fifteen minutes. It is written to be heard, with no tables. It leans on the same checked facts as the longer Brussels episode. For the full story, play "The Story of Brussels".

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.label: Welcome
paragraphs: Anna: Morning. You're in Brussels. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. You've got a day, and we've got fifteen minutes.
Anna: Think of it as the briefing before the mission.
Ben: Three things to know about the city. Five things worth seeing. Three stories for your pocket. And one plan for when it rains.
Anna: It will rain.
Ben: It's Brussels. It might rain while we're talking.
Anna: Okay. Start me off. What is this place?

chapters.title: The big picture
chapters.label: The big picture
paragraphs: Ben: Two things at once. A small, very old Belgian city that grew up on a muddy river. And the main home of the European Union.
Anna: And those two don't look much alike.
Ben: Not at all. In one walk, you go from a medieval guild square to a glass office tower full of EU officials.
Anna: Let's do the mud first.
Ben: The river is called the Senne. And the name of the city comes from an old word meaning a home in the marsh.
Anna: Charming.
Ben: Honest, at least. People settled along that river, merchants on the road between Flanders and Cologne stopped here, and a market town grew.
Anna: How old are we talking?

Ben: The date people usually give is around the year nine seventy-nine. A Frankish nobleman called Charles moved the relics of a saint named Gudula to a chapel on an island in the river. Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.
Anna: Is that exactly true?
Ben: Historians say the story is probably tidier than the reality.
Anna: But the party was already booked.
Ben: The date stuck. Then came centuries of other people's empires. Burgundy, Spain, Austria, France, the Netherlands.
Anna: Brussels has had a lot of landlords.
Ben: And in 1830, a revolution. Belgium becomes its own country, with Brussels as the capital.
Anna: And the second thing? The EU.

Ben: After the Second World War, Belgium was one of the six countries that founded what became the European Union. Brussels ended up with the European Commission and the Council, and the Parliament does much of its work here too.
Anna: Which is why there are so many flags.
Ben: And so many languages. Which is the third thing.
Anna: Go on.

Ben: Brussels is officially bilingual, French and Dutch. Every street sign has both. In daily life, most people speak French, but you'll hear Dutch, English, and dozens of other languages. Nearly four in ten residents hold a foreign passport.
Anna: So don't be surprised if someone switches language mid-sentence.
Ben: Don't be surprised. And don't feel bad about starting in English.
Anna: I'll start in English and smile a lot.
Ben: A solid strategy.

chapters.title: Five things worth seeing
chapters.label: Five things worth seeing
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. If I only had a day. What are the five?

Ben: One. The Grand Place. A paved square, about sixty-eight meters by a hundred and ten, surrounded by guild houses with gilded decoration, and a Gothic town hall with a tower about ninety-six meters high.
Anna: The heart of the city.
Ben: And here's the surprise. Most of it isn't medieval.
Anna: What?
Ben: In August of 1695, a French army under Marshal Villeroi shelled the city for two days, and most of the square was destroyed. Only the stone shell of the town hall and a few fragments survived.
Anna: But it looks perfect.
Ben: The guilds and owners rebuilt it in about four years. So when you look at those golden facades, you're looking at a very fast, very proud recovery. UNESCO listed it in 1998.
Anna: Four years. My kitchen has taken longer.
Ben: Your kitchen didn't have the guilds competing.
Anna: Fair. Number two.
Ben: The Manneken Pis. A small bronze boy, about fifty-five centimeters tall, relieving himself into a fountain basin on a street corner, a few minutes from the Grand Place.
Anna: And I bet you a coffee that you'll say "that's it?" out loud.
Ben: Everyone does. People are always disappointed by how small he is.
Anna: I win.
Ben: You haven't even been there yet. But he has a wardrobe of about a thousand costumes, which have their own museum nearby.
Anna: A thousand outfits. For a statue.
Ben: And there are two or three competing legends about why he exists. My favorite is the baby duke of Leuven, who supposedly relieved himself on enemy troops from a basket in a tree.
Anna: A tiny duke, in a tree, in a basket.
Ben: Winning a battle.
Anna: Number three.

Ben: The Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert. A glass-roofed shopping arcade, opened in June of 1847, designed by an architect named Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar. It's about two hundred and thirteen meters long and has three sections. The King's, the Queen's, and the Princes' galleries.
Anna: And it's still a shopping arcade?
Ben: With chocolate shops, a theater, a cinema, bookshops, and the Taverne du Passage. It's also where the Lumière brothers' films were shown in public in Brussels, in 1896.
Anna: Number four.
Ben: The Boulevard Anspach and the Bourse. Underneath that wide pedestrian boulevard, the Senne is still flowing, in a tunnel.
Anna: They buried a river.

Ben: Between 1867 and 1871. The river was polluted and flooded, so the city covered it over and built grand boulevards on top, modeled on Paris. The Bourse, the old stock exchange, went up between 1868 and 1873. And since 2015, the boulevards around it have been mostly car-free.
Anna: A river under a pedestrian street. Brussels does like to hide things.
Ben: And five. The Atomium.
Anna: The giant atom.
Ben: A giant steel model of an iron crystal, built for the 1958 World's Fair. You can ride up inside it for a view over the city. It's out on the northern edge, so it's a metro ride away.
Anna: That's a half-day trip.
Ben: It is. So pick one or two of these and enjoy them, rather than rushing through all five.
Anna: Rushing through Brussels. Never works.
Ben: Never.

chapters.title: Three stories to carry in your pocket
chapters.label: Three stories to carry in your pocket
paragraphs: Anna: Facts are great, but I want stories. Three I can tell over a coffee.
Ben: The coffee you won.
Anna: The coffee I won.
Ben: Story one. A night raid.
Anna: Ooh.

Ben: In 1356, the Count of Flanders invades Brussels and takes it. A citizen called Everard t'Serclaes, from one of the great families, leads a night raid with a small band of men. They slip into the city and drive the Flemish garrison out.
Anna: A local hero.
Ben: A very local one. There's a monument to him in the Rue Charles Buls, just off the Grand Place. And the tradition is that you touch the bronze for luck.
Anna: I'll be touching it.
Ben: Everyone does. It's very shiny.
Anna: Story two?
Ben: A night at the opera.
Anna: Two nights, two stories. I like the pattern.

Ben: On the twenty-fifth of August, 1830, there's a performance at the Théâtre de la Monnaie of a popular French opera called The Mute Girl of Portici. It's about a revolt against Spanish rule in seventeenth-century Naples, and it has a stirring duet about love of country.
Anna: And the audience took it personally.

Ben: They poured out into the street, and the unrest turned into a revolution. Within weeks, the southern provinces of the Netherlands had broken away, and Belgium was an independent country with Brussels as its capital.
Anna: From a duet to a country.
Ben: In a few weeks.
Anna: I can't get my neighbors to agree on a bin schedule.

Ben: Story three is smaller. Saint Gudula, the patron saint of the city. The legend says she walked to church before dawn, carrying a lantern. The devil kept blowing it out, and each time, an angel lit it again.
Anna: So the patron saint of a capital is a woman, a lantern, and a very persistent angel.
Ben: Persistent is the word. It tells you something about the city's character.
Anna: Stubbornness, again.
Ben: It comes up a lot.

chapters.title: Beyond the old center
chapters.label: Beyond the old center
paragraphs: Anna: And if I have more than a day? Or I'm sick of cobblestones?
Ben: Then go and look at three other Brussels. The first is Art Nouveau.
Anna: Curves and flowers.

Ben: In the eighteen-nineties, a young architect named Victor Horta built a townhouse for a professor called Emile Tassel. Iron columns shaped like plant stems, stairs that curl like vines, and light pouring down from above. In 1893 and 1894. It's widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.
Anna: And there's a museum.
Ben: The Horta Museum, in Saint-Gilles, in the house where he lived and worked. Several of his houses are now UNESCO World Heritage. If you want just one museum, I'd pick that.
Anna: What's the second Brussels?
Ben: Comics.
Anna: Tintin!

Ben: A young Brussels cartoonist named Georges Remi, who signed his work Hergé, published the first adventure of a young reporter with a quiff of red hair, in a children's supplement, in January of 1929.
Anna: That quiff is iconic.
Ben: And Belgium's comic strip tradition has made Brussels a world capital of the form. You'll find big comic murals on the sides of buildings around the center, if you keep your eyes up.
Anna: Eyes up. Got it. And the third?
Ben: The European quarter. Take the metro to Schuman station and walk out. You'll face the Berlaymont, the star-shaped headquarters of the European Commission.
Anna: It's not exactly cute.
Ben: It's not charming in the way the Grand Place is. But it tells you what the city is for now.
Anna: A slightly different kind of landmark.
Ben: A different kind, and every bit as much part of the story.

chapters.title: A few things to know
chapters.label: A few things to know
paragraphs: Anna: Practical stuff. What's the vibe?
Ben: A city of cafés and small museums, and the weather is changeable. Carry a light jacket. The center is quite walkable, with cobbled streets and hills, so wear good shoes.
Anna: And the food everybody talks about?

Ben: Belgian beer culture was recognized by UNESCO in 2016. Chocolate, waffles, and fries are everywhere. And the praline is traditionally credited to a Brussels chocolatier named Neuhaus, who has a shop in the Galeries.
Anna: Tourist traps?
Ben: The streets right around the Grand Place can be crowded and pricey. Walk two or three streets away and you'll usually find something better.
Anna: And if it rains?
Ben: Then go indoors, and Brussels is good at that. The Galeries are covered. There are museums. And a lot of cafés that exist just to give you somewhere to wait the weather out.
Anna: So what's the one thing to take away from all this?
Ben: That Brussels gets knocked down and rebuilt, and keeps its sense of humor. A small boy on a fountain, in a different costume every week, tells you most of it.
Anna: Right. Go have a good day.
Ben: And if you want the whole story, the long episode will be waiting for you tonight.
Anna: And if it rains?
Ben: Then you've got the Galeries, and a very good waffle.

episodes.title: Walking Brussels' Lower Town
episodes.blurb: A stop-by-stop walk from the Manneken Pis through the Grand Place and the Galeries to the buried river and the island where Brussels began. Allow about two hours with pauses.
hints: About a 10-minute walk from Brussels-Central station. The statue is on the corner of Rue de l'Étuve and Rue du Chêne.
Walk up Rue de l'Étuve and into Rue Charles Buls, where the t'Serclaes monument is. The square opens up at the end of the street.
Leave the square by the Rue des Bouchers, the restaurant street. The galleries open off it, a few minutes on.
Come out of the galleries and walk toward the wide Boulevard Anspach. The Bourse is the big building with the lions.
Carry on from the Bourse through the small streets. The square has an old brick market hall in the middle and bars all around.
episodes.notes: A walking tour of the old center, about a kilometer and a half in all, in five stops. Each chapter is one stop, so you can pause between them, and the audio carries on as you walk. Streets and landmarks are described loosely, so keep a map open as well. The stops are close together, and you can do the whole route in a morning. Opening hours, queues and any construction change often, so check them on the day.

chapters.title: Welcome and how this works
chapters.label: Welcome and how this works
paragraphs: Anna: Hello, and welcome to a walk. I'm Anna.
Ben: And I'm Ben. This is a walking tour of the lower town of Brussels, the oldest part of the city, in five stops.
Anna: And the idea is that you're not sitting down.

Ben: You're out on the street, with headphones, or a speaker in your pocket. Each chapter is one stop. We tell you where you are, what you're looking at, and the story behind it. Then we point you toward the next one.
Anna: And if I want to stand there and stare?
Ben: Press pause. Stare as long as you like. The tour waits for you.
Anna: What do I need?

Ben: Comfortable shoes, because it's cobblestones. Something for the weather, because Brussels changes its mind. And a map on your phone, because we describe where things are, but we'd rather you not get lost.
Anna: And I'll make a bet with you, right now. Somebody on this walk will say "it's smaller than I thought."
Ben: Within five minutes. You'll win that one.
Anna: I love an easy bet.
Ben: One more thing. This walk is really about a river.
Anna: A river? In the middle of the city?
Ben: Used to be. We'll get there.
Anna: He says "we'll get there" a lot.
Ben: Because we do.
Anna: Okay, so where do we start?
Ben: With a small boy and a very large crowd. Our first stop is the Manneken Pis. From Brussels-Central station, it's roughly a ten-minute walk, and it's a few minutes from the Grand Place.
Anna: And the whole route?
Ben: About a kilometer and a half. Allow two hours with pauses. More if you stop for a coffee.
Anna: Which you should.
Ben: Which you absolutely should.
Anna: Right. Shoes on. Let's go.

chapters.title: Stop 1: The Manneken Pis
chapters.label: Stop 1: The Manneken Pis
paragraphs: Anna: Okay. If there's a crowd, lots of phones, and something very small in the middle, you've found it.
Ben: He stands at the corner of the Rue de l'Étuve and the Rue du Chêne. A bronze figure of a little boy, about fifty-five centimeters tall, relieving himself into a stone basin.
Anna: Fifty-five centimeters. That's less than two feet.
Ben: And somebody around you just said "it's smaller than I thought."
Anna: I win.
Ben: You win. Now take a look at the setting. He's on a corner, on a wall, behind railings. This isn't a monument in a grand square. It's a street fountain that became a symbol.
Anna: How old is he?

Ben: The first mention of a fountain figure of a boy goes back to the thirteen-hundreds. The bronze statue was made in 1619 by the Brabant sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder. And here's a detail that surprises people. The one in front of you is a replica.
Anna: A replica?
Ben: The original is kept in the Brussels City Museum, on the Grand Place. Which is where we're going next.
Anna: Why a replica?
Ben: Because he keeps getting stolen.
Anna: A statue that keeps getting kidnapped.
Ben: Greatest hits. A legend says English soldiers took him in the seventeen-forties, and he was found in a town called Geraardsbergen. The French grenadiers allegedly tried another theft in 1747.
Anna: Allegedly.
Ben: In 1817, a freed convict named Antoine Licas stole him and broke him into eleven pieces. He was repaired and recast. In 1963, students from Antwerp hijacked him for five days.
Anna: Five days. What did they do with him?
Ben: I'd rather not know. And in the nineteen-sixties he disappeared again, and divers recovered him from a canal in 1966.
Anna: A canal.
Ben: Which is why there's a replica on the street, and the original is somewhere safe and dry.
Anna: Okay, but why is a boy on a fountain doing that?

Ben: There are several legends, and nobody can prove any of them. The best known says that Duke Godfrey the Third of Leuven, a two-year-old, was hung in a basket from an oak tree to encourage his troops during a battle in 1142. And he urinated on the enemy.
Anna: A baby duke. Doing military service.
Ben: Another legend says a boy put out a burning fuse that was meant to blow up the city walls. Another says he put out a fire. Take your pick.
Anna: Which one do I tell my friends?
Ben: The baby duke. It's the funniest.
Anna: And then there's the wardrobe.

Ben: This is the part I love. He has about a thousand costumes. The thousandth was presented in 2018. They're changed regularly, for special occasions, for visiting delegations, for anniversaries. A little sign near the statue often tells you who he's dressed as today.
Anna: A boy with a thousand outfits.
Ben: More than I own.
Anna: More than I own, and I like clothes.
Ben: And they're all on display. Since 2017, there's a museum for them called GardeRobe MannekenPis, at number nineteen on the Rue du Chêne, just around the corner.
Anna: GardeRobe. I see what they did there.
Ben: Garde-robe is French for wardrobe. Belgians like their puns.
Anna: What does this tiny statue tell me about Brussels?

Ben: That the city has always had a sense of humor about itself. A capital of Europe whose most famous symbol is a boy doing something naughty. And everyone is fine with it. They dress him up and give him a birthday.
Anna: So pause here. Stay a minute. Watch the crowd.
Ben: They all do exactly the same thing. They look, they laugh, they take a photo, and they leave.
Anna: Okay. When you're ready, we head toward the Grand Place. It's only a few minutes away.
Ben: Follow your map, or the crowds. On the way, you'll pass the Rue Charles Buls. In it, there's a bronze monument to a man named Everard t'Serclaes.
Anna: The one we should touch.
Ben: Yes. I'll tell you why when we get there.

chapters.title: Stop 2: The Grand Place
chapters.label: Stop 2: The Grand Place
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, you've turned a corner and the street opens up. And now you're in it.

Ben: Stand somewhere near the middle and turn all the way around. This is the Grand Place. In Dutch, the Grote Markt. A paved square, about sixty-eight meters by a hundred and ten, and every side is covered in decoration.
Anna: I'm going to use the word "gold" a lot.
Ben: Please do. Gilded statues, gilded cornices, gilded ornaments on top of every building.
Anna: Why is it all so ornate?

Ben: Because of who built it. This was the marketplace of a rich trading city, and the houses around the square belonged to the guilds, the associations of craftsmen and merchants. The bakers, the brewers, the butchers, the tanners, the boatmen, the painters. They competed with each other to have the grandest house on the square.
Anna: A very medieval show-off contest.
Ben: Except it isn't medieval. Not most of it. Here's the thing that surprises people.
Anna: Go on.

Ben: In August of 1695, during the Nine Years' War, a French army of about seventy thousand men under Marshal Villeroi bombarded Brussels. The aim was to draw enemy forces away from a siege at Namur. They shelled the city for about two days. Most of the Grand Place was destroyed. Only the stone shell of the town hall and a few fragments of other buildings survived.
Anna: Wow. So what we're looking at...

Ben: Was rebuilt in about four years. The guilds put their houses back, under rules from the city council and the governor, in an exuberant baroque style. So these golden facades are about three hundred and thirty years old, not seven hundred.
Anna: And they look better than ever.
Ben: That's what Brussels does. It gets knocked down, and then it builds something even better, to spite whoever did it.
Anna: Let's talk about the town hall.
Ben: That's the Gothic building with the tall tower. The one old building left. It was built in stages, between 1401 and 1455, and the tower is about ninety-six meters tall.
Anna: And there's someone on top.

Ben: A golden Saint Michael, about two point seven meters tall, slaying a dragon. He's the patron saint of the city. What you see is a copy from the nineteen-nineties. The original is inside the City Museum.
Anna: Another copy.
Ben: Brussels loves a backup.
Anna: Now look at the tower carefully, I'm told.

Ben: Compare the two halves of the facade. The tower isn't in the center. It's off to one side, and the building isn't symmetrical. There's a famous story that the architect found out and threw himself off the tower in despair.
Anna: Oh no.
Ben: It's almost certainly a legend.
Anna: Thank goodness.

Ben: Let's turn around. Opposite the town hall is the building with the neo-Gothic facade, with lots of pointed arches. It's called the King's House, or the Maison du Roi. In Dutch, the Broodhuis, the Bread House.
Anna: Bread house? Not very royal.

Ben: It was named for the bread market that once stood on the site. It was rebuilt in neo-Gothic style between 1874 and 1896, and since 1887 it's housed the Brussels City Museum, where that little boy is kept in his original form.
Anna: So the real Manneken Pis lives in the Bread House.
Ben: In a museum with a very good view of his own fan club.
Anna: And the guild houses.

Ben: Have names. Each has a name, and often a symbol. Number one is Le Roy d'Espagne, the King of Spain, which was the house of the bakers. Number five is La Louve, the she-wolf, the archers' house. Number eight, L'Étoile, the star, is a small and rather modest one. And number nine is Le Cygne, the swan, which belonged to the butchers.
Anna: The butchers got the swan. Fair enough.

Ben: Now, a thing you might want to plan your trip around. The Ommegang. A costumed pageant held on the square in late June or early July, which re-enacts the Joyous Entry of Charles the Fifth and his son Philip in 1549. UNESCO recognized it in 2019.
Anna: And the flower carpet!

Ben: Every two years in August, around Assumption Day, for three or four days, they cover part of the square with a carpet of nearly a million flowers. Begonias or dahlias. About twenty-four meters by seventy-seven.
Anna: A carpet made of a million flowers.
Ben: Someone has to plant them.
Anna: And the Grand Place has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
Ben: It has. And we promised the t'Serclaes monument.
Anna: Yes! The lucky bronze.

Ben: A short walk away. Remember, in 1356, the Count of Flanders invades and takes Brussels. A citizen named Everard t'Serclaes leads a night raid with a small band of men, slips into the city, and drives the Flemish garrison out.
Anna: A local hero.
Ben: The monument, on the Rue Charles Buls, shows him lying dead. Touch the bronze, the tradition says, and you'll have luck. You can see where millions of hands have polished it.
Anna: Millions of hands. Hope they washed.
Ben: I'd use hand sanitizer afterward. And then take the luck.
Anna: Pause here as long as you like. Look up, look around, go into a café on the edge of the square if you want.
Ben: When you're ready, we're heading north to a very different kind of place. A covered arcade.
Anna: Walk with the Grand Place behind you, toward the little streets with all the restaurants.
Ben: That's the Rue des Bouchers, the butchers' street. Now it's lined with restaurants with menus on the pavement. A word of advice. It's touristy. Look, and keep walking.

chapters.title: Stop 3: The Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert
chapters.label: Stop 3: The Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert
paragraphs: Anna: Okay, you've found it. You've stepped from a cobbled street into a glass tunnel.
Ben: Look up. That's a glass roof, held up by a delicate cast-iron frame, arching over a long shopping street. This is the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert.
Anna: It's gorgeous.

Ben: About two hundred and thirteen meters long. It opened on the twentieth of June 1847, inaugurated by King Leopold the First and his two sons. The architect was Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar, who designed and built it between 1846 and 1847.
Anna: And it's often described as...

Ben: One of the first truly public covered shopping arcades in Europe. Paris had its famous covered passages, but this one was built as a public street, open to everyone. Its motto, in Latin, is Omnibus omnia.
Anna: Everything for everybody.
Ben: That's the idea. A very nineteenth-century dream. A clean, dry, well-lit street where anyone could stroll, shop, and be seen.
Anna: Dry. In Brussels. That's a luxury.
Ben: The rain isn't going to get you in here.
Anna: And it's three galleries.

Ben: Three sections. The Galerie du Roi, the King's Gallery. The Galerie de la Reine, the Queen's Gallery, which is the longer one. And a smaller side passage called the Galerie des Princes, the Princes' Gallery.
Anna: Who's in them now?

Ben: Chocolate shops, leather goods, a bookshop, a theater, and a cinema. The Royal Theater of the Galleries opened in the King's Gallery on the seventh of June 1847, just before the arcade itself. And a cinema, the Cinéma des Galeries, opened in the Queen's Gallery in 1939.
Anna: And chocolate. I'm counting on chocolate.

Ben: You'll find it. One of the best known names here is Neuhaus. Tradition credits a Neuhaus, a Brussels chocolatier, with inventing the praline, the filled chocolate, in the early twentieth century. The shop is right here in the gallery.
Anna: I'm sorry, the praline was invented here?
Ben: According to tradition. As with the Manneken Pis, I'd call it a good story with some truth in it. But the shop is real, and I think it's worth a visit.
Anna: I'll check the truth. Carefully. With samples.
Ben: A scientific method.
Anna: And the cafés?
Ben: The Taverne du Passage, in the Queen's Gallery, was called the Café des Arts until 1892, and it was a meeting place for writers and artists. It's still a restaurant, with a classic Belgian menu.
Anna: And film history.
Ben: On the first of March, 1896, the Lumière brothers' films were shown to the public in Brussels in these galleries, just a few months after their first public screening in Paris.
Anna: So this is where Brussels first saw the movies.
Ben: In a glass-roofed passage. I like that.
Anna: And the galleries are protected.
Ben: Listed as a historic monument in 1986, and they're on UNESCO's tentative list for World Heritage.
Anna: Give me one thing to look for.

Ben: Look up at the roof, then look down at the pavement. The architect designed the whole thing as one piece, from the cast-iron frame to the shop fronts. It's a rare place where a nineteenth-century dream is still working.
Anna: And I'm told there's a little girl around here.

Ben: Yes. Back on the Rue des Bouchers there's a narrow alley called the Impasse de la Fidélité, the dead end of Fidelity. At the end of it is a tiny bronze figure of a squatting girl, about fifty centimeters tall.
Anna: The Manneken Pis's sister!
Ben: Jeanneke Pis, installed in 1987. Behind a little grille, so she's often hard to see.
Anna: A bit of equality.
Ben: In a way.
Anna: Pause here. Have a coffee, buy some chocolate.
Ben: When you're ready, we're heading toward a very grand building and the story of a vanished river.
Anna: Leave the galleries and walk west, toward the wide boulevard.
Ben: You'll see the building long before you reach it. It looks like a small palace.

chapters.title: Stop 4: The Bourse and the buried river
chapters.label: Stop 4: The Bourse and the buried river
paragraphs: Anna: You've reached a big building with columns, lions, and lots of statues, on a square with a wide pedestrian street running past.
Ben: This is the Place de la Bourse, and the building is the Bourse, the old stock exchange. Built between 1868 and 1873, on the site of a former butter market. The architect was Léon-Pierre Suys.
Anna: It looks like a palace.

Ben: An eclectic style, a mix of neo-Renaissance and Second Empire. You can see the lions at the entrance, by the Jacquet brothers, and figures along the facade symbolizing Art, Agriculture, Industry, and Science. And inside, the caryatids were carved with the help of a young Auguste Rodin, who worked in Brussels at the time.
Anna: Rodin. Here.
Ben: A young sculptor, working on a commission. Not the Thinker yet.
Anna: Still working on his résumé.
Ben: But you asked about the river.
Anna: I did. I've been very patient.
Ben: You have. Turn and look down the long pedestrian street. That's Boulevard Anspach. And what I want you to imagine is that it's a river.
Anna: A river?

Ben: The Senne. The river that made Brussels. The name of the city means a home in the marsh, remember. For centuries, the Senne flowed through the middle of the city, and by the eighteen-hundreds it was a disaster. An open sewer, choked with refuse. It flooded regularly. And it carried cholera.
Anna: So they buried it.

Ben: The reforming mayor Jules Anspach decided to cover it. In 1865, he chose a design by Léon Suys, the same architect who built the Bourse, to vault the river and build grand boulevards on top. Between 1867 and 1871, the river was covered.
Anna: And the boulevard is named after him.
Ben: Yes. Wide, straight, and lined with imposing buildings, modeled on the boulevards of Paris, which Baron Haussmann was building at the same time. The Bourse was the centerpiece.
Anna: So we're standing on top of a river.
Ben: We are. It's still down there, in a tunnel, flowing under your feet. Most visitors never know.
Anna: We got there.
Ben: We did. Told you.
Anna: Was it a triumph?

Ben: A mixed one. The city got clean water, better health, and a grand new center. But hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods along the river were torn down, and whole communities were pushed out.
Anna: That's a real cost.
Ben: And it's one reason so many people here care about preserving what's left.
Anna: What's the boulevard like now?

Ben: On the twenty-ninth of June 2015, the central boulevards were closed to traffic between the Place de la Bourse and the Place de Brouckère, creating a big pedestrian zone. It's been a place to walk, sit, and have a drink ever since. There was a lot of argument at first. Now most people seem to like it.
Anna: And inside the Bourse?

Ben: The upper floors have housed a museum called Belgian Beer World since September 2023, and the main hall was opened to the public for the first time then. If you like beer, it's worth knowing about. Belgian beer culture was recognized by UNESCO in 2016.
Anna: And I'd like to say something about the steps.

Ben: Yes. After the attacks of the twenty-second of March, 2016, the steps and the square in front of the Bourse became a place where people came to grieve. They wrote messages in chalk on the pavement and left candles and flowers. It became a kind of living memorial, and people still come here to remember.
Anna: It's good to stand quietly for a moment.
Ben: It is. This is a place where the city gathers, in good times and in bad.
Anna: Pause here. Look at the building, look down the boulevard, and think about the river underneath.
Ben: When you're ready, we have one more stop. A few minutes' walk to the west, and it's where the city began.
Anna: Head toward the Place Saint-Géry.
Ben: It's a short way from the Bourse, in the direction of the old center, among narrow streets and small bars.

chapters.title: Stop 5: Place Saint-Géry, where Brussels began
chapters.label: Stop 5: Place Saint-Géry, where Brussels began
paragraphs: Anna: This one isn't grand. It's a pleasant square, with cafés, and an old brick hall in the middle.
Ben: And it might be the most important stop on the tour. Because this is where Brussels started. Or at least, where the story says it did.
Anna: The island.

Ben: Remember the river. Before it was buried, the Senne divided into channels here, forming little islands in the marsh. And the tradition is that around the year five eighty, a holy man named Gaugericus, known in French as Saint Géry, the bishop of Cambrai, built a small chapel on an island in the river.
Anna: Right here?
Ben: Close to where you're standing. The square is named after him. Historians are cautious, because the sources are later and uncertain, but it's a good candidate for the seed of the city.
Anna: And the name of the city?
Ben: The earliest forms look something like Bruocsella. Most scholars read it as a home in the marsh, or a dwelling by the swamp.
Anna: A very honest name.
Ben: It's what a farmer would call a wet bit of ground. And you're standing on that wet ground. It's just been paved over and covered up.
Anna: So that's the story.

Ben: That's the story. Around the year nine seventy-nine, Charles, the exiled Carolingian duke, is said to have built a fortification on an island in the river, and moved the relics of Saint Gudula to the chapel. That's the date usually given for the founding of Brussels.
Anna: With a caution.

Ben: With a caution. Modern historians say the story rests on sources written long afterward, and that the city probably grew gradually, over several generations. But it's the story that stuck, and Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.
Anna: Happy birthday, to a date that might be wrong.
Ben: They had cake anyway.
Anna: And there's an old hall.

Ben: The brick building in the middle of the square is the old market hall, the Halles Saint-Géry, close to where the island once was. In the nineteenth century, it was a covered market. Now it's an exhibition and event space, with a café, and the square around it is full of bars.
Anna: A good place to sit.

Ben: A very good place. And a nice way to end. The city started in a swamp, on an island, with a chapel and a market. It grew into a capital, it rebuilt itself after a bombardment, it buried its river, and now people sit outside in the sun and drink beer on the spot where it began.
Anna: A full circle.
Ben: It is. Take a moment. Order something. Look at the old hall, and then look at the paving stones and imagine the water.

chapters.title: Wrap-up
chapters.label: Wrap-up
paragraphs: Anna: That's the tour. What have you walked?

Ben: About a kilometer and a half, in five stops. A fountain boy with a thousand outfits. A square rebuilt in four years. A glass-roofed arcade from 1847. A boulevard over a buried river. And a little square on the island where it all began.
Anna: What's the theme?
Ben: That Brussels is a city of things that got broken and rebuilt, buried and rediscovered. And that it doesn't take itself too seriously.
Anna: If you still have energy, what's next?

Ben: If you want more of the story, the long episode, The Story of Brussels, goes into the dukes, the guilds, the Habsburgs, the revolution and the Belle Époque. And for a short version of everything, play Brussels in Fifteen Minutes.
Anna: And if you want to do this again?
Ben: Ask for another walk. There's a whole upper town on the hill, with the royal palace, the museums, and a different story.
Anna: Thank you for walking with us.
Ben: Safe travels, and enjoy your coffee.

episodes.title: The Story of Luxembourg (one narrator)
episodes.blurb: From a Roman-era fortress and a medieval dynasty to the Gibraltar of the North, a steel nation and a modern financial centre.
episodes.notes:
This script runs roughly an hour and a quarter to an hour and a half at a normal speaking pace, split into eight chapters of roughly nine to thirteen minutes each. Each chapter stands on its own, so you can stop and start anywhere, and you can paste one chapter at a time into an audio app, since many apps cap how much text they accept at once.

Everything from the Welcome section onward is written to be heard, not read: no tables, no footnotes, and years and numbers placed where they sound natural.

Text-to-speech voices sometimes stumble on Luxembourgish and French names, such as Alzette, Vauban, Ermesinde and Echternach. If one sounds wrong, swap in a phonetic spelling before you generate the audio, for example Al-zet for Alzette.

On accuracy: the 1839 partition, the 1942 conscription figures, the 2025 abdication and the current government were checked against sources listed at the end. Older dates and details come from standard histories. They are reliable, but check anything you plan to repeat in print.

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.label: Welcome
paragraphs: Welcome. Over the next hour or so, we are going to tell the story of one of the strangest and most successful countries in Europe: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

It is small. You could drive across it in about an hour. Its population is smaller than that of many a single city. And yet it has been fought over by emperors and kings for more than a thousand years. It has been a fortress, a province, a battlefield, a steel empire, a banking center, and one of the founding members of the European Union. It is the last grand duchy in the world.

How did a tiny territory on the edge of the great powers end up with all of that history? The answer is a story of rock, iron, borders, and stubbornness. It is a story of a people who, in the words of their own national motto, want to remain what they are.
We will move in order, from the Stone Age to the present day. Settle in, and let's begin with a swap of land beside a river.

chapters.title: Before Luxembourg
chapters.label: Chapter 1: Before Luxembourg
paragraphs: Let's begin with a puzzle: when was Luxembourg born? Some people say 1815, when the Grand Duchy was created at the Congress of Vienna. Others say 1839, when its modern borders were drawn in London. Others point to 1867, when the great powers guaranteed its independence. But the story we are telling really starts in the year nine sixty-three, with an exchange of land beside a river. And before that exchange, there are thousands of years we should not skip.

Our first character has no name. Archaeologists call him Loschbour man, after the rock shelter near the village of Heffingen where his skeleton was found in 1935. He lived about eight thousand years ago, when this land was covered in dense forest and people survived by hunting, fishing and gathering. When scientists sequenced his DNA, decades after his discovery, the result made headlines. It suggested that this early European had dark skin and blue eyes, a combination that overturned a lot of assumptions about what the first Europeans looked like.

After Loschbour man came farmers, who arrived from the southeast and cleared fields along the river valleys. Then came the age of metal, first bronze and later iron. By the last centuries before Christ, the land of Luxembourg belonged to a Celtic people called the Treveri.

The Treveri left a remarkable monument: a fortified hilltop town called the Titelberg, in the far southwest of today's country, close to the French border. It sat on a high plateau, with ramparts around it, and it was a center for metalworking and trade. Imagine a town of craftsmen and warriors, with a view across the countryside, and one of the richest cavalry traditions in Gaul.

Then Rome arrived. The first written reference to this territory comes from Julius Caesar himself, in his account of the Gallic Wars. Around the middle of the first century before Christ, Caesar fought the Treveri, and after years of rebellion and repression, the region was swallowed into the Roman Empire.

The Romans founded a city on the Moselle river, just across what is now the German border: Augusta Treverorum, today's Trier. Within a few generations it became one of the great cities of the western empire. At one point it was the home of emperors, and its Roman gates and baths still stand. The land that would become Luxembourg was Trier's backyard. It was farmland and forest, crossed by Roman roads and dotted with country estates.

One of those roads ran from the city of Reims, in what is now France, to Trier. Along it, near today's village of Dalheim, grew a small Roman town with a theater. At Echternach and at Diekirch, wealthy landowners built grand villas. At Diekirch, a Roman mosaic from one of those houses survives, laid out in colored stone. Life was settled, Latin-speaking and, for a few centuries, secure.

Then the empire cracked. In the third and fourth centuries, raiders pushed across the Rhine, and Roman power along the frontier began to wear away. By the end of the fifth century, the region had passed to the Franks, a Germanic people whose king, Clovis, was building a new kingdom out of the ruins of Roman Gaul. Luxembourg's land became part of the Frankish heartland, in the eastern half that was later called Austrasia.

Christianity came with the Franks, and with a handful of remarkable missionaries. The most important for our story is a monk named Willibrord, born in Northumbria, in England, and trained in Ireland. He crossed the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians, and in the year six ninety-eight he founded a monastery at Echternach, on land given to him by a noblewoman from the Trier area. Willibrord died in 739 and was buried there.
